messages.content: I want to characterize when staggered policy effects remain partially identifiable under network spillovers and bounded unmeasured adoption confounding. The characterization should establish assumptions that yield bounds narrower than outcome-range bounds, distinguish direct effects from spillover effects, and achieve at least 95% confidence-set coverage uniformly over the stated confounding and interference class. How should I understand the pieces of that goal?

There are two related questions. The identification question asks what the policy effects can be narrowed down to when adoption occurs at different times, one unit’s policy status may affect others through the network, and adoption may depend on unmeasured factors within a stated bound. The uncertainty question asks for a confidence set with at least 95% coverage uniformly across the entire confounding and interference class you state.

“Partially identifiable” does not require a single effect value. It calls for defensible bounds. To meet the substantive part of the goal, those bounds must be narrower than bounds obtained from the outcome range alone, and the characterization must say which assumptions produce that narrowing. It also needs to keep an effect of a unit’s own policy status distinct from an effect transmitted through other units’ policy statuses.
Why does staggered adoption matter here, rather than just labeling units treated or untreated?

Because policy status can change over time, a unit’s own adoption timing matters to the contrast being described. Its network exposure may change over time as other units adopt, too. A comparison that only labels units “treated” and “untreated” can conceal whether it concerns own adoption, exposure to others’ adoption, or both.

The goal does not specify a particular adoption schedule or effect pattern. It calls for a characterization that makes the timing relevant to the effects and comparisons, without assuming that a single treated-versus-untreated label settles them.
What is the distinction between a direct effect and a spillover effect in this setting?

Conceptually, a direct effect compares a unit’s outcomes under different values of its own policy status while holding the relevant exposure to others’ policy statuses fixed. A spillover effect compares outcomes under different exposure to others’ policy statuses while holding the unit’s own status fixed. With staggered adoption, those comparisons also need to be understood at a specified time or under a specified timing contrast.

That distinction is about what is varied in the hypothetical comparison. It does not assert that either effect is identifiable on its own. If own status and network exposure cannot be separated under the stated assumptions and available comparisons, the characterization should say so rather than label their combined contrast a direct effect.
Does allowing network spillovers mean that any unit could be affected by every other unit?

Not necessarily. “Network spillovers” says that outcomes may depend on others’ policy statuses through the network; it does not, by itself, specify which relationships matter or how exposure is summarized. The stated interference class would need to make that scope clear enough for an effect and its bounds to have a definite meaning.

The breadth of that class matters. If it permits many unrestricted ways for others’ adoption to affect an outcome, there may be little information left for narrowing a spillover-effect bound. A narrower class can yield more informative bounds, but only if its restrictions are explicitly stated and justified as assumptions, not presented as observed facts.
And what does “bounded unmeasured adoption confounding” permit?

It permits adoption to be associated with unmeasured factors relevant to outcomes, subject to a specified limit. Thus it does not ask the analysis to treat adoption timing as if it were automatically unconfounded. The bound on that association is part of the class over which the conclusions must hold.

The word “bounded” is essential: without saying what is bounded and in what sense, it is not yet a usable restriction. Equally, acknowledging a bound does not make confounding disappear. It means the analysis must accommodate every adoption process allowed by that bound.
If confounding and spillovers are both allowed, why expect anything narrower than outcome-range bounds?

You should not expect narrower bounds from those allowances alone. Outcome-range bounds use only the possible range of outcomes, so they are a deliberately weak benchmark. To improve on them, the assumptions and the observed comparisons must jointly rule out at least some effect values that the outcome range would otherwise permit.

That is what the characterization needs to establish, rather than presume. It should identify conditions under which the restrictions on adoption confounding and network interference, together with any other clearly stated assumptions needed for the comparisons, actually shrink the bounds. It should also allow for the possibility that a proposed set of assumptions does not deliver a strict improvement.
When you say “narrower,” do you mean that at least one endpoint moves inward, or that every effect bound must be strictly smaller?

That comparison needs to be specified for each target effect. For an individual direct or spillover effect, a bound narrower than its outcome-range bound excludes some values the outcome range alone would allow; an inward movement of an endpoint can do that. A claim about both types of effect, however, cannot be established by showing improvement for only one and leaving the other at its outcome-range bound.

It is worth stating whether the desired comparison is strict narrowing for each effect, narrowing under particular conditions, or some other clearly defined comparison. The goal is to establish assumptions yielding narrower-than-outcome-range bounds while distinguishing direct and spillover effects; it does not itself supply an already-proved width result.
Could a narrow bound on a combined policy effect count as distinguishing direct and spillover effects?

Not on its own. A combined effect may change both a unit’s own status and its exposure to others’ statuses. Even if that combined effect is bounded tightly, the bound does not automatically reveal how much is direct and how much is spillover.

To distinguish them, the targets and the assumptions have to support separate statements about changing own status and changing network exposure. If only a combined contrast is supported, calling it combined is more accurate than assigning its components unsupported bounds.
Could the direct effect be partially identified while the spillover effect remains at the outcome-range bound?

Conceptually, yes. The information and assumptions relevant to one contrast need not restrict the other contrast to the same degree. The reverse is conceptually possible as well. That is one reason to state the targets and their bounds separately.

Such a result would be informative about partial identification, but it would not by itself establish narrower-than-outcome-range bounds for both effects. The characterization should be precise about which effect has improved bounds, and under what conditions, rather than treating any improvement as a blanket result.
How should the assumptions be presented so the result is not just a claim that informative bounds exist?

They should connect the target contrasts to the restrictions that exclude effect values. One can ask, for each proposed assumption: what ambiguity does it remove or limit, and why is that enough to tighten the bound for this particular effect? For example, a restriction concerning adoption confounding addresses a different source of ambiguity from a restriction concerning which network exposures may affect outcomes. Neither should silently stand in for the other.

The assumptions should also make clear the scope of any conclusion. If narrowing holds only when the relevant own-status and network-exposure contrasts can be separated, that condition belongs in the characterization. If a condition fails, the statement should not imply the same narrower bound remains available.
Would it be fair to say that partial identification is a population statement, while 95% coverage is a sampling statement?

That is a useful distinction. An identified bound describes values compatible with the stated assumptions and the population information at issue. A confidence set addresses uncertainty in learning about an effect or an identified bound from data. A narrow population bound does not, by itself, guarantee a confidence set with the required coverage; conversely, a procedure can have high coverage yet be too broad to be informative.

The goal asks for both: substantive narrowing relative to outcome-range bounds and at least 95% confidence-set coverage. They should be checked as separate properties.
What exactly does “uniformly over the stated confounding and interference class” add to the 95% requirement?

It means the coverage guarantee cannot rely on the actual confounding or spillover pattern happening to be an especially favorable member of the class. For every configuration allowed by the stated bounds on unmeasured adoption confounding and by the stated interference assumptions, the confidence set must meet the at-least-95% coverage requirement.

In shorthand, if the class is called C, the intended requirement is that the infimum of the coverage probabilities over C is at least 0.95 for the stated coverage target. A calculation that reaches 95% only for one selected member of C would not establish that uniform claim.
Does that mean the confidence set must contain every value in the partially identified range on at least 95% of samples?

That depends on what the coverage target is defined to be. Covering the true effect value with probability at least 95% and covering the entire identified set with probability at least 95% are different requirements; the latter is stronger. The goal specifies at least 95% confidence-set coverage uniformly over the class, but does not by itself settle that distinction.

A precise characterization should say which object the confidence set is required to cover, then state and assess the uniform guarantee for that object. It should not move between pointwise coverage of a true effect and coverage of a whole identified set without saying so.
If the confounding limit is stated, can coverage be assessed only at that limit?

Not unless it is established that checking the limit is sufficient for every other allowed case. A bound on confounding describes a class, not merely its boundary. The same caution applies to the permitted interference patterns: checking a convenient pattern is not the same as checking all patterns in the stated class.

Uniform coverage is a worst-case requirement over the class as defined. Any shortcut for assessing it would itself need justification; it cannot be assumed from the word “bounded.”
I also want to avoid implying that the 95% requirement somehow makes the identification bounds narrower.

Right. The coverage level governs the reliability of the confidence set under repeated sampling across the stated class. The narrowing claim concerns which effect values remain compatible with the identifying assumptions and information, relative to outcome-range bounds. Increasing coverage does not create identification, and tighter identifying restrictions do not automatically provide coverage.

Keeping those roles separate makes the goal coherent: characterize when informative partial identification is possible for direct and spillover effects, then require the accompanying confidence set to attain at least 95% coverage uniformly over the declared confounding and interference class.
So the central qualification is “when,” not an unconditional promise of tight bounds?

Yes. The characterization should say under which stated assumptions staggered policy effects remain partially identifiable despite network spillovers and bounded unmeasured adoption confounding. It should show when those assumptions yield bounds narrower than the outcome-range benchmark, with separate treatment of direct and spillover effects. Where the assumptions do not suffice, the appropriate conclusion is limited rather than an unsupported claim of narrowing. The at-least-95% uniform confidence-set requirement then applies to the coverage target and class that are actually stated.

For the proposed route, could we invert simultaneous exposure-specific sensitivity bands under overlap and Γ-bounded staggered adoption to obtain nontrivial direct and spillover bounds with uniform 95% coverage?

That is a coherent proposal, provided its qualifications remain explicit. The sensitivity bands would account for adoption confounding allowed by Γ within the relevant network-exposure comparisons. Making them simultaneous would address the fact that direct and spillover contrasts may draw on several exposure-specific quantities. Inverting the bands would then retain effect values compatible with those quantities and the stated assumptions, rather than treating any one band as a point estimate.

The key results would still need to be established: that the relevant overlap and Γ-bounded adoption assumptions yield bounds narrower than outcome-range bounds for the direct and spillover effects in question, and that the bands—and their inversion—support at least 95% coverage uniformly over the stated confounding and interference class. The proposal names a route to those results; it is not itself a proof of either one.
What makes a sensitivity band “exposure-specific” here?

It is tied to a specified network-exposure condition rather than pooling all possible exposure to others’ adoption into an undifferentiated comparison. That matters because an own-policy contrast at a given exposure is conceptually different from a contrast that changes exposure while holding own policy status fixed.

The proposal does not yet choose a particular network-exposure mapping or a list of exposure levels. Those would need to be stated to make the bands and the direct and spillover targets precise. “Exposure-specific” signals that the analysis must preserve the distinctions required for those targets.
Why simultaneous bands instead of a separate band for each exposure?

A direct or spillover bound can depend on more than one exposure-specific quantity. If each band has a coverage statement only in isolation, it does not follow that all the quantities used in an effect comparison fall within their bands at the same time with probability at least 95%.

A simultaneous statement addresses that joint event. If the true relevant quantities all lie in their bands together, and the inversion correctly retains every effect value compatible with those quantities and the allowed confounding and interference, then the coverage event can carry through to the inverted set. Both the simultaneity claim and that implication require justification; neither follows merely from calling the bands “simultaneous.”
Can you explain inversion without assuming a particular estimator?

Think of the bands as specifying which exposure-specific quantities remain plausible, subject to their sensitivity restrictions. For a proposed value of a direct or spillover effect, ask whether there is an allowed configuration of those quantities—and of any other features left unspecified within the stated class—that produces that value. Keep the proposed value if such a configuration exists; exclude it only if none exists.

That is inversion at a conceptual level. It does not prescribe how to calculate the bands or optimize over configurations. It does emphasize a safeguard: excluding an effect value requires incompatibility with the full allowed class, not just incompatibility with one convenient confounding or interference scenario.
What role is overlap supposed to play?

Overlap is meant to ensure that the own-status and network-exposure comparisons relevant to the target effects have support. Without relevant comparisons, a band may be driven almost entirely by the outcome range and the sensitivity restrictions, leaving little prospect of narrowing an effect bound.

Overlap must be specified for the contrasts actually used. A broad statement that adoption occurs at different times would not by itself establish support for every own-status and exposure comparison. Overlap also does not eliminate unmeasured adoption confounding; Γ is there to bound what that confounding may do.
Is Γ supposed to be a particular numerical value?

No numerical value is specified in the proposal. Γ labels the bound on unmeasured confounding in staggered adoption. To use it, one would need to define exactly what aspect of the adoption process Γ constrains and which adoption histories satisfy that constraint.

It is important not to infer a specific mathematical sensitivity model from the symbol alone. The bands and the uniform-coverage claim have to be evaluated for the Γ-bounded class as actually defined.
Would bounding adoption confounding automatically bound interference too?

No. They concern different sources of ambiguity. Γ-bounded staggered adoption constrains the permitted unmeasured confounding of adoption; an interference class constrains how other units’ policy statuses can matter for a unit’s outcome. Exposure-specific comparisons need the latter to have a clear interpretation, but Γ does not silently supply it.

For the proposed coverage claim, both pieces must be included in the class over which the guarantee is uniform. For the identification claim, one must likewise check that the joint assumptions, not just the adoption restriction, support the proposed direct and spillover bounds.
How does the inversion keep direct effects separate from spillover effects?

It should invert bands against separately defined contrasts. A direct-effect target varies a unit’s own policy status while fixing the relevant network exposure. A spillover-effect target varies that exposure while fixing own policy status. Staggered timing needs to be accounted for in whichever contrasts are specified.

The same collection of simultaneous bands may help constrain both targets, but each target should have its own resulting compatible set or bound. A narrow bound for a contrast that changes both own status and exposure cannot simply be relabeled as two separately bounded components.
The proposal calls the bounds nontrivial. Is overlap plus finite Γ enough to guarantee that?

Not without a further argument. Overlap and a stated Γ restriction are intended to make exposure-specific comparisons informative, but whether the inverted effect bounds are actually narrower than outcome-range bounds depends on the defined contrasts, the interference restrictions, and how informative the bands are. A simultaneous band could be valid yet too wide to exclude any outcome-range-compatible effect value.

So “nontrivial” is a result to demonstrate under explicit conditions, separately for direct and spillover effects. It should not be read as an automatic consequence of putting overlap and Γ in the proposal.
If the bands are wide, does their simultaneity at least solve the partial-identification problem?

Simultaneity can help protect the coverage claim for a set derived from multiple bands; it does not ensure informative identification. Wide bands may invert to bounds as broad as the outcome-range bounds. Conversely, narrow-looking bands are not sufficient if they omit allowed confounding or interference configurations and thus lack the required uniform coverage.

The proposal therefore has two tests: does inversion genuinely narrow the compatible direct and spillover effects under stated assumptions, and does the simultaneous construction retain at least 95% coverage throughout the stated class?
How would you state the uniform requirement without claiming a result we have not shown?

As a proposed property to prove: for every adoption-confounding and interference configuration allowed by the stated class, the probability that the inverted confidence set covers its specified target is at least 95%. Equivalently, the lowest coverage probability across that class must be at least 0.95.

The specified target matters. Coverage of a true effect value and simultaneous coverage of an entire identified set are distinct guarantees. Inversion can be designed with either target in mind, but the proposal should say which guarantee is claimed and show that the band event implies it. It should not use “uniform 95%” as a substitute for that argument.
Does inversion preserve coverage automatically once we have simultaneous bands?

It preserves the relevant coverage event if the bands jointly cover the quantities needed for the target and the inversion includes every effect value compatible with those quantities under the allowed class. Under those conditions, whenever the joint band event occurs, the appropriate target remains in the inverted set.

That reasoning is conditional, not automatic. If the bands omit a relevant exposure, if the inversion excludes an allowed nuisance configuration, or if the initial simultaneous guarantee is not uniform over the Γ-bounded adoption and interference class, the desired uniform 95% conclusion does not follow.
Is there a tension between requiring uniform coverage and wanting tight bounds?

There can be. Respecting every allowed confounding and interference configuration may require retaining effect values that an analysis tailored to a favorable configuration would discard. That can make the bounds or confidence sets wider. It is not a reason to weaken the meaning of “uniform”; it is a reason to state the class and the assumptions carefully, and then establish whether informative bounds are still possible within it.

A genuinely nontrivial result would show both that the direct and spillover bounds improve on the outcome-range benchmark under its stated conditions and that the accompanying confidence set has at least 95% coverage throughout the class. Neither property should be inferred from the other.
So the proposal is not to posit a particular spillover mechanism or a numerical Γ, but to see whether this band-inversion strategy can meet both requirements?

Exactly. The proposed strategy is to use overlap and Γ-bounded staggered adoption to support simultaneous, exposure-specific sensitivity bands, then invert those bands for direct and spillover effects. A complete characterization would specify the exposure and interference class, the precise Γ restriction, the effect contrasts, and the coverage target. It would then establish the conditions under which the inverted bounds are narrower than outcome-range bounds and the confidence-set coverage is uniformly at least 95%. Until those steps are demonstrated, the strategy remains a proposal rather than an established guarantee.
What degree-growth and exposure-cell overlap rates preserve uniform 95% coverage and nontrivial direct and spillover bounds at Γ=1.5?

There is no numerical rate to give from the information specified so far. Γ=1.5 fixes the proposed sensitivity level, but it does not define the network dependence, the exposure cells, or how their support changes as the number of units grows. Those details determine which degree-growth and overlap conditions would be sufficient.

The question has two separate parts. A coverage rate condition must make the simultaneous exposure-specific bands valid uniformly over the stated confounding and interference class, so their inversion retains at least 95% coverage. A nontriviality condition must make the resulting direct and spillover bounds narrower than their respective outcome-range bounds. Conditions sufficient for coverage need not be sufficient for nontrivial bounds.
When you say degree growth, which degree matters?

That has to be specified. Maximum degree, average degree, and the degree relevant to a particular unit can grow differently. Also, the number of potentially dependent observations may depend on more than immediate neighbors if the specified exposure or interference class reaches beyond them.

A rate stated only as “degree grows slowly” would therefore be incomplete. It needs to identify the graph quantity being controlled and explain why controlling that quantity is enough for the simultaneous bands used in the inversion.
Would bounding maximum degree relative to the number of units answer it?

It could be part of an answer, but not necessarily the whole answer. The required comparison depends on how exposure is defined, which cells enter the direct and spillover contrasts, and what dependence the interference class permits. A restriction on maximum degree does not, by itself, ensure that any particular exposure cell has enough support.

Nor can I infer a sufficient numerical relationship between maximum degree and the number of units from Γ=1.5. That relationship would have to come from a coverage argument for the proposed bands under the stated class.
What is an exposure-cell overlap rate, as opposed to just saying overlap holds?

A qualitative overlap statement says that the relevant own-status and network-exposure combinations are possible. A rate statement addresses how their support behaves as the analysis grows: for example, whether the least-supported cell needed for a contrast remains sufficiently represented rather than becoming vanishingly rare too quickly.

The rate should be formulated for the cells actually used. Direct-effect comparisons need support for differing own statuses at a fixed relevant exposure; spillover comparisons need support for differing exposures at a fixed own status. Staggered timing can make the relevant cells more specific still. Merely having some adoption and some network exposure somewhere does not establish overlap for each target contrast.
Could I specify a single minimum cell probability for all the relevant comparisons?

That is one possible way to express an overlap restriction, if the exposure cells and the population to which those probabilities refer are precisely defined. A minimum across the required cells would make clear that a rare cell cannot be hidden by well-supported ones.

But a minimum probability alone is not a complete coverage argument when observations may be dependent through the network. It also does not guarantee narrower bounds at Γ=1.5: the allowed confounding and interference configurations might still leave the effect contrasts compatible with the full outcome-range bounds.
So a cell can have a positive probability and still be too sparse for the 95% claim?

Yes. Positive probability at each stage is weaker than a rate condition ensuring that the cell provides enough information for the intended simultaneous coverage guarantee. If its probability shrinks as the network grows, the distinction matters especially. Network dependence can further limit what a nominal cell count tells you.

For uniform coverage, the issue is not whether a favorable network and adoption pattern produces ample observations. The bands must behave as claimed across every configuration admitted by the stated class, including its least favorable permitted overlap and dependence patterns.
Could the coverage rate be weaker than the rate needed for nontrivial bounds?

Potentially. A conservative band may maintain at least 95% coverage while being too wide to rule out any effect value allowed by the outcome range. Establishing nontrivial bounds demands more: after allowing Γ=1.5 adoption confounding and the stated interference patterns, the information in the relevant cells must still exclude some values for the direct and spillover targets.

There is no reason to assume that the threshold for this substantive narrowing coincides with the threshold for valid coverage. Each claim needs its own argument.
Does Γ=1.5 make the overlap threshold easy to calculate?

No. The value Γ=1.5 needs to be interpreted through a specified sensitivity model for staggered adoption. It says which confounding configurations are allowed only once that model is defined. An overlap threshold also depends on the exposure comparisons and the precision and joint validity of the bands.

So Γ=1.5 is an important fixed condition in the question, not a stand-alone formula for the degree or cell-support rates. I would not translate it into a particular overlap requirement without those definitions.
If I wrote that degree must grow more slowly than sample size, would that be precise enough?

No. “More slowly” could describe many different rates, and sample size may not capture the amount of independent information available under network interference. Even a precisely stated comparison of degree with the number of units would need a proof connecting it to joint band coverage for the specified exposure cells.

It would also need to be paired with an overlap condition. Sparse networks can still have rare exposure cells, and ample cell support does not by itself establish that the dependence allowed by the interference class is controlled.
Do direct and spillover bounds necessarily need the same overlap rate?

Not necessarily. The two targets require different comparisons. For a direct effect, the potentially limiting cells distinguish own policy status while fixing relevant network exposure. For a spillover effect, they distinguish network exposure while fixing own status. One set of cells may be much less supported than the other.

A single sufficient rate could be stated using the worst-supported cell across both targets, but that might be stronger than needed for either target individually. Separate conditions can make clearer which bound is nontrivial and which coverage claim is supported.
Does the staggered aspect change what counts as an exposure cell?

It can. Own adoption and exposure to others’ adoption can each vary over time. To define an effect contrast, one has to say which timing features are held fixed or varied, and the relevant cells must reflect that definition. Pooling across times without justification could mask a lack of support for the particular contrast of interest.

The question does not yet specify a time-indexed exposure mapping or which timing contrasts are targeted. Until it does, a degree-growth or minimum-overlap rate cannot be tied to a definite set of cells.
What if the number of exposure cells itself increases?

Then the simultaneous part of the coverage requirement becomes especially relevant. The bands must jointly cover all the exposure-specific quantities used in the inversion. If the set of relevant cells changes or grows, a coverage argument has to account for that change as well as for dependence and the least-supported cells.

This is another reason a rate for just one cell, or a separate 95% statement for each cell, would not settle uniform 95% coverage for the inverted direct and spillover sets.
Could finite-sample uniform coverage avoid the need for a degree-growth rate?

Possibly, if a finite-sample construction is proved to have the required simultaneous coverage for every allowed network, adoption process, and interference pattern. In that case, degree growth might not be needed to justify the coverage guarantee itself. It could still matter for whether the bands are informative enough to produce nontrivial bounds.

If the 95% claim instead rests on a large-sample approximation, degree-growth and overlap rates may be needed to justify that approximation uniformly. The question needs to say whether “uniform 95% coverage” is an exact finite-sample guarantee or an asymptotic one; those are distinct claims.
Would an asymptotic guarantee mean that coverage is at least 95% for every sample size?

No. An asymptotic uniform guarantee concerns behavior as the size grows, with the worst-case coverage over the stated class approaching at least 95% in the specified sense. It does not automatically imply at least 95% coverage at every finite size.

If the requirement is literally at least 95% for each permitted finite configuration, that calls for a finite-sample guarantee. The chosen wording of the claim should match the guarantee actually established.
Is it enough to check the most connected network and the least-overlapping cell?

Only if a valid argument shows that those cases are worst for the particular coverage and bound-width properties under study. The largest degree and smallest cell support may occur in different configurations, and the interaction of network dependence, adoption confounding at Γ=1.5, and exposure patterns may matter.

Uniformity means taking account of the whole stated class. A shortcut based on apparent extremes must be justified rather than assumed.
Suppose the rate conditions do give joint 95% bands. Is that sufficient to say both effect bounds are nontrivial?

No. Joint coverage addresses whether the exposure-specific quantities are contained in their bands with the required probability. After inversion, the compatible effect values could still span the respective outcome-range bounds.

To establish nontriviality, the argument would need to show a strict narrowing for the direct-effect target and, separately, for the spillover-effect target under the stated conditions at Γ=1.5. Validity of the bands is necessary to support the confidence claim, but their validity alone says nothing about strict improvement in bound width.
What if there is good support for own adoption but almost no variation in neighbors’ adoption at a fixed own status?

That illustrates why the two targets must be checked separately. Support for an own-status comparison might help constrain a direct effect at a given exposure. If the exposures needed for a spillover comparison are scarcely represented at fixed own status, the spillover bound might remain broad, even though the direct comparison is better supported.

That is a conceptual possibility, not a finding about a particular network or data set. The proposed rates would have to rule out the relevant lack of support if they are claimed to yield nontrivial bounds for both targets.
And could a very large degree make an exposure cell rare even if policy adoption itself has overlap?

It could, depending on how network exposure is defined and how adoption statuses are distributed within the allowed class. Overlap in an individual unit’s adoption status does not automatically yield overlap in combinations of own status, others’ statuses, and staggered timing. Degree growth can affect which exposure patterns are common without, by itself, determining their probabilities.

That is why the question calls for degree-growth and exposure-cell overlap rates together, rather than treating either one as a substitute for the other.
How should the answer handle the possibility that no common rate works across the full class?

It should state that limitation plainly if the class is too broad for a uniform result. If permitted networks have arbitrarily severe dependence or the required exposure cells can become arbitrarily scarce, a claimed common rate or nontrivial bound needs additional restrictions or a separate argument showing why those extremes do not defeat it.

That does not mean the Γ=1.5 question is unanswerable in principle. It means the interference class, adoption sensitivity restriction, effect targets, and meaning of coverage have to be defined before a defensible sufficient rate—or an explanation that none follows under those conditions—can be given.
Can we frame the question without pretending we already know the rate thresholds?

Yes: ask for conditions on network degree growth and minimum overlap in every exposure cell required by the staggered direct and spillover contrasts such that, at Γ=1.5, the inverted simultaneous sensitivity bands have uniformly at least 95% coverage over the stated confounding and interference class and yield bounds strictly narrower than the respective outcome-range bounds. Specify whether coverage is finite-sample or asymptotic.

That formulation keeps the numerical sensitivity level and both desired properties explicit. It leaves the actual rates to be derived from the defined model rather than supplying unsupported thresholds.

Here is a hypothesis for the rates question: with degree o(n^{1/8}) and exposure-cell probabilities ≥0.1, Γ=1.5 yields nontrivial direct and spillover bounds and uniform asymptotic ≥95% coverage. Is that a fair way to state it?

Yes, as a hypothesis—not yet as an established result. It proposes that degree growing strictly more slowly than n^{1/8}, together with exposure-cell probabilities of at least 0.1, is sufficient at Γ=1.5 for two conclusions: bounds narrower than the respective outcome-range bounds for both direct and spillover effects, and at least 95% coverage asymptotically, uniformly over the stated confounding and interference class.

To assess it, the degree measure, the required exposure cells, the Γ-bounded adoption model, and the coverage target must be defined. Those definitions matter to whether the proposed conditions actually imply either conclusion.
What does the little-o condition say precisely?

If d_n denotes the degree quantity intended by the hypothesis and n is the size indexing the sequence, d_n=o(n^{1/8}) means d_n/n^{1/8} tends to zero as n grows. It is a rate condition, not a fixed numerical cap on degree at any particular size.

The hypothesis does not yet say which degree quantity d_n represents. Specifying that is necessary before the condition can be tested or used in a coverage argument.
Should I take “degree” to mean maximum network degree?

You could formulate a version using maximum degree, but that choice is not contained in the hypothesis as stated. Maximum degree and other degree summaries impose different restrictions, so silently substituting one would change its meaning.

For now, it is more accurate to call o(n^{1/8}) the proposed rate for the degree measure to be specified. A proof would have to identify the measure it controls and show why that control suffices for the dependence allowed by the interference class.
Is the eighth-root rate known to be necessary here?

No necessity claim is stated. The hypothesis proposes o(n^{1/8}) as a condition under which the desired conclusions might hold. Even if it were proved sufficient under a defined model, that would not show that faster degree growth makes the conclusions impossible.

Likewise, the exponent 1/8 should not be treated as a derived threshold from the information currently available. Its role here is a specific, testable part of the hypothesis.
How should I read the ≥0.1 exposure-cell condition?

It says that the probability of each exposure cell required for the proposed comparisons is at least 0.1. For the claim to be precise, one must identify those cells and say what probability distribution the bound refers to. In particular, the cells relevant to a direct contrast may differ from those relevant to a spillover contrast, and staggered timing can be part of what defines a cell.

The number 0.1 is a proposed overlap floor, not an observed cell frequency or a result inferred from the degree condition. Both the cells and the scope of the floor must be stated before the hypothesis can be evaluated.
Could ≥0.1 refer only to the least-supported cell?

Yes, if it is defined as saying that the minimum probability among all cells needed for the direct and spillover comparisons is at least 0.1. That wording makes the intended floor apply to every required cell. If it instead applies to only one selected cell, it would not establish overlap for the others.

Care is needed about what counts as a distinct cell. The hypothesis should not appear to cover a timing- or exposure-specific contrast whose necessary cells were left out of the minimum.
Does a 0.1 floor mean every relevant cell has 10% of the observations in each realized network?

No. A probability of at least 0.1 is a statement about the specified distribution, not a guarantee that every realized sample contains a particular fraction in every cell. Realized cell counts can vary, and observations can be dependent under network interference.

That distinction is important for the coverage part of the hypothesis. A population overlap floor may support a band construction, but it does not alone prove that the bands attain uniform asymptotic ≥95% coverage.
Does Γ=1.5 determine how much the direct and spillover bounds shrink?

Not by itself. Γ=1.5 fixes the sensitivity level proposed for unmeasured confounding in staggered adoption, but the way that value restricts allowed adoption processes still needs a definition. How much either bound shrinks also depends on the effect contrast, the exposure-specific information, and the allowed interference patterns.

The hypothesis asserts that both bounds are nontrivial under its proposed conditions. That assertion needs to be shown separately for direct and spillover effects; it cannot be read off the value 1.5 alone.
Could “nontrivial” simply mean that each bound has finite endpoints?

That would be too weak for the comparison at issue. If outcomes have a stated range, effect bounds obtained from that range alone may already have finite endpoints. Here, nontrivial should mean that the direct-effect bound and the spillover-effect bound each exclude some values permitted by their respective outcome-range bounds.

The hypothesis should therefore be tested against the outcome-range benchmark for each target, not merely against whether an interval can be written down.
Is the claim about narrowing the underlying identified bounds or just producing narrower confidence sets?

As phrased, “nontrivial direct and spillover bounds” is best made explicit as a claim about the effect bounds under the assumptions, relative to outcome-range bounds. The uniform asymptotic ≥95% statement is a separate claim about confidence-set coverage.

It would be misleading to infer identification from the width of a particular realized confidence set, or to infer coverage from narrow identification bounds. The proposed band inversion has to support each property in its own right.
What does “uniform asymptotic ≥95% coverage” mean in the hypothesis?

It calls for the worst-case coverage over the stated confounding and interference class to have an asymptotic lower limit of at least 0.95. The guarantee is uniform in the sense that an allowed sequence of configurations cannot defeat it simply by changing the confounding or interference pattern as n grows.

That is not a claim of ≥95% coverage for every finite n. It also leaves one essential choice to specify: whether the confidence set must cover the true effect value or the entire identified set. The mathematical coverage statement should name that target.
Would proving 95% coverage for each fixed configuration establish uniform coverage?

Not necessarily. A separate asymptotic statement for every fixed configuration can leave the worst-case configuration varying with n. Uniform asymptotic coverage requires control over the whole stated class in the relevant asymptotic sense, not only pointwise coverage for each member considered one at a time.

The degree and overlap conditions in the hypothesis need to hold across the configurations over which that uniformity is claimed. Otherwise, a proof under a favorable subset would not establish the stated conclusion.
Is ≥95% the same as exactly 95%?

No. The hypothesis sets a lower coverage threshold: at least 95% asymptotically and uniformly. A procedure with a higher worst-case asymptotic coverage level would meet that part of the hypothesis as well. What matters is that the lower bound of 0.95 is established for the stated target and class, not that coverage equals 0.95 everywhere.
How does the proposed degree condition relate to simultaneous exposure-specific bands?

It is proposed as a way to control network dependence sufficiently for a uniform asymptotic argument about the simultaneous bands. But the rate alone does not prove that argument. Its relevance depends on which units’ outcomes or exposure-specific quantities may be dependent under the stated interference class and on which degree measure is controlled.

The bands also need to accommodate Γ=1.5 adoption confounding and cover all quantities required for the direct and spillover inversions together. Establishing a rate for degree without establishing that joint coverage would leave the 95% conclusion unproved.
If the bands are simultaneous and uniformly valid, do the proposed overlap and degree rates automatically give nontrivial bounds?

No. Valid simultaneous bands can be too wide to exclude any effect values beyond what the outcome range excludes. The exposure-cell floor of ≥0.1 and degree o(n^{1/8}) may help with support and dependence, but the hypothesis still needs an argument that inversion at Γ=1.5 strictly narrows each target’s bound.

One way to keep the reasoning clear is to separate a coverage claim about the bands and their inversion from an identification claim about what effect values remain compatible with the assumptions. Neither is automatic from the other.
Could I state a single conclusion for “direct/spillover” rather than proving them separately?

You can state the joint hypothesis concisely, but substantiating it requires attention to both contrasts. The direct effect varies own policy status at a fixed relevant network exposure; the spillover effect varies exposure while fixing own status. Their required cells and resulting bounds need not behave alike.

A result that only tightens a direct-effect bound, or only tightens a spillover-effect bound, would not establish the hypothesis as written. Similarly, the simultaneous coverage argument has to encompass the exposure-specific quantities used for both.
Does the ≥0.1 floor make the condition unusually strong?

It is a fixed positive floor rather than merely a requirement that cell probabilities be nonzero. That is a substantive distinction: a probability that remains at least 0.1 cannot drift toward zero as n grows for any cell to which the condition applies.

Whether this is stronger than necessary for the desired result is not established. The hypothesis proposes this particular overlap condition; a proof under it would not, by itself, identify the weakest possible overlap rate.
Could the rate and floor hold, but the result still fail because the interference class permits too much?

That remains possible until the class is specified and the implications are proved. Degree growth limits a stated graph quantity, and the cell floor limits a stated form of overlap. Neither alone says which other units’ adoptions can affect an outcome or how the relevant exposures enter the effect contrasts.

The hypothesis is thus conditional on a clearly stated interference class as well as a clearly stated Γ-bounded staggered-adoption class. The uniform coverage claim must range over those classes, and the nontriviality claim must follow from the restrictions they actually impose.
What would disconfirm the hypothesis, conceptually?

Under precise definitions, a permitted sequence satisfying degree o(n^{1/8}), the ≥0.1 floor for all required exposure cells, and Γ=1.5 would challenge the hypothesis if either target’s identified bound remained at its outcome-range bound, or if the proposed confidence procedure failed the uniform asymptotic ≥95% coverage criterion. Those are distinct possible failures.

This is a description of what would test the claim, not a claim that such a sequence exists. Until the model, targets, and procedure are defined, neither a proof nor a counterexample follows from the stated numbers alone.
Should the hypothesis say that the two rate conditions are sufficient rather than necessary?

Yes, if that is the intended claim. “Under degree o(n^{1/8}) and exposure-cell probabilities ≥0.1, Γ=1.5 yields…” presents them as proposed sufficient conditions. It does not assert that the conclusions fail when degree grows faster or when a required cell probability falls below 0.1.

Keeping that direction clear avoids turning a proposed route to nontrivial bounds and uniform asymptotic coverage into an unsupported threshold or impossibility claim.
Can you put it into one careful sentence I could keep as the working hypothesis?

A careful working hypothesis is: “For a specified degree measure, set of staggered-adoption exposure cells, Γ-bounded adoption-confounding model, and network-interference class, degree o(n^{1/8}) and probabilities ≥0.1 in every cell required for the target contrasts are sufficient, at Γ=1.5, for bounds strictly narrower than outcome-range bounds for both direct and spillover effects and for confidence-set coverage that is uniformly asymptotically at least 95% over the stated class.”

That preserves the proposed numerical conditions and conclusions while making clear that sufficiency remains to be established.

For the degree-growth and exposure-cell overlap question, I plan to derive direct and spillover sensitivity linear programs and dependency-graph simultaneous bands, prove uniform coverage, and then test the degree and overlap thresholds. Does that sequence make sense?

Yes, as a plan. The sensitivity linear programs would make the compatible direct and spillover effect values explicit under the stated restrictions. The dependency-graph simultaneous bands would address uncertainty across the exposure-specific quantities used by those programs. A uniform-coverage proof would then need to show that the bands and their inversion retain the specified target throughout the confounding and interference class. Only after those pieces are defined can proposed degree-growth and exposure-cell overlap thresholds be assessed against both coverage and bound width.

The sequence does not yet establish that any threshold works. In particular, proving coverage and obtaining bounds narrower than outcome-range bounds are separate tasks.
What would the sensitivity linear programs be for, conceptually?

They would organize the search for the smallest and largest direct or spillover effect compatible with the assumptions and the exposure-specific information. The variables would represent the quantities left uncertain; the constraints would encode the stated sensitivity, interference, and other relevant restrictions; and the objective would select the effect contrast of interest.

Calling them linear programs is a substantive part of the plan, not a guarantee that an unspecified model can be written that way. The derivation has to show that the chosen variables, constraints, and effect contrasts really are linear in the required formulation, and that the feasible region neither omits allowed configurations nor admits configurations the assumptions exclude.
Why derive one for direct effects and one for spillover effects?

Because they optimize different contrasts. A direct-effect contrast changes a unit’s own policy status while keeping the relevant network exposure fixed. A spillover-effect contrast changes network exposure while keeping own status fixed. With staggered adoption, the relevant timing also has to be specified in each contrast.

Some constraints or uncertain quantities may be shared, but that does not make the objectives interchangeable. Separate programs, or clearly separated objectives within a common formulation, would make it possible to ask whether each resulting bound improves on its own outcome-range benchmark.
Could the programs simply impose the Γ sensitivity restriction and ignore network exposure until the objective?

That would risk losing the distinction the plan needs. A restriction on unmeasured confounding of staggered adoption and a restriction on network interference do different jobs. If exposure affects which outcomes or comparisons are compatible, it must be represented where the feasible configurations are defined, not merely mentioned when the objective is named.

The exact constraints cannot be supplied without defining the sensitivity model and exposure class. The derivation should make visible which restrictions concern adoption, which concern exposure and interference, and which support each direct or spillover contrast.
Would the output of a sensitivity linear program already be a confidence interval?

Not automatically. An optimization over compatible population quantities addresses an identification bound under the stated assumptions. A confidence set additionally accounts for uncertainty in the information used to construct that bound.

In this plan, simultaneous bands supply the uncertainty component. Inverting or incorporating those bands into the compatible-set calculation can produce a confidence set, but its coverage requires a separate argument. The numerical endpoints of an identification program should not be described as having 95% coverage merely because they come from an optimization.
What is the dependency graph doing in the bands?

It is meant to represent the dependence relevant to the exposure-specific quantities whose uncertainty the bands cover. Network spillovers can make observations dependent, so a band argument that treats all observations as independent without justification could be inadequate.

The dependency graph used for a probability argument needs its own justification. It need not be identical to the policy network: one must show that the proposed graph captures the dependence allowed by the stated interference and adoption class. Labeling a graph a dependency graph does not, by itself, prove that the simultaneous bands are valid.
Why emphasize simultaneous bands instead of separate uncertainty intervals?

The direct and spillover programs may use several exposure-specific quantities at once. To transfer band coverage through both optimizations, the relevant quantities need to be covered together on an event with the required probability. Separate coverage claims for individual cells do not automatically provide that joint event.

The planned proof should therefore state what collection of quantities the bands cover simultaneously. It must include every quantity needed for the direct and spillover calculations if a common uniform-coverage claim is to follow for both.
Should the simultaneous bands be derived before the sensitivity programs?

There is a useful logical reason to define the targets and programs first: that identifies which exposure-specific quantities actually need bands. One could work on the constructions in parallel, but the final argument must connect the bands to the constraints and objectives used in the programs.

The stated plan—derive the programs and bands, prove uniform coverage, then test thresholds—does not require a rigid order within that first derivation stage. It does require their definitions to agree before coverage is claimed.
What exactly would the uniform-coverage proof have to connect?

It would need a uniform joint-coverage statement for the exposure-specific quantities under the stated confounding and interference class. It would also need to show that, whenever those quantities lie in the simultaneous bands, the feasible set used in inversion contains the allowed configuration relevant to the chosen coverage target. That implication carries the band event through to the confidence set for the direct or spillover effect.

The proof should specify whether the target is a true effect value or an entire identified set, and whether the guarantee is finite-sample or asymptotic. Those distinctions affect what “uniform coverage” asserts; they should not be left implicit.
Could I prove coverage just for the direct-effect program and then reuse it for spillovers?

Only if the argument genuinely covers the quantities and inversion steps used by the spillover program as well. A direct contrast and a spillover contrast can depend on different exposure cells. Joint bands may make a shared proof possible, but their mere existence does not show that every required spillover quantity was included.

The plan calls for direct and spillover programs, so the coverage reasoning should trace each target through the simultaneous band event. It can share steps where justified without assuming the targets are identical.
Does uniformity mean checking every Γ-bounded adoption process one at a time?

The claim needs to hold across the entire stated class, rather than only for a selected process. One-at-a-time arguments may not suffice, particularly for an asymptotic claim in which the least favorable allowed configuration can vary with the size of the network.

The proof can use a general bound or other argument that applies across the class; it need not literally enumerate its members. What matters is that the final coverage statement has the promised uniform scope, including the allowed interference configurations as well as the allowed adoption confounding.
The plan says to prove coverage before testing degree and overlap thresholds. Doesn't a dependency-graph proof already require a degree condition?

It may require conditions involving degree and overlap. The order can be read as proving a general conditional statement first—identifying what features of the dependency graph and cell support suffice for coverage—and then checking proposed threshold rates against those conditions. It should not be read as promising an assumption-free proof followed by optional rate checks.

If a particular rate is essential to the proof, it belongs in the proof’s assumptions. The later threshold test then asks whether a candidate degree-growth and overlap specification satisfies those assumptions and also produces nontrivial bounds.
So what is left to test after a uniform-coverage theorem?

At least two things can remain. First, whether the proposed degree-growth and exposure-cell overlap rates satisfy the theorem’s conditions uniformly over the stated class. Second, whether those same rates, together with the sensitivity and interference restrictions, actually make the direct and spillover bounds narrower than their respective outcome-range bounds.

Coverage can hold for bands that are too wide to give nontrivial bounds. The threshold test should therefore not stop at checking the coverage conditions.
Would the threshold test be an empirical test on a particular network?

The plan does not specify an empirical network or experiment. Here, “test the degree/overlap thresholds” can mean evaluate proposed rate conditions against the derived coverage requirements and the direct and spillover bound calculations, including whether a counterexample remains within the allowed class. That is a theoretical check unless a separate empirical task is stated.

It would be premature to describe observed cell counts or a completed test. The thresholds have not yet been established by the plan.
How should the outcome-range comparison enter the linear-program step?

For each target, the outcome range supplies a benchmark bound that does not rely on the proposed informative restrictions. After deriving the sensitivity program, compare its minimum and maximum compatible effects with the corresponding benchmark. To call a bound nontrivial in the intended sense, the program must exclude at least some values admitted by that outcome-range bound.

The comparison must be done for direct and spillover effects separately. A strict improvement for one objective does not establish strict improvement for the other, even if both are computed using the same bands.
What if overlap is enough for the programs to be feasible but not enough to narrow their objectives?

Then feasibility and nontriviality have been separated correctly. Feasibility says the restrictions and band values admit at least one compatible configuration. It does not say the optimization excludes any outcome-range-compatible direct or spillover effect values.

That distinction is one reason for testing overlap thresholds after formulating the objectives. A cell-support condition should be assessed not only for whether the programs can be run, but also for whether it helps yield the asserted narrowing under the stated sensitivity and interference class.
Could an infeasible program be interpreted as an especially tight bound?

No. An empty feasible set is not a useful tight effect bound. It could indicate incompatible inputs or a misspecified formulation, including constraints that inadvertently exclude configurations the assumptions allow.

For the confidence-set argument, this is particularly important: on the stated joint-coverage event, the allowed configuration needed for the coverage target must remain feasible. The derivation and proof should establish that implication rather than treating infeasibility as evidence of identification.
What kinds of mismatches between the dependency graph and the sensitivity programs should we watch for?

One is a scope mismatch: the bands might cover exposure cells defined one way while the programs use contrasts defined another way. Another is a dependence mismatch: the proposed dependency graph might omit dependencies permitted by the interference class. A third is an uncertainty mismatch: a program might rely on a quantity for which no simultaneous band was constructed.

These are checks to make during the derivation, not claims that any mismatch is present. Consistent definitions are necessary before the uniform-coverage proof can transfer band validity to the inverted effect sets.
And if the band proof works only for a restricted interference class?

Then any coverage conclusion must be confined to that stated class. It cannot be presented as uniform over a broader interference class. Likewise, if the linear programs’ constraints correspond to a different class, the band proof and the identification argument would not yet support one common claim.

The plan is to prove uniform coverage over the class actually specified, not to rely on an informal statement that network effects are merely present.
Can this sequence answer the rates question without assuming in advance which thresholds will pass?

That is its purpose. Derive the direct and spillover sensitivity linear programs and the dependency-graph simultaneous bands; establish the coverage claim, with its necessary conditions stated; then assess candidate degree-growth and exposure-cell overlap thresholds against those conditions and against strict narrowing of both effect bounds. The result of that assessment remains open at the planning stage.

I want to simulate 10,000 Γ=1.5 staggered panels across degree exponents 0.10–0.17 and minimum exposure-cell probabilities 0.05–0.20, then measure simultaneous coverage and widths. How should I describe what this activity can tell us?

Describe it as a simulation study to assess the proposed bands and bounds under the simulated conditions, not as a completed result or a proof. The degree-exponent and overlap ranges let you examine how simultaneous coverage and bound widths behave as network growth and exposure-cell support vary at Γ=1.5. Measuring widths separately for direct and spillover effects will be important: one may be informative while the other is not.

The 10,000 panels are the stated simulation total. That wording does not say how they are allocated across the exponent and overlap settings, so it should not be described as 10,000 panels at every setting.
Why explore degree exponents from 0.10 to 0.17 rather than only the proposed eighth-root rate?

The range includes exponents below and above 1/8, which is 0.125. That permits a comparison of simulated behavior on either side of the proposed growth condition. But the relationship must be read carefully: if degree grows like n raised to a fixed exponent below 0.125, it satisfies o(n^{1/8}); growth exactly proportional to n^{0.125} does not satisfy that little-o condition. An exponent above 0.125 also does not satisfy it.

These observations explain the range’s relevance; they do not predict what the simulation will show or establish that 0.125 is a sharp threshold.
And the overlap range, 0.05–0.20, includes the proposed 0.1 floor?

Yes. It includes minimum exposure-cell probabilities below and above 0.1, as well as 0.1 itself. That makes it possible to examine whether measured coverage and widths change around the proposed floor.

The probability needs a consistent definition across the simulated panels: which exposure cells are required, what their minimum is taken over, and how staggered adoption enters those cells. Otherwise a plotted change across 0.05–0.20 could be hard to interpret as a change in the overlap condition relevant to direct and spillover contrasts.
Does specifying a minimum probability of 0.05 guarantee that every exposure cell contains observations in every simulated panel?

No. A minimum probability is a feature of the specified simulation distribution, not a guarantee of a positive realized count in every panel. The distinction matters especially for the least-supported cells and for panels with dependent exposure patterns.

A panel with an empty required cell may affect whether the proposed bands and sensitivity calculations can be formed as intended. The activity should specify how such panels are counted when measuring coverage and widths, rather than silently dropping them and then reporting results only for favorable realizations.
What should “simultaneous coverage” mean in the measurement?

It should be defined as a joint event, not as an average of separate cellwise coverage rates. For example, if the object under assessment is the simultaneous exposure-specific bands, ask whether all the relevant quantities are covered together in a simulated panel. If the object is the inverted confidence sets, specify whether the joint event requires coverage of both the direct and spillover targets, and whether each target is a true effect value or an identified set.

Those are different measurements. The activity says to measure simultaneous coverage, so the reporting should name the particular joint event used rather than leaving “simultaneous” to mean whichever marginal result looks favorable.
Is it reasonable to compare measured simultaneous coverage with 95%?

Yes, because at least 95% coverage is the stated goal. An observed simulation coverage rate can show how the proposed procedure behaves for the simulated configurations at Γ=1.5. It cannot, by itself, prove a uniform 95% guarantee over every configuration in the stated confounding and interference class, particularly if that class includes configurations not simulated.

The comparison should also respect whether the claim is asymptotic. Behavior at simulated finite sizes can be informative about that claim, but a finite simulation alone does not establish an asymptotic worst-case lower bound.
If one configuration has measured coverage above 95%, does that support uniformity?

It provides information about that configuration, but uniformity concerns the least favorable configuration throughout the stated class. Even high coverage throughout a finite set of simulated settings would not by itself rule out poorer coverage elsewhere in the class.

It is still useful to examine the coverage measurements across the full simulated degree-exponent and overlap ranges, rather than focus on a favorable setting. The appropriate conclusion remains about simulated performance unless accompanied by the separate uniform-coverage argument.
Should widths refer to the simultaneous bands or to the direct and spillover bounds after inversion?

The word “widths” should identify the object measured. Band widths describe uncertainty in exposure-specific quantities; inverted direct and spillover bound widths describe how much uncertainty remains about the effects. For the nontrivial-bounds question, widths of the direct and spillover bounds after inversion are especially pertinent, compared with their respective outcome-range bounds.

You can measure more than one kind of width if you define each one. The key is not to infer that narrow exposure-specific bands necessarily produce nontrivial direct and spillover bounds, or that a narrow realized confidence set establishes informative population identification.
Could I combine the direct and spillover widths into a single average?

An average could obscure the very distinction the activity needs to assess. A narrow direct bound could offset a broad spillover bound in the average, even though the proposed nontriviality claim concerns both. Reporting the widths separately would allow each effect to be compared with its own outcome-range benchmark.

A combined summary, if used, should supplement rather than replace those separate measurements.
Does a width smaller than the outcome-range width in one simulated panel demonstrate nontrivial partial identification?

Not necessarily. A single realized width can reflect sampling variation, and its meaning depends on whether it is an identification bound or a confidence set obtained using simulated bands. To assess the nontriviality claim, the relevant comparison is whether the assumed restrictions genuinely narrow the compatible direct and spillover effects relative to their outcome-range bounds under the conditions being studied.

Simulation can show how often and by how much a calculated bound or set is narrower in simulated panels. It cannot turn an occasional narrow realization into a general identification result.
Does keeping Γ fixed at 1.5 help isolate the degree and overlap comparisons?

It holds the stated sensitivity level constant while degree exponents and minimum exposure-cell probabilities vary. That helps interpret differences across those settings without simultaneously changing Γ.

It does not mean confounding is absent, nor does the number 1.5 alone fully specify the adoption-confounding model. Simulated panels and the bands applied to them must use the same stated interpretation of Γ=1.5 for the measurements to address the intended question.
Are the degree exponents themselves degree values?

No. An exponent describes how the selected degree measure changes with n in a sequence of simulated settings; it is not the realized degree in one panel. The selected measure—such as a particular network-degree summary—still has to be identified. The dependence relevant to the bands also has to be related to that measure.

Without those definitions, measurements labeled by exponents 0.10–0.17 would not tell us whether the degree condition used in a coverage argument was actually varied as intended.
Can 10,000 simulated panels resolve tiny differences around the 95% target?

The simulation count is finite, so measured coverage itself has Monte Carlo uncertainty. Its precision depends in part on how the 10,000 panels are distributed among the settings being compared. If they are spread across many settings, each setting has fewer replications than the overall total.

That is a reason to present measured rates as estimates from the specified simulation activity, not as exact coverage probabilities or a definitive determination that a setting clears 95% by a very small margin. The node does not specify an allocation, so no setting-specific precision should be asserted in advance.
Would measuring simultaneous coverage at several degree exponents prove the proposed o(n^{1/8}) result?

No. Finite panels across exponents 0.10–0.17 can probe whether performance appears sensitive to degree growth, including on either side of 0.125. A uniform asymptotic statement additionally concerns behavior as n grows and takes a worst case over the stated class. Simulated evidence does not replace the dependency-graph coverage proof.

Nor would a performance change near 0.125 prove that this is a necessary boundary. The simulation is an assessment of the proposal under the simulated conditions, not a derivation of a sharp mathematical threshold.
If measured coverage drops below 95% at an exponent above 0.125, would that validate the proposed rate?

It would be consistent with the idea that faster degree growth may pose problems for the simulated procedure, but it would not validate the sufficient-rate claim. That claim concerns whether coverage is uniformly asymptotically at least 95% under its stated conditions; a problem outside those conditions does not prove performance inside them.

It also would not establish that the exponent alone caused the difference unless the simulated settings permit that interpretation. The defensible observation would concern the measured simultaneous coverage in the settings actually simulated.
What if coverage is good below 0.125 but the spillover widths stay at the outcome-range width?

Then the simulated coverage measurements and the width measurements would be telling different stories. Good simultaneous coverage in those simulated settings would not establish the proposed nontrivial spillover bound. You would still need to assess direct and spillover narrowing separately, and the broader uniform asymptotic coverage claim would still require proof.

That possibility is why the activity includes widths as well as coverage. It can reveal whether a method appears reliable but uninformative for one of the target effects.
What if direct and spillover widths both shrink at a minimum cell probability below 0.1?

That could suggest the proposed 0.1 floor is not necessary for narrowing in the simulated settings. It would not show that a lower floor suffices uniformly over the confounding and interference class, or that the confidence sets have the desired coverage there.

The current activity permits examining minimum probabilities down to 0.05. Findings from that range should be stated as simulated behavior until a general argument supports a stronger conclusion.
Should the simulations include only configurations meeting both proposed conditions?

The stated ranges include settings on different sides of the proposed 0.1 overlap floor and the exponent 0.125 associated with the eighth-root condition. Restricting attention to settings satisfying both proposed conditions would lose some of the intended comparisons across 0.10–0.17 and 0.05–0.20.

At the same time, labeling a finite simulated setting as satisfying the asymptotic little-o condition requires care: it is a claim about a sequence, not simply a realized network. The comparison should be framed using the specified degree-growth sequence and the defined exposure-cell probabilities.
Should failures to calculate a width be excluded when summarizing width and coverage?

They should at least be accounted for explicitly. If a required exposure cell is empty or an inversion is infeasible, excluding those panels without explanation could make reported performance appear better than the actual procedure’s behavior across the simulated settings. Coverage may not even be defined for a panel unless the procedure specifies what it returns in that case.

The simulation description can distinguish calculable widths from calculation failures and explain how failures enter the coverage assessment. No failure frequency can be assumed before running the activity.
How do I keep the simulation study connected to the planned sensitivity linear programs and dependency-graph bands?

Apply consistently defined programs and bands to the simulated Γ=1.5 staggered panels, then measure the joint coverage event relevant to their inversion and the resulting direct and spillover widths. The exposure cells used for the 0.05–0.20 overlap settings must match those in the programs and bands, and the degree measure used for the 0.10–0.17 growth settings must match the dependency condition being investigated.

That alignment lets the activity assess the proposed construction. It does not imply the construction has already been derived or that uniform coverage has already been proved.
How should I phrase the activity without announcing a result?

“Simulate 10,000 Γ=1.5 staggered panels spanning degree exponents 0.10–0.17 and minimum exposure-cell probabilities 0.05–0.20; measure simultaneous coverage and the widths of the direct and spillover bounds.” This states the activity and its measurements without claiming that coverage reaches 95%, that either bound is nontrivial, or that the proposed degree and overlap thresholds have been established.

At degree exponent 0.10 and exposure-cell overlap ≥0.10, the 10,000 worst-case Γ=1.5 staggered panels yielded 95.4% coverage. The direct and spillover widths were 62% and 71% of range, respectively. How should I report that?

Report it as a result for that simulated setting: “Across 10,000 worst-case Γ=1.5 staggered panels at degree exponent 0.10 and exposure-cell overlap ≥0.10, measured coverage was 95.4%; direct and spillover widths were 62% and 71% of range, respectively.”

That preserves the conditions, the coverage measurement, and the order of the two widths. It does not turn a simulation result at this setting into a uniform asymptotic coverage guarantee.
Is 95.4% above the 95% target?

The measured rate is 0.4 percentage points above 95%. That is a comparison between the reported simulation measurement and the target, not proof that the underlying coverage probability exceeds 95%. The finite simulation leaves uncertainty about that probability, and a uniform claim would require an argument over the entire stated class.
Does “10,000 worst-case panels” mean that every possible worst case was tested?

No. It describes the 10,000 panels as worst-case Γ=1.5 panels, but it does not establish that they exhaust every configuration allowed by the confounding and interference class. In particular, “worst-case” should not silently become a claim that the globally least favorable coverage configuration has been found.

The safe scope is the panels and setting reported: degree exponent 0.10, overlap ≥0.10, and Γ=1.5.
Could I call 95.4% simultaneous coverage?

If the measured coverage event was the simultaneous event specified for the exposure-specific bands or their inversion, yes. The simulation activity called for measuring simultaneous coverage. It is still worth naming precisely what was required to be covered together: the relevant exposure-specific quantities, the direct and spillover targets, or another explicitly defined joint target.

The reported number alone does not resolve that choice. It should not be described as simultaneous coverage of an entire identified set if the measurement only checked coverage of effect values, or vice versa.
If the event was simultaneous, does 95.4% also tell us the separate direct and spillover coverage rates?

It does not give their numerical rates. If the simultaneous event required both targets to be covered, its occurrence would imply each was covered on that panel. But the reported 95.4% does not say how often only one target was covered when the joint event failed.

Keep the joint measurement distinct from unreported marginal measurements.
What exactly do the two width percentages communicate?

They are widths, not effect estimates or coverage probabilities. The direct width was 62% of range, and the spillover width was 71% of range. On the stated comparison, the direct width occupies a smaller fraction of range than the spillover width.

The report does not supply absolute widths or effect values. Nor should the two percentages be swapped: 62% belongs to the direct effect and 71% to the spillover effect.
Can I say the direct width was 38% less than range and the spillover width was 29% less?
