Yes, as arithmetic descriptions of the stated width ratios: 100% minus 62% is 38%, and 100% minus 71% is 29%. Make clear that these are reductions in width relative to the same range used for the reported ratios, not reductions in effect size.

The original 62% and 71% figures are less susceptible to confusion about the reference and are sufficient on their own.
Would it be accurate to say the direct effect itself was 62% of range?

No. The reported quantity is the width of the direct-effect bound or set, expressed as 62% of range. An effect value could be positive, negative, or otherwise positioned within a bound; width does not identify its value or position.

The same distinction applies to the spillover figure of 71%.
Does the smaller direct width mean the direct effect is more certain than the spillover effect?

It says that the reported direct width is smaller relative to range in this setting. “More certain” can suggest a broader conclusion about estimation precision, identification, or coverage that the two ratios alone do not establish. The direct and spillover targets may also have different relevant comparisons.

A precise statement is simply that the direct and spillover widths were 62% and 71% of range, respectively, in these panels.
Should I describe the widths as narrower than outcome-range bounds?

You can make a width comparison if “range” in the reported percentages is the corresponding outcome-range width for each target. On that reading, 62% and 71% are each below 100% of their respective benchmarks. State the reference explicitly rather than assuming readers know what “range” denotes.

The numerical result remains a measurement at this simulated setting. It does not by itself establish that the underlying bounds are strictly narrower for every configuration admitted by the stated class.
Does the exponent 0.10 describe the degree observed in each panel?

No. It is the reported degree exponent for the setting, not a numerical degree for an individual unit or panel. To interpret it as a growth rate, the degree measure and its relation to panel size would need to be specified.

The reported evidence does not include realized degree values. Calling 0.10 a realized degree would change the meaning of the result.
How does 0.10 compare numerically with 1/8?

One eighth is 0.125, so 0.10 is smaller. If a specified degree measure grows proportionally to n^0.10 along a sequence, it grows more slowly than n^{1/8} in the little-o sense. The result here, however, reports measurements for panels at degree exponent 0.10; that numerical comparison alone does not establish an asymptotic coverage theorem.
Does overlap ≥0.10 mean every realized panel had at least 10% of its observations in each required exposure cell?

Not from the wording alone. An exposure-cell overlap condition expressed as a probability of at least 0.10 concerns the specified probabilities. Realized cell shares can differ across panels, especially when exposures are dependent through a network.

The finding should retain the stated “overlap ≥0.10” condition without silently recasting it as a guarantee about every realized cell count.
Can we compare this coverage measurement with settings at other degree exponents or overlap values?

Not numerically from the result given here. It reports 95.4% coverage and the two widths for degree exponent 0.10 with overlap ≥0.10. It supplies no measurements for other settings, so it does not establish a trend across degree exponents or exposure-cell probabilities.

Even though those quantities were dimensions of the simulation activity, results for unreported settings should not be inferred from this one.
Would 95.4% across 10,000 panels mean 9,540 covered panels?

If the reported percentage is exact and each panel contributes one binary coverage event, 95.4% of 10,000 is 9,540 covered events. If the percentage was rounded or coverage was aggregated differently, the exact count cannot be recovered solely from the percentage.

The coverage rate as reported—95.4%—is the unambiguous figure to retain.
Can I infer a margin of error for the 95.4% figure from the panel count alone?

Not responsibly without specifying how the panels were generated and how the coverage events relate across them. A calculation that assumes independent, identically distributed binary events would add assumptions not stated in the result.

It is enough to distinguish the observed 95.4% from an exact coverage probability. The number of panels conveys the simulation scale, but it does not alone prove that the true coverage probability clears 95%.
Does this establish uniform asymptotic ≥95% coverage?

No. The observation concerns 10,000 simulated panels at the stated Γ=1.5 setting. Uniform asymptotic coverage is a worst-case statement over a defined confounding and interference class as size grows. Neither coverage outside the reported setting nor the required asymptotic lower bound follows solely from this measurement.

A uniform-coverage proof would have to address that broader claim separately. The simulation result can be reported in full without presenting it as that proof.
Does the phrase “worst-case Γ=1.5” at least make the coverage result uniform within the simulated panels?

It identifies how the panels are described, but uniform coverage is not the same as an aggregate coverage rate across a collection labeled worst-case. Uniformity requires the guarantee to hold for each allowed configuration in the stated class, including the least favorable ones under the defined coverage criterion.

If several configurations contributed panels, the pooled 95.4% would not on its own give the coverage rate for each configuration. The result as stated is a measured rate for the 10,000 panels, no more and no less.
Is it fair to separate what was measured from what remains unestablished?

Yes. What was measured is specific: at degree exponent 0.10 and overlap ≥0.10, 10,000 worst-case Γ=1.5 staggered panels yielded 95.4% coverage, with direct and spillover widths of 62% and 71% of range. What that sentence does not establish is a coverage guarantee for every allowed confounding and interference configuration or an asymptotic result.

That separation does not diminish the reported measurements; it keeps their scope clear.
Could you give me a compact wording that retains the numbers and the limitation?

“At degree exponent 0.10 and exposure-cell overlap ≥0.10, 10,000 worst-case Γ=1.5 staggered panels yielded 95.4% measured coverage; direct and spillover widths were 62% and 71% of range, respectively. These are results for the simulated panels, not a uniform asymptotic coverage guarantee.”

Given the simulated coverage, I want to retain Γ=1.5, exposure-cell overlap ≥0.10, and degree o(n^{1/8}) as proof targets. The simulation supports feasibility, not uniformity. Is that the right distinction?

Yes. The decision is to keep those three conditions as targets for a proof, not to treat them as established sufficient conditions. The simulated coverage makes the proposed approach worth pursuing under the examined conditions, but it does not establish coverage uniformly over the stated confounding and interference class.

The proof still has to show what follows at Γ=1.5 when the relevant exposure-cell probabilities are at least 0.10 and the specified degree measure is o(n^{1/8}).
What does retaining them as proof targets commit us to?

It commits the proposed argument to examining those stated conditions: Γ=1.5 for the adoption-confounding sensitivity restriction, ≥0.10 for the required exposure-cell probabilities, and o(n^{1/8}) for the specified degree measure. The aim is to determine whether they support the desired direct and spillover bounds and the uniform coverage claim.

It does not commit us to asserting that the proof succeeds, that the conditions are necessary, or that their numerical thresholds are sharp.
When I say the simulation supports feasibility, what should “feasibility” mean here?

Read it modestly: the simulated coverage supports the feasibility of pursuing this proposed set of proof targets. It is evidence that the proposed approach can be examined meaningfully, not a theorem about every allowed configuration.

It should not be taken to mean that the sensitivity linear programs are feasible for all possible inputs, that every exposure cell is populated in every panel, or that uniform coverage has been verified. Those are different claims.
Why isn't simulated coverage enough for uniformity if the panels were designed to be challenging?

Because uniformity quantifies over the entire stated confounding and interference class. However challenging the simulated panels are, a measured coverage rate over them does not establish the required coverage level for every allowed configuration, including configurations that may not have been simulated.

That is the specific limit preserved by the decision: simulated coverage supports feasibility of the proof direction, not the uniform coverage conclusion itself.
Could I still say the simulation proves coverage at Γ=1.5?

No. Γ=1.5 identifies the sensitivity level retained as a proof target. A simulated coverage measurement describes performance in the simulated panels; it does not prove a coverage guarantee at that level over the full class.

A careful statement is that simulated coverage supports feasibility at the proposed setting, while coverage—particularly uniform coverage—remains to be proved.
Does the retained overlap threshold refer to observed cell shares or cell probabilities?

It refers to exposure-cell overlap ≥0.10 as a condition to be made precise in the proof. In the formulation under discussion, the natural reading is a probability floor for every exposure cell required by the direct and spillover contrasts, rather than a guarantee about each realized panel’s cell shares.

The proof must specify the cells and the probabilities to which the floor applies. Retaining the threshold does not resolve those definitions by itself.
And degree o(n^{1/8}) remains a growth condition, not a cap at one panel size?

Correct. For the degree measure ultimately specified, o(n^{1/8}) means its ratio to n^{1/8} tends to zero as n grows. It is an asymptotic condition, not a fixed degree limit for a single panel.

Keeping it as a proof target also does not specify whether the measure is maximum degree or another degree summary. The argument must identify the measure it needs.
Is the decision claiming that the three conditions are jointly sufficient for at least 95% uniform coverage?

No. It retains their joint sufficiency as something to establish, not something already established. The coverage objective is at least 95% uniformly over the stated class, but the decision explicitly separates that objective from what simulated coverage can show.

A proof would need to justify the simultaneous bands and their inversion under the precise Γ restriction, overlap condition, and degree-growth condition, with the interference class and coverage target stated.
Should direct and spillover bounds remain separate proof targets too?

Yes. The proposed conditions are being retained in pursuit of the original distinction between direct and spillover effects. Showing that one bound is narrower than its outcome-range benchmark would not establish the same for the other.

The decision does not say either result has been proved. It preserves the conditions under which the separate narrowing claims can be investigated.
Could we describe ≥0.10 and o(n^{1/8}) as the minimum requirements?

No. Calling them minimum requirements would assert necessity or sharpness that this decision does not establish. They are retained proof targets: proposed conditions under which to seek a result.

A proof under those conditions would show sufficiency for whatever conclusion it actually establishes. It would not, by itself, show that a lower overlap floor or faster degree growth cannot work.
Does retaining Γ=1.5 imply that the same claim will hold at every other sensitivity level?

No. The retained target is specifically Γ=1.5. Whether an argument extends to another sensitivity level would require its own justification. The decision neither asserts such an extension nor compares results across levels.
What would a successful coverage proof have to say that the simulated coverage cannot?

It would have to state a coverage target and establish the at-least-95% guarantee in the intended sense across all configurations in the specified Γ=1.5 confounding and interference class that satisfy the proof conditions. If the intended claim is uniform asymptotic coverage, it must control the worst case over that class as n grows.

Simulated coverage is a measurement over simulated panels. It cannot supply that quantification over the whole class, even when it motivates attempting the proof.
If the proof needs a stronger overlap condition, does this decision already rule that out?

No. Retaining ≥0.10 as a proof target means attempting to establish the desired result with that floor. It is not a declaration that the result must hold under it. If an argument cannot establish the claim at that floor, the decision itself does not supply the missing result.

For now, there is no need to announce a different condition or a judgment about whether one is required.
How should I avoid letting the feasibility statement sound like a completed theorem?

Use language such as “supports pursuing” or “is consistent with feasibility,” and immediately name the limitation: it does not establish uniform coverage. Then call Γ=1.5, overlap ≥0.10, and degree o(n^{1/8}) proof targets rather than proven thresholds.

That phrasing retains the positive role of the simulated coverage without converting a finite assessment into a guarantee for the full class.
Could the proof establish coverage but leave nontrivial bound widths unresolved?

Yes. Coverage and width are separate properties. A uniformly valid confidence set could remain as wide as the outcome-range benchmark for a direct or spillover effect. Retaining these conditions as proof targets therefore does not merge the coverage and nontriviality questions.

The desired characterization would need to establish narrowing for each effect as well as the coverage claim. The decision does not report that either task is complete.
Can you state the decision in one sentence without overclaiming?

Retain Γ=1.5, exposure-cell overlap ≥0.10, and degree o(n^{1/8}) as proof targets for the direct and spillover bounds and uniform coverage claim; simulated coverage supports the feasibility of pursuing those targets but does not establish uniformity.

StaggerNetSim v1 contains Γ=1.5 panel simulations, degree and overlap grids, simultaneous-coverage estimates, and separate direct- and spillover-bound-width tables. How should I describe the artifact?

Describe StaggerNetSim v1 as an artifact that brings those four components together: panel simulations at Γ=1.5, grids for degree and exposure-cell overlap, estimates of simultaneous coverage, and separate tables of direct- and spillover-bound widths. That says what it contains without implying that the artifact itself proves a coverage guarantee or establishes a degree or overlap threshold.
Why mention the degree and overlap grids explicitly?

They identify the dimensions along which the simulated results can be examined. A coverage estimate or width entry is easier to interpret when the corresponding degree and overlap setting is clear. Merely saying that the artifact contains simulations would conceal those dimensions.

The description does not, however, specify the values in the grids or say that every possible combination has a result. Those details should come from the artifact rather than be inferred from the word “grids.”
Does Γ=1.5 apply to the panel simulations or to every item in the artifact?

The explicit statement is that StaggerNetSim v1 contains Γ=1.5 panel simulations. The coverage estimates and width tables are presented as contents of the same artifact, but that short description does not independently define how every entry was calculated. If you want to say that a particular estimate or table entry was calculated at Γ=1.5, that linkage should be clear from the artifact’s definitions.

For a brief description, calling it an artifact containing Γ=1.5 panel simulations and the listed grids, estimates, and tables preserves exactly what is stated.
What is the distinction between a simultaneous-coverage estimate and a uniform coverage guarantee?

A simultaneous-coverage estimate is a measured frequency for a specified joint coverage event in the simulations. “Simultaneous” means the event covers all the quantities or targets included in that event together, rather than evaluating each one separately.

A uniform guarantee is a claim about coverage throughout a stated class of confounding and interference configurations. The existence of estimates in StaggerNetSim v1 does not, on its own, establish that broader guarantee. The artifact description should retain the word “estimates.”
Can I just write that StaggerNetSim v1 contains coverage results?

You can, but “simultaneous-coverage estimates” is more precise. “Coverage results” might be read as a demonstrated guarantee or as separate coverage figures for different effects. The artifact’s stated content is estimates of simultaneous coverage; naming them that way preserves both their joint nature and their evidentiary scope.
Should the artifact specify what is covered simultaneously?

That would make its estimates interpretable. The joint coverage event should say which exposure-specific quantities or effect targets have to be covered together, as well as what counts as coverage. Without that definition, two readers could attach different meanings to the same estimate.

The current description does not supply that definition, so I would not claim that the estimates cover a particular set of targets unless StaggerNetSim v1 actually specifies it.
Why separate the direct and spillover width tables?

Direct and spillover effects represent different contrasts, and their bounds need not have the same width. Separate tables let readers examine each without a combined number concealing a wide bound for one effect behind a narrow bound for the other.

The tables report bound widths, not effect values. Their separation also does not imply that either type of bound is nontrivial at every grid setting.
If both tables have entries for a setting, can I conclude that both effects are identified there?

No. A bound-width entry tells you how wide a reported bound is under its stated definition. It does not by itself say whether the bound is narrower than the relevant outcome-range bound, whether the underlying target is point identified, or whether an accompanying confidence set has the desired coverage.

Those conclusions require the appropriate benchmark and definitions. The artifact description establishes that separate width tables are present, not what every entry proves.
Should the width tables state their reference range?

Yes, if widths are reported relative to a range. Readers need to know whether an entry is an absolute width or a fraction of a specified benchmark, and which benchmark applies to each target. Direct and spillover widths should not be treated as interchangeable merely because both appear in tables.

That is advice on interpreting or documenting the tables, not an assertion about the format of entries already in StaggerNetSim v1.
Does the word “grid” mean that the estimates are valid between the listed settings?

No. A grid identifies settings at which results may be organized or reported. Results between those settings would require additional calculations or a justified argument; they do not follow from the existence of the grid alone.

The same caution applies to a putative threshold: coverage estimates at grid settings cannot, without further reasoning, establish a degree-growth or overlap condition valid across an entire class.
Could I call StaggerNetSim v1 a proof artifact?

That would overstate the contents as described. It is an artifact containing simulations, grids, estimates, and width tables. Those materials can inform assessment of a proposed proof target, but the description does not say that it contains a proof or establishes uniform coverage.

Calling it a simulation artifact is more faithful to the listed contents.
Does “v1” indicate that any particular method or numerical finding has been finalized?

No such conclusion follows from the version label. “StaggerNetSim v1” is the artifact’s specific name here. It does not, by itself, tell us that an estimator, an inference method, or a numerical threshold has been finalized.
How can someone use the separate tables alongside the simultaneous-coverage estimates without conflating them?

They can ask two questions at a given reported setting: what does the simultaneous-coverage estimate say about the specified joint event in the simulations, and what do the direct and spillover width entries say about the sizes of their respective bounds? Those are related assessments, but they measure different properties.

A favorable coverage estimate does not force narrow bounds, and narrow reported widths do not establish coverage. Keeping the estimate and the two width measures distinct is the main interpretive safeguard.
Does the artifact description tell us whether the degree grid controls maximum degree?

No. It says there is a degree grid, but does not identify the degree measure used. To connect that grid to a degree-growth claim, the measure and its interpretation would have to be specified. I would not label it a maximum-degree grid solely from the artifact description.
Similarly, does the overlap grid tell us exactly which exposure cells have to meet its condition?

Not by itself. The relevant cells depend on how network exposure and the direct and spillover contrasts are defined. To interpret an overlap setting, one needs to know which exposure-cell probabilities it constrains and whether that includes every cell required by the reported comparisons.

The description confirms the presence of an overlap grid; it does not supply that underlying exposure definition.
Can the artifact be cited as showing how coverage and widths vary with degree and overlap?

It can be described as containing the degree and overlap grids, simultaneous-coverage estimates, and separate width tables needed to examine that question. Saying how they *vary* would require reading the entries and reporting the patterns they actually show. The fact that the components are present does not establish a trend or a direction of change.
What if someone reads a width table as a table of estimated direct or spillover effect magnitudes?

Then clarify that its entries are bound widths, not estimated effect magnitudes. A width measures the span of compatible or reported values under the table’s definition; it does not locate the effect on the outcome scale. The distinction should be explicit for both the direct-bound-width table and the spillover-bound-width table.
Is there a concise description that preserves the artifact’s exact scope?

“StaggerNetSim v1 contains Γ=1.5 panel simulations, degree and overlap grids, simultaneous-coverage estimates, and separate direct- and spillover-bound-width tables.” If needed, add: “The estimates describe simulated performance; the artifact’s listed contents do not themselves establish uniform coverage.”

I want to use the StaggerNetSim v1 panels to audit sensitivity-band inversion under adversarial adoption odds, measuring minimum simultaneous coverage and direct and spillover widths. What should the audit actually assess?

It should assess whether the exposure-specific sensitivity bands, when inverted under the adversarial adoption odds being examined, retain the intended targets together and what widths the resulting direct and spillover bounds have. Minimum simultaneous coverage asks for the lowest measured joint coverage across the audited configurations, rather than an average that could conceal a poorly performing configuration.

This is an activity to carry out, not a reported result. The StaggerNetSim v1 panels provide the simulation material, but measurements from them would not alone prove uniform coverage over an entire confounding and interference class.
What is adversarial about the adoption odds?

The idea is to examine adoption-odds configurations that challenge the sensitivity bands and their inversion while remaining within the adoption-confounding restriction being audited. “Adversarial” should not mean allowing arbitrary odds outside that restriction; doing so would test a different claim.

The phrase does not specify how the odds are selected or which configurations are most challenging. The audit would need to state the allowed odds and the set over which it searches before its minimum-coverage measurement can be interpreted.
Since StaggerNetSim v1 contains Γ=1.5 panels, can I say the audit is at Γ=1.5?

You can identify the panels being used as the Γ=1.5 panels in StaggerNetSim v1. If the audit is described as testing inversion at Γ=1.5, the adversarial adoption odds and the sensitivity bands must use the same defined interpretation of that restriction. The label alone does not specify the admissible odds or show that the inversion respects them.
Is the minimum simultaneous coverage the fraction of panels on which both effects are covered?

That is one possible joint coverage event, if the audit defines coverage in terms of both direct and spillover targets being contained in their inverted sets on the same panel. Another possible event concerns joint coverage of all exposure-specific quantities by the bands. Those events are related, but they are not identical.

The audit should name the event it measures. It should also say what the minimum is taken over—such as the adversarial adoption-odds configurations examined—rather than using “minimum” to mean the outcome of a single panel, where coverage is simply present or absent.
Why measure the minimum rather than just report coverage pooled over all the panels?

A pooled rate can be high even if one audited odds configuration has noticeably lower simultaneous coverage. Taking the minimum across the configurations actually assessed focuses attention on that weaker observed performance, which is relevant when investigating a uniform-coverage claim.

The distinction is scope: the measured minimum is over the audited configurations. It is not automatically the minimum over every configuration permitted by the full confounding and interference class.
If the audit examines challenging odds, does its measured minimum become a uniform guarantee?

No. Challenging audited configurations can make the assessment more informative, but they do not establish that no unexamined allowed configuration has lower coverage. A uniform guarantee requires an argument spanning the stated class, not just a minimum over simulated cases.

The audit can be described as probing the proposed uniform-coverage property under adversarial adoption odds. Its measurements remain simulation measurements unless a separate proof supplies the broader guarantee.
Where does band inversion itself enter, instead of merely auditing the bands?

The audit needs to follow the bands through the inversion step. It should check the joint band-coverage event and the resulting direct and spillover sets under the same panel and odds configuration, with the relevant coverage target specified. That allows a distinction between bands failing to cover a needed exposure-specific quantity and an inversion failing to retain a target despite the needed quantities lying inside the bands.

Those are possible diagnostic categories, not findings about StaggerNetSim v1. An assessment limited to the bands alone would not fully audit sensitivity-band inversion.
Would an inversion failure mean that a direct or spillover bound is too wide?

Not necessarily. A failure to retain the coverage target would be a coverage problem; a bound that is wide may still cover that target. Conversely, a narrow-looking bound might exclude it. Width and coverage therefore have to be measured separately.

The audit calls for both the minimum simultaneous coverage and direct and spillover widths precisely because a favorable result on one measure would not establish a favorable result on the other.
Should direct and spillover widths be kept separate in the audit?

Yes. The inversion addresses distinct contrasts: own policy status at fixed relevant network exposure for a direct effect, and network exposure at fixed own status for a spillover effect. Their inverted bounds can have different widths under the same adversarial adoption odds.

A combined width could conceal that difference. Separate measurements also make clear which contrast, if either, is informative relative to its own outcome-range benchmark.
Can a width measurement tell me whether the bound is nontrivial?

Only with an explicit reference. To assess nontriviality, compare a direct-bound width with the appropriate outcome-range bound for that direct target, and a spillover-bound width with the appropriate benchmark for that spillover target. A width without its reference does not establish narrowing.

It also matters whether the measurement is of an underlying sensitivity bound or of a confidence set formed using the simultaneous bands. Both can have widths, but they answer different questions. The audit should label the quantities it reports.
If a wide band leads to a wide inverted spillover bound, should I treat that as an adoption-odds problem?

Not automatically. The width may reflect the information available for the relevant exposure contrast, the allowed sensitivity restriction, the band uncertainty, or the specified interference class. The audit can examine how the inverted width behaves across its adversarial odds configurations, but an association in those measurements does not, by itself, identify a single cause.

The useful distinction is between what was varied in the audit and what the reported width actually measures.
Should the same adversarial odds be used when examining direct and spillover effects?

If the aim is a joint audit for a single allowed configuration, the direct and spillover inversions should be evaluated against a consistent underlying adoption-odds configuration. That makes their joint coverage event interpretable. The two targets may still respond differently because their contrasts use different exposure-specific quantities.

If the minimum is sought separately for each effect, those minima could occur under different configurations. Neither separate minimum alone would determine the minimum simultaneous coverage of both targets.
Does overlap matter even though this activity specifically mentions adversarial adoption odds?

Yes, because the panels and the inversions involve exposure-specific comparisons. The degree and overlap grids in StaggerNetSim v1 can identify the settings at which coverage and widths are measured. Challenging adoption odds do not replace the need to know which exposure cells support the direct and spillover contrasts.

For an interpretable audit, the odds configurations, exposure-cell definitions, and bands being inverted should refer to compatible versions of the same staggered-panel setting.
Could I take the lowest coverage estimate anywhere in StaggerNetSim v1 and call that the minimum for this audit?

Only if those estimates measure the audit’s specified simultaneous event under the relevant adversarial adoption odds and every setting over which you intend to take the minimum. A lowest entry from an existing collection of estimates is not automatically the minimum for a newly defined audit of inversion.

State the domain of the minimum explicitly. A minimum over selected panels or grid settings is a minimum over those selections, not necessarily over all allowed odds or all network configurations.
How should calculation failures be treated when measuring minimum coverage and widths?

The audit should say what the inversion returns when a required calculation cannot be made, rather than silently excluding that panel or odds configuration. Otherwise the measured coverage could describe only the cases in which the procedure happened to produce a set. A width is undefined if no bound is returned, and it should not be assigned a favorable value without a stated rule.

This is an interpretive requirement for the planned measurement; it does not assert that any such failures occur in the StaggerNetSim v1 panels.
What would it mean if the bands jointly cover the needed quantities but the inverted set misses an allowed effect?

That would indicate a problem in the connection between the band event and the inversion for that audited case. An inversion intended to retain every effect compatible with covered quantities and the allowed restrictions should include the effect represented by an allowed configuration when those quantities are jointly covered.

The audit can check that implication. It should not infer it solely from the bands’ measured coverage, because the inversion’s handling of the sensitivity restrictions and effect contrasts matters too.
And if the inversion covers both effects under every audited odds configuration?

That would describe performance within the audited configurations, assuming the joint coverage event and configurations are clearly defined. It would not establish that the same happens for every configuration in the full confounding and interference class. Nor would coverage alone show that either inverted bound is narrower than its outcome-range bound.

That is why the audit also measures direct and spillover widths and keeps the scope of its minimum explicit.
How can I phrase the activity in a way that does not imply its findings are already known?

“Use the StaggerNetSim v1 panels to audit sensitivity-band inversion under adversarial adoption odds, measuring minimum simultaneous coverage across the audited configurations and reporting direct and spillover bound widths separately.” This describes the intended assessment, not its outcome. Any resulting minimum would be an audited simulation measurement, not by itself a uniform-coverage theorem.
The audit found that under cohort-correlated, Γ=1.5-bounded adoption odds and 0.10 overlap, band inversion covered both effects in only 92.8% of 10,000 trials. How should I interpret that finding?

It is a measured joint-coverage shortfall in that audited setting. In 10,000 trials with cohort-correlated adoption odds bounded at Γ=1.5 and overlap of 0.10, the inverted bands covered both the direct and spillover effects together in 92.8% of trials. That is 2.2 percentage points below the at-least-95% coverage target.

The result raises a concrete concern about coverage of the inversion under those adoption odds. It is still a simulation result, not by itself a proof about asymptotic coverage or every configuration in the stated confounding and interference class.
Does “covered both effects” mean each effect separately had 92.8% coverage?

No. The 92.8% refers to the joint event: both effects were covered in the same trial. It does not give either effect’s separate coverage rate. On a trial where the joint event failed, the direct effect, the spillover effect, or both may have been missed; the stated result does not distinguish those cases.
Can I call the result 92.8% simultaneous coverage after inversion?

Yes, if you make clear that “simultaneous” refers to covering both effects with the inverted sets in the same trial. That is more precise than saying only “band coverage,” which a reader might take to mean joint coverage of the exposure-specific quantities before inversion.

The observation is specifically about band inversion covering both effects, not a reported coverage percentage for the original bands alone.
Why does the cohort-correlated feature matter to the description?

It identifies the adoption-odds configuration under which the 92.8% measurement arose. The finding should not be described as if the adoption odds lacked that cohort correlation or as if every Γ=1.5-bounded configuration necessarily produces the same rate.

The stated evidence does not specify how the cohort correlation was constructed or which part of the procedure it affected. Those details would be needed to explain a mechanism for the shortfall, rather than simply identify the setting in which it was observed.
Does Γ=1.5-bounded mean these odds are outside the sensitivity class?

No. The description says the adoption odds are Γ=1.5-bounded. It would be contrary to that description to dismiss the finding by calling the odds unbounded or outside the stated Γ restriction.

Whether all other assumptions needed for a particular uniform-coverage claim also apply is a separate question. The result alone does not specify every feature of the interference class or the degree condition.
How should I express the comparison with the 95% target without overstating it?

You can say, “Measured simultaneous coverage after inversion was 92.8%, below the 95% target, in 10,000 trials under cohort-correlated, Γ=1.5-bounded adoption odds and 0.10 overlap.” That reports the observed shortfall directly.

Avoid turning it into a statement that the underlying coverage probability is known exactly to be 92.8%, or that a uniform asymptotic guarantee has been mathematically disproved solely by these trials.
Does the 10,000-trial count make the shortfall definitive?

It establishes the scale of the reported audit, but a finite set of trials still produces a measured rate rather than an exact coverage probability. Assessing uncertainty in that rate would require information about the trial design and how coverage events relate across trials; that is not supplied here.

You need not calculate an uncertainty interval to report the finding accurately. The warranted statement is that the observed joint coverage was 92.8% of 10,000 trials.
If 92.8% was reported exactly, would that correspond to 9,280 trials covering both effects?

If each of the 10,000 trials contributed one binary joint-coverage event and 92.8% is exact rather than rounded, then yes: 0.928 × 10,000 is 9,280. The reported percentage is the safer figure if its rounding or aggregation is not specified.
Could the 92.8% tell us which of the direct and spillover sets needs work?

Not on its own. Because it is a joint coverage measurement, it does not attribute the missed trials to the direct effect, the spillover effect, or both. It also does not say whether the underlying exposure-specific bands missed needed quantities or whether the inversion failed to retain an allowed effect when those quantities were covered.

Those distinctions would require additional diagnostic measurements. The current finding supports the narrower statement that coverage of both effects together fell short in the audited trials.
Were the resulting direct and spillover bounds wide or narrow under these cohort-correlated odds?

Their widths are not reported in this finding. The coverage rate cannot supply them: a set can be wide and still miss a target, or narrow and cover it. Likewise, coverage below 95% does not tell us whether either bound was narrower than its outcome-range benchmark.

The stated evidence concerns simultaneous coverage after inversion at 0.10 overlap under the specified adoption odds, not a direct- or spillover-width result.
Can I infer the network degree exponent for these 10,000 trials?

No degree exponent is specified for this finding. It would be inaccurate to attach one to the 92.8% figure based only on the description given. The reported conditions are cohort-correlated, Γ=1.5-bounded adoption odds and 0.10 overlap.
Does this mean band inversion can never attain 95% coverage?

No. It shows that the audited inversion covered both effects in only 92.8% of these 10,000 trials under the stated conditions. It does not establish an impossibility result for every band construction, inversion rule, adoption-odds configuration, or interference class.

At the same time, it should not be set aside when discussing the proposed 95% goal. The measured shortfall is directly relevant to whether this audited construction supports that goal under cohort-correlated, Γ=1.5-bounded adoption odds.
Is the issue that the sensitivity level Γ=1.5 is too permissive?

The observation does not isolate a cause. Γ=1.5 defines the bound applying to the audited adoption odds, but the finding alone does not show that this value, rather than the band construction, the inversion, or another specified feature of the audit, caused the shortfall.

It is sound to identify the sensitivity level as part of the conditions and the 92.8% as the observed coverage. A causal diagnosis would need information not present in this result.
Does overlap of 0.10 guarantee that the joint coverage should have reached 95%?

No. The overlap condition specifies support for the relevant exposure cells, but it is not itself a coverage guarantee. The reported result illustrates that at 0.10 overlap, under the stated cohort-correlated and Γ=1.5-bounded odds, the audited inversion’s measured joint coverage was 92.8%.

That observation does not establish what would happen at another overlap level or under another adoption-odds configuration.
Could I average this rate with coverage from other settings and report that average as the relevant result?

An average across settings would answer a different question. The 92.8% rate is the reported measurement for this cohort-correlated, Γ=1.5-bounded setting with 0.10 overlap. Averaging could conceal a shortfall for this setting, which matters when the goal is coverage uniformly over a class rather than good average coverage across selected settings.

If a separate aggregate is reported, it should not replace or be presented as the coverage rate for these 10,000 trials.
Does a measured rate below 95% contradict the claim of at least 95% coverage in each finite simulated setting?

It is an observed rate below 95%, so it does not provide empirical confirmation of that claim for this setting. But a finite observed rate below 95% is not, without further assumptions, a proof that an underlying probability cannot be at least 95%. The distinction between a simulated frequency and a probability guarantee still applies.

For an asymptotic uniform claim, there is an additional distinction: a finite-panel audit alone does not determine the worst-case limiting coverage as size grows. The shortfall is an important coverage concern, not a complete asymptotic theorem.
What is the strongest concise conclusion supported by the finding?

In the audited 10,000 trials with cohort-correlated, Γ=1.5-bounded adoption odds and 0.10 overlap, band inversion simultaneously covered the direct and spillover effects in 92.8% of trials, below the 95% target. The finding identifies a measured shortfall for that setting; it neither supplies separate effect-specific coverage or widths nor, on its own, resolves uniform asymptotic coverage.

Here is a hypothesis: for independent cohorts, degree o(n^{1/8}), and exposure-cell overlap ≥0.10, worst-case cohort-block Γ=1.5 bands ensure uniform ≥95% coverage and nontrivial direct and spillover bounds. How carefully should I state it?

State it explicitly as a hypothesis whose two conclusions remain to be established. It proposes that independent cohorts, the specified degree-growth restriction, and the overlap floor suffice for worst-case cohort-block bands at Γ=1.5 to deliver uniform coverage of at least 95% and bounds narrower than the respective outcome-range bounds for both direct and spillover effects.

Each term needs a definition before the claim can be proved: what is independent across cohorts, which degree measure is o(n^{1/8}), which exposure cells have probability at least 0.10, what configurations the cohort-block bands treat as worst case, and what object the confidence sets cover. None of those definitions should be silently filled in by the numerical conditions alone.
Does “independent cohorts” mean that units within each cohort are independent too?

No. Independence across cohorts does not imply independence among units within a cohort. In a network setting, within-cohort outcomes or exposure quantities may still be dependent to the extent permitted by the specified interference and adoption model.

The hypothesis needs to identify the objects whose cohort blocks are independent. Otherwise the phrase cannot by itself justify a coverage calculation for the bands.
What makes the bands cohort-block bands?

The phrase indicates that the uncertainty argument treats cohorts as blocks, rather than assuming all unit-level contributions are independent. For that to be more than a label, the construction must say what belongs to each block and how the independent-cohort assumption applies to those blocks.

It also needs to account for dependence that remains within a block. The hypothesis does not specify a particular band formula or blocking procedure, so I would describe that structure conceptually rather than claim it has already delivered coverage.
What does “worst-case” add to the cohort-block construction?

It signals that the bands are intended to accommodate the least favorable configurations within the specified Γ=1.5 cohort-block adoption-confounding class, not merely a convenient odds configuration. But the class and the operation that makes the bands worst-case must be stated. Taking a worst case over one feature of adoption odds would not automatically account for every allowed network-interference or dependence pattern.

The adjective is therefore part of the proposed construction, not a substitute for showing that the resulting coverage guarantee holds uniformly over the class named in the hypothesis.
Could the cohorts be independent even when the network connects units in different cohorts?

That depends on what is asserted to be independent. If the quantities used in the bands can depend on policy statuses or outcomes across cohort boundaries, cross-cohort links may undermine an independence argument unless the stated exposure and interference assumptions account for them. The existence of a cohort label alone would not settle the issue.

The hypothesis must make the independent-cohort condition compatible with the network dependence actually permitted. It does not specify whether cross-cohort links are present or absent, so neither case should be assumed.
Does independent cohorts reduce the need for a degree condition?

Not automatically. Cohort independence and degree growth control different aspects of dependence. The first concerns what is independent across blocks; the second is a proposed restriction on a network-degree quantity. If network dependence remains relevant within blocks or for the exposure-specific quantities, the degree condition may still play a role.

To justify both conditions, the coverage argument should say what each controls. It should not presume that either restriction makes the other redundant.
How should I interpret o(n^{1/8}) without picking a degree measure yet?

For a degree quantity d_n that must be specified, d_n=o(n^{1/8}) means d_n/n^{1/8} tends to zero as n grows. It is a property of a sequence, not a maximum degree allowed for any single network.

The hypothesis has not identified whether d_n refers to the original network, a graph used to represent dependence among band contributions, or a particular summary such as maximum degree. Picking one without explanation would change the proposed condition.
Is n necessarily the number of cohorts?

Not from the hypothesis as worded. Since the statement combines cohort independence and network degree growth, it must specify what n indexes and how the number and sizes of cohorts behave as n grows. Otherwise an asymptotic interpretation of o(n^{1/8}) is ambiguous.

The numerical exponent 1/8 should be retained, but it cannot carry a coverage argument until the indexing sequence and degree quantity are clear.
Could I say the eighth-root rate is the largest permissible rate?

No. The hypothesis proposes o(n^{1/8}) as a sufficient condition to investigate. It does not assert that faster growth is impossible to accommodate or that 1/8 is a sharp boundary. Even a proof under this condition would not, by itself, establish necessity.
What does the overlap floor ≥0.10 have to cover?

Every exposure cell needed to define and support the direct and spillover contrasts for which the hypothesis claims nontrivial bounds. A direct contrast needs the relevant own-policy statuses at a fixed exposure; a spillover contrast needs the relevant exposures at a fixed own-policy status. Staggered adoption may make timing part of those cells.

The hypothesis must specify the cell definitions and the distribution under which their probabilities are at least 0.10. The floor is a probability condition, not an assertion that each realized cohort or panel contains at least 10% of its observations in every required cell.
Should the floor hold within every cohort, or only across the population?

That choice is not settled by the stated hypothesis. A population-level minimum and a within-each-cohort minimum impose different restrictions, especially for cohort-block bands. The proof must say which version its coverage and bound-width arguments need.

It would overstate the hypothesis to claim a within-cohort floor without defining one. Equally, a proof that requires within-cohort overlap should not present its conclusion as if an aggregate ≥0.10 floor alone were sufficient.
Does Γ=1.5 constrain the cohort correlation as well as the adoption odds?

Γ=1.5 is identified here as the sensitivity level for the worst-case cohort-block bands, but the statement does not give a mathematical definition of what Γ bounds. In particular, the number alone does not say that all within-cohort dependence is bounded by 1.5.

The adoption-odds restriction, the independent-cohort assumption, and any permitted within-cohort dependence should be distinguished. A coverage proof must use the definitions actually imposed, not an inferred meaning for Γ.
If the bands are called worst-case, can they guarantee 95% coverage by construction?

Not just by being called worst-case. A band may optimize over the stated odds restriction and still fail to cover the relevant exposure-specific quantities jointly with the required probability if, for example, its dependence argument does not apply to the allowed class. The hypothesis asserts a guarantee that would need proof.

The proof should show both that the proposed bands genuinely encompass the relevant Γ=1.5 configurations and that their simultaneous sampling coverage is at least 95% uniformly under the defined cohort and network assumptions.
What makes the coverage uniform rather than just 95% in one cohort-block configuration?

Uniformity requires the at-least-95% guarantee across every configuration in the stated confounding and interference class that satisfies the hypothesis’s conditions, not merely a selected configuration of cohort-block odds or network exposures. A construction calibrated for one configuration could behave differently for another allowed one.

The guarantee also needs a named coverage target: for example, covering the true direct and spillover effects together is different from covering both entire identified sets. “Uniform ≥95%” is incomplete until the target, class, and finite-sample or asymptotic interpretation are specified.
Since degree o(n^{1/8}) is asymptotic, must the 95% statement be asymptotic too?

The presence of a growth-rate assumption suggests an asymptotic argument may be intended, but the hypothesis does not explicitly state that coverage is asymptotic. It would be important to choose the intended form. A uniform asymptotic lower bound of at least 95% is not the same as coverage of at least 95% at every finite n.

Neither form should be attributed to the proposed bands without a proof. If the intended conclusion is asymptotic, say so in the hypothesis; if it is finite-sample, the argument must establish that stronger claim.
Why would simultaneous bands matter for both effects?

The two contrasts may use several exposure-specific quantities. If the bands jointly cover all quantities needed for both contrasts, an inversion that retains every effect compatible with those quantities and the allowed restrictions can transfer that joint event into coverage of the inverted sets.

This is a conditional argument. Separate 95% statements for individual quantities do not automatically give 95% simultaneous coverage, and correctly constructed bands do not excuse an inversion that excludes an allowed configuration. The hypothesis concerns the resulting direct and spillover claims together.
Could a uniform coverage proof alone establish that the bounds are nontrivial?

No. Bands can be conservative enough to cover uniformly and still leave direct or spillover effects bounded only by the outcome range. Nontriviality requires a separate comparison showing that the restrictions exclude some outcome-range-compatible values for each target effect.

For this hypothesis, the proof would need to address the direct and spillover widths individually. A narrower direct bound cannot stand in for a narrower spillover bound.
Does “nontrivial” mean point identification of both effects?

No. It means informative partial identification: each bound is strictly narrower than the respective outcome-range bound, without requiring a single value. The direct and spillover effects remain distinct targets, and neither need be point identified for the hypothesis’s width claim to hold.
Could cohort blocking make coverage better while making the bounds wider?

Conceptually, a construction that accounts for more allowed dependence or odds configurations may be more protective of coverage yet yield wider inverted sets. That possibility is exactly why the two parts of the hypothesis must be checked separately. It does not predict the performance of the proposed cohort-block bands.

The claim as stated is stronger than coverage alone: it asks for uniform ≥95% coverage and nontrivial bounds for both effects under the specified conditions.
Would it be enough to show the direct and spillover widths shrink for one possible exposure pattern?

That would show narrowing for that pattern, not a general nontriviality result under all conditions the hypothesis purports to cover. The width claim needs a clearly stated scope. If strict narrowing requires additional features beyond cohort independence, degree o(n^{1/8}), overlap ≥0.10, and the defined Γ=1.5 and interference restrictions, those features must be included in the assumptions rather than left implicit.

It is possible to state a narrower conditional result, but it should not be presented as proving the hypothesis in its broader form.
Can simulations of these bands settle the uniform part?

Simulation can examine measured simultaneous coverage and widths under simulated cohort-block configurations, including ones chosen to be challenging. It cannot on its own show coverage for every allowed configuration in the stated class or establish an asymptotic worst-case bound. It can still help evaluate whether the hypothesis is plausible and identify where a proof needs care.

The conclusion “ensure uniform ≥95% coverage” remains a proposed theorem-level claim, not something conferred by calling the odds or bands worst-case.
Could I formulate a useful proof checklist without claiming it has been satisfied?

Yes. Define the cohort-level independence assumption and its compatibility with the permitted network interference; specify n, the degree measure, and the exposure cells subject to the ≥0.10 floor; define the Γ=1.5 adoption-odds class and the cohort-block worst-case bands; identify what must be covered simultaneously; then show coverage uniformly over the stated class and strict narrowing relative to outcome-range bounds for each of the direct and spillover targets.

That is a list of obligations for assessing the hypothesis, not a declaration that any of them has been proved.
Can you state the hypothesis in one sentence that preserves the conditions but avoids presenting it as a result?

“We hypothesize that, for independent cohorts with a specified degree measure satisfying o(n^{1/8}) and probabilities of at least 0.10 in every required exposure cell, worst-case cohort-block bands at Γ=1.5 yield uniform coverage of at least 95% for the stated target and nontrivial, separately identified bounds for direct and spillover effects.” The cohort, interference, sensitivity, and coverage definitions remain to be specified and the two conclusions remain to be proved.

I want to derive worst-case cohort-block critical values at Γ=1.5 and test 10,000 adversarial panels for joint coverage and direct and spillover widths. What are the two parts of this activity meant to do?

The derivation is meant to specify how the cohort-block bands are calibrated while allowing the adoption odds permitted by Γ=1.5. The test then applies the resulting construction to 10,000 adversarial panels and measures two different properties: whether the relevant targets are covered jointly, and how wide the resulting direct and spillover bounds are.

Both are activities to perform, not reported findings. Calling the critical values “worst-case” states the intended calibration; the derivation must show what class the worst case ranges over and why the values protect the stated joint coverage event.
What is a critical value doing in a cohort-block band?

A critical value sets how far the band extends to account for sampling uncertainty in the quantities being covered. A cohort-block construction must calibrate that extension using a dependence structure appropriate to the stated cohort assumptions, rather than silently treating every unit-level contribution as independent.

Its precise form cannot be inferred from the activity alone. Deriving it means defining the band statistic, the relevant blocks, and the allowed configurations against which the critical value is calibrated.
Does Γ=1.5 itself supply the critical value?

No. Γ=1.5 fixes the stated sensitivity level for the allowed adoption odds; it is not a numerical critical value for statistical uncertainty. The critical value would depend on the defined band construction, joint coverage event, and cohort-block dependence assumptions as well as on how the Γ=1.5 restriction enters the worst-case calculation.

Keeping those roles separate prevents an adoption-confounding bound from being mistaken for a coverage calibration.
What must be shown before calling a derived value worst-case?

The derivation must identify the permitted configurations and show that the calibration accounts for the least favorable ones relevant to the stated coverage event. Selecting an adoption-odds configuration that looks extreme is not, by itself, a demonstration that it is worst for joint coverage.

The scope matters too. A critical value that is worst-case over a specified adoption-odds set is not automatically worst-case over a broader interference or dependence class. Its description should match the class actually handled.
How do cohorts enter the calculation without assuming away network dependence?

The construction needs to state what the cohort blocks contain and which block-level quantities, if any, can be treated as independent. Dependence allowed within blocks still has to be accommodated. If the network exposure or interference assumptions allow dependence across blocks, the derivation must address that rather than relying on the cohort labels alone.

The activity names cohort-block critical values but does not give those definitions. Establishing that the proposed block structure is valid is part of deriving them.
Should the critical values protect each exposure-specific band separately, or all the bands used by the effects together?

They should be calibrated for the joint event needed by the intended inference claim. If direct and spillover inversion uses multiple exposure-specific quantities, separate marginal calibrations do not automatically protect all of them together at the target coverage level.

The derivation should identify the full collection being covered simultaneously. That makes it possible to test whether the inverted sets cover both effect targets jointly, rather than assuming a collection of separate bands supplies joint protection.
What exactly should count as joint coverage in the 10,000-panel test?

For the effect-level measurement, a trial would count as jointly covered only if the inverted sets contain both the specified direct-effect target and the specified spillover-effect target in that same panel. The targets need to be defined: covering two true effect values and covering two entire identified sets are different events.

One can also inspect whether all required exposure-specific quantities lie in their bands, but that is a band-level event. The test should label the event whose joint-coverage rate it reports rather than conflating the bands’ coverage with coverage after inversion.
Why test adversarial panels instead of only typical ones?

Adversarial panels are intended to challenge the coverage and width properties under configurations permitted by the assumptions. They can expose behavior that would be obscured by concentrating on convenient panels.

The test must still specify what makes a panel adversarial and keep it within the class being evaluated. Testing 10,000 such panels does not prove that they exhaust every allowed configuration or that the smallest measured coverage is the global worst case.
Does the activity mean 10,000 panels for every adoption-odds configuration?

No allocation is specified. It says to test 10,000 adversarial panels. That should not be silently expanded into 10,000 panels per configuration or per network setting. If results are broken down by setting, the number contributing to each reported rate should be made clear when the test is carried out.
Would you test the critical values alone or the whole inversion procedure?

Both links matter. The critical values determine the cohort-block bands; the inversion turns those bands and the sensitivity restrictions into sets for the direct and spillover effects. To assess joint effect coverage, the test must carry each panel through the construction being evaluated, not stop after computing a critical value.

Examining the intermediate band event can be useful for interpreting a coverage failure, but it does not replace measuring coverage of the inverted effect sets.
What might it mean if the bands cover their quantities but joint effect coverage fails?

It would call for scrutiny of how inversion translates covered exposure-specific quantities into compatible direct and spillover effects. If the intended inversion retains every allowed configuration whenever those quantities are covered, the joint band event should protect the appropriate effect target. A failure of that implication could indicate a mismatch in targets, constraints, or implementation.

That is a diagnostic possibility, not a claim about what the planned 10,000-panel test will find.
What should the two width measurements represent?

They should represent the widths of the reported direct and spillover bounds or sets after applying the specified band-inversion procedure, with the object named precisely. Report them separately because they concern different contrasts and can behave differently in the same panel.

If the question is whether the bounds are nontrivial, each width needs its own outcome-range benchmark. A width measurement by itself does not tell you whether the corresponding effect bound is narrower than that benchmark.
Could we combine the widths into one number since joint coverage involves both effects?

A combined number would risk concealing a wide spillover bound behind a narrower direct bound, or vice versa. Joint coverage is one event, but the width question still concerns two separately defined effects. Keeping the widths separate makes it possible to assess whether each one is informative.

A supplemental combined measure would not replace the direct and spillover width results specified in the activity.
If a larger critical value improves coverage, should we expect narrower bounds?

No. Widening the bands through a larger critical value may help retain targets, but it can also widen the sets obtained by inversion. That is why the activity measures joint coverage and both widths rather than treating either as a proxy for the others.

The test may reveal a coverage–width tradeoff under the adversarial panels, but its direction or magnitude is not known in advance.
How should this test relate to the proposed independent-cohort, degree-growth, and overlap conditions?

If the purpose is to assess the cohort-block hypothesis under independent cohorts, degree o(n^{1/8}), and overlap ≥0.10, the tested panels and the derived critical values must be matched to precise definitions of those conditions. In particular, the degree measure, what n indexes, the required exposure cells, and the independence assertion need to agree between the derivation and the panel test.

Testing panels described only as adversarial would not, without that alignment, tell us whether the proposed conditions were actually assessed. Nor would agreement within those conditions establish that they are necessary or sharp.
Can a test on 10,000 panels establish uniform ≥95% coverage?

Not by itself. It can estimate joint coverage under the adversarial configurations represented in those panels and compare that measurement with 95%. A uniform guarantee ranges over every configuration in the stated class; if the claim is asymptotic, it additionally concerns its behavior as size grows.

The worst-case critical-value derivation is where a class-wide argument would need to be supplied. The panel test probes the construction rather than replacing that argument.
Should we call the smallest observed joint-coverage rate the worst-case coverage?

Call it the minimum measured joint coverage over the tested configurations, if coverage is estimated separately for those configurations. “Worst-case coverage” without qualification could imply that the minimum over the entire allowed class was found, which the finite test does not show.

If only one pooled rate is calculated across all 10,000 panels, it is a pooled measurement, not a minimum across configurations. The reporting should reflect how the measurement was actually defined.
How do calculation failures enter the joint-coverage and width measurements?

The procedure needs a stated rule for a panel in which a required band or inverted set cannot be calculated. Silently dropping such a panel could change the meaning of the measured joint coverage, while assigning it a narrow width would be misleading. A width should be identified as unavailable if no set is returned, unless the procedure defines an alternative output.

This is a reporting and design issue for the proposed test; it does not assert that calculation failures will occur.
What is the most accurate one-sentence description of the activity?

Derive worst-case cohort-block critical values under the specified Γ=1.5 adoption-odds class, then test the resulting band inversion on 10,000 adversarial panels, measuring joint coverage of the direct and spillover targets and reporting their bound widths separately.
At n=800, cohort-block bands achieved 93.6% joint coverage across 10,000 independent-cohort Γ=1.5 panels, with degree exponent 0.10 and overlap 0.10. How should I report the finding?

Report it as a measurement for that setting: “At n=800, cohort-block bands achieved 93.6% joint coverage across 10,000 independent-cohort Γ=1.5 panels with degree exponent 0.10 and overlap 0.10.” This retains the sample-size index, panel count, construction, and conditions without extending the result beyond the panels examined.
What does “joint coverage” convey here?

It says that coverage was measured for a joint event, rather than reported separately for each quantity. If the event was defined as covering both the direct and spillover targets in the same panel, the 93.6% is the fraction of panels in which both were covered together. The report should name the event if that definition is available; the percentage alone does not give separate coverage rates for the two targets.
Could I say each effect had 93.6% coverage?

No. A joint rate does not identify either marginal rate. When the joint event fails, one target or both could be missed. The stated finding reports 93.6% joint coverage, not effect-specific coverage percentages.
Does “independent-cohort panels” mean every observation within a cohort was independent?

No. Independence across cohorts does not, by itself, imply independence within each cohort. The finding identifies the panels as independent-cohort panels but does not supply a unit-level independence claim. It is best to retain that wording without broadening it.
And does it mean the 10,000 simulation trials were independent of one another?

That is not specified by the phrase. “Independent-cohort” describes a feature of the panels; it does not necessarily describe how the 10,000 trials were generated relative to one another. Keep those two kinds of independence distinct.
How should I read the degree exponent 0.10 at n=800?

It identifies the degree-growth setting used for these panels. It is not a realized degree of 0.10, and the finding does not provide individual degree values. Because this result is reported at n=800, it also cannot, by itself, establish how the bands behave along a growing sequence of panel sizes.
Does overlap 0.10 say that exactly 10% of each panel fell into every relevant exposure cell?

No. An overlap setting of 0.10 should not be recast as an exact realized share in every cell of every panel. If overlap is defined through exposure-cell probabilities, realized cell shares can vary. The finding states the overlap setting, not the cell counts observed in each panel.
Should I write overlap ≥0.10 instead?

The reported finding says overlap 0.10. Unless the measurement was explicitly taken over settings satisfying a floor of at least 0.10, keep “overlap 0.10” in the result sentence. Changing it to “≥0.10” could make a result at one setting sound like a result across a wider set of settings.
What does Γ=1.5 tell the reader about these panels?

It identifies the sensitivity level associated with the reported panel setting. The number does not, on its own, specify the mathematical adoption-odds restriction or the cohort-block critical-value calculation. Those definitions would have to accompany a technical account; the concise measurement can retain the Γ=1.5 label without supplying unstated details.
If the percentage is exact, how many of the 10,000 panels were jointly covered?

If each panel contributes one binary joint-coverage event and 93.6% is exact, the count is 9,360 panels. If the percentage was rounded or calculated through a different aggregation, the exact count cannot be recovered from it alone. Reporting 93.6% across 10,000 panels avoids that ambiguity.
Can I infer an uncertainty interval for the coverage rate just from 93.6% and 10,000?

Not without assumptions about how the trial-level events were generated and related to one another. A particular uncertainty calculation would require a stated simulation design. The finding gives the measured fraction and the number of panels; it does not give an uncertainty interval for an underlying coverage probability.
Does this measurement describe coverage at other values of n?

No. The reported result is at n=800. It supplies no coverage measurements at other sizes, so it does not establish a trend with n or a limiting coverage rate. Those would be different claims from the one-panel-size measurement given here.
Can it establish uniform coverage over every permitted adoption and network configuration?

A measured rate across these 10,000 panels does not, by itself, quantify coverage for every configuration in a broader stated class. The panels show the performance recorded in this specified setting. A class-wide statement would require its own argument about the configurations it covers.
Were the direct and spillover bounds narrow in these panels?

The finding does not report their widths. Joint coverage says whether the specified targets were covered together; it does not determine how wide either bound was. No direct-versus-spillover width comparison can be drawn from the 93.6% figure alone.
Could I infer that the cohort-block critical values were calculated correctly because there is a coverage figure?

The figure shows a measured outcome after applying the cohort-block bands, but it does not document the critical-value derivation or verify each step of the calculation. Describing the bands as cohort-block bands is supported; declaring their calibration correct would require information beyond this finding.
What is the safest compact version for a results table?

“n=800; independent-cohort Γ=1.5 panels; degree exponent 0.10; overlap 0.10; 10,000 trials; cohort-block-band joint coverage 93.6%.” That presents the reported measurement and its conditions without adding unreported effect-specific rates, widths, or results for other settings.
Could we invert finite-sample worst-case tests over independent-cohort Γ-bounded adoption laws, using exposure overlap and bounded drift to obtain narrower direct and spillover intervals?

That is a proposal worth formulating precisely. For each candidate direct or spillover effect, the idea is to test whether it is compatible with the allowed adoption laws and other stated assumptions, calibrating the test against the worst case in that class. Inversion retains candidate effects that the tests do not exclude.

The proposed advantages remain to be established. Finite-sample worst-case calibration could support a uniform coverage claim if the tests genuinely control rejection for every allowed configuration. Exposure overlap and bounded drift are proposed sources of information for narrowing the intervals, but their presence alone does not prove that either interval is narrower than its outcome-range bound.
What does finite-sample change about the coverage claim?

A finite-sample claim applies at each sample size covered by the stated conditions; it does not rely on coverage approaching its target as the sample grows. To obtain confidence-set coverage of at least 95% by test inversion, the relevant tests would need to have rejection probability no greater than 5% under every configuration of the null allowed by the stated class.

That is a requirement for the proposed construction, not a result already supplied by calling a test finite-sample or worst-case.
What is the worst case taken over?

At minimum, it must encompass the independent-cohort adoption laws permitted by the specified Γ bound, including allowed unmeasured adoption confounding. It also has to account for any nuisance features and network-interference configurations relevant to the claimed uniform coverage. The exact set must be stated: “worst-case” has no protective force beyond the configurations actually included in calibration.

For a candidate effect, the test should remain valid even under the allowed configuration most unfavorable to its error control. It should not be calibrated only to a convenient adoption law.
Does Γ refer to a particular value here?

No numerical Γ is specified in this proposal. It refers to a defined bound on the allowed adoption laws. The construction would need to state what aspect of staggered adoption that bound constrains and how to determine whether a law belongs to the class.

The symbol by itself does not define the sensitivity model, supply a test statistic, or guarantee coverage.
Does independent cohorts mean policy adoption is independent for every unit?

No. Independence of cohorts is not the same as independence of units within a cohort. A cohort can retain dependence allowed by the adoption and network assumptions. The proposal needs to specify which cohort-level objects are independent and whether the interference class permits cross-cohort effects that would conflict with the independence used by the test.

Without that compatibility, treating cohort blocks as independent for calibration would be an additional, unjustified assumption.
If the test is calibrated over all Γ-bounded adoption laws, is network interference automatically covered?

No. A restriction on adoption laws describes how policy adoption may occur under bounded confounding. Network interference describes how others’ policy statuses may affect outcomes. Both can affect the distribution of a test statistic and the interpretation of a direct or spillover contrast.

A uniform coverage claim over a confounding and interference class must account for both parts. Taking a worst case over adoption laws alone is insufficient if permitted interference configurations can change the test’s rejection behavior.
How does test inversion produce an interval?

For a specified effect target, consider candidate values across its possible range. Test each candidate under the stated class, and retain those not rejected by the applicable worst-case test. The retained values form an inverted confidence set; if they constitute an interval, its endpoints give the reported interval.

One should not assume the inverted set is an interval merely because an interval is desired. Its shape depends on the test and the effect definition. If an interval is reported from a more complicated retained set, any operation used to turn it into an interval must preserve the intended coverage.
Would we run the same inversion for direct and spillover effects?

The general logic can be shared, but the targets must stay distinct. A direct contrast changes a unit’s own policy status while holding the relevant network exposure fixed. A spillover contrast changes exposure to others’ policy statuses while holding own status fixed. Staggered timing also needs to be specified for each contrast.

Those targets may require different comparisons or different nuisance configurations. Each interval must be justified for its own effect rather than treating an interval for a combined policy contrast as both a direct and a spillover result.
When the null leaves confounding and interference unspecified within their bounds, how should a candidate effect be tested?

The null is then composite: a candidate effect may be compatible with more than one allowed adoption and interference configuration. A valid test must control its rejection probability for every configuration in that composite null. One conceptual route is to calibrate the rejection rule conservatively against the configuration that would make erroneous rejection most likely.

Inversion should exclude a candidate only according to such a valid rule. Excluding it because one selected nuisance configuration fits poorly would not show that the candidate is incompatible with every allowed configuration.
Is finding the worst case in the test just the same as finding the narrowest effect bound?

No. Worst-case test calibration protects against erroneous rejection under allowed laws. Narrowing an effect bound concerns which effect values the assumptions and information can exclude. A conservatively calibrated test may have the desired coverage yet retain a wide range of candidate values.
