The proposal needs separate arguments for error control and for intervals narrower than the outcome-range benchmark. Optimizing for one does not automatically deliver the other.
What is exposure overlap contributing?

It is meant to ensure support for the exposure-specific comparisons needed to distinguish own-policy effects from spillovers. For a direct contrast, relevant own-status values must be supported at the exposure held fixed. For a spillover contrast, relevant exposures must be supported at the own status held fixed. Staggered timing can further define which comparisons are required.

Overlap must be specified for those cells, not asserted generically. It makes comparisons possible, but it does not eliminate Γ-bounded confounding or guarantee that inversion will yield narrow intervals.
Does overlap have to mean a fixed probability floor?

Not necessarily from this proposal. It calls for exposure overlap without specifying a numerical floor or a rate. A formal version must say what probabilities are bounded, for which exposure cells, and whether the condition is required at each relevant time or for a specified aggregate contrast.

Different overlap assumptions can have different implications for finite-sample test calibration and interval width. The proposal does not select one merely by using the word “overlap.”
What is bounded drift supposed to restrict?

That must be defined rather than inferred. “Bounded drift” indicates a limit on how some relevant quantity may change across the comparisons used in the staggered setting, but the proposal does not specify which quantity, the comparisons across which it drifts, or the size of the bound.

Its proposed role is to prevent unconstrained changes from explaining away the effect contrasts. It should not be treated as equivalent to exposure overlap, the Γ bound on adoption laws, or a restriction on network interference. Each assumption needs its own meaning and justification.
If drift is bounded, can I treat outcomes at different adoption times as interchangeable?

No. A bound on drift allows some change, subject to its stated limit; it does not generally set that change to zero. Nor does the phrase alone identify which outcomes or times can be compared.

The effect definitions and tests would need to incorporate the permitted drift. Treating observations at different times as interchangeable without an explicit assumption would impose a stronger condition than “bounded drift.”
Could bounded drift narrow the spillover interval without narrowing the direct interval?

Conceptually, the restrictions and available comparisons might constrain the two contrasts differently. Whether bounded drift helps either interval depends on how it is defined and enters the direct and spillover tests. The proposal does not establish that its contribution is equal for both.

For a claim of narrower direct and spillover intervals, each needs a comparison with its respective outcome-range interval. An improvement for only one would not establish the full proposed narrowing.
Do the intervals need to be narrower in every finite sample for the proposal to succeed?

That is not specified, and it is an important distinction to settle. A population identification bound narrower than an outcome-range bound, an inverted confidence interval that is narrower with high probability, and an interval that is narrower for every possible sample are different claims. Finite-sample coverage alone does not imply any of them.

If the intended statement is about the reported finite-sample intervals, it should say under what conditions and in what sense their widths are smaller. If the intended statement is about underlying partial-identification bounds, that should be established separately from coverage.
How would a uniform 95% argument work in outline?

First define the coverage target—such as the true direct and spillover effect values, or their entire identified sets—and the full allowed confounding and interference class. Then show that, at each sample size covered by the claim, the test of any true candidate has rejection probability at most 5% for every relevant configuration. Inverting those tests would retain the coverage target with probability at least 95% in the stated sense.

If both effects must be covered together, the error control must protect the joint event. Two separately valid 95% inverted sets do not automatically have 95% simultaneous coverage.
Can worst-case tests address joint coverage without assuming the two effect estimates are independent?

Potentially, yes. A joint rejection rule can be calibrated for the combined direct-and-spillover target under the allowed dependence, rather than multiplying separate coverage probabilities or presuming independence. The derivation would have to show the resulting rule controls erroneous rejection across the class.

Independent cohorts do not imply that the two effect targets or their test statistics are independent. The proposal should not rely on that implication unless it is separately established.
Could a test be finite-sample valid but yield only outcome-range intervals?

Yes. It could retain every candidate value that the outcome range permits while still making no erroneous exclusions. That would satisfy coverage but not the proposed informative narrowing.

Exposure overlap and bounded drift are intended to make narrower intervals possible, yet a proof must demonstrate that they actually exclude some outcome-range-compatible values for each specified contrast under the Γ-bounded adoption and interference class.
What would prevent us from claiming a worst-case guarantee over a class broader than independent cohorts?

The calibration would be justified only for the class it actually handles. If its finite-sample argument uses independence across cohorts, it cannot automatically extend to laws with dependence across those cohorts. Likewise, a restriction on adoption odds cannot silently stand in for unrestricted network interference.

The stated guarantee should match the adoption, cohort, drift, overlap, and interference assumptions used in the test. Broader coverage would require a broader argument.
Is this proposal a claim that finite-sample tests have already resolved the degree-growth issue?

No. The proposal specifies a different route—finite-sample worst-case tests over independent-cohort Γ-bounded adoption laws, with exposure overlap and bounded drift—but does not state a degree-growth threshold or prove that network dependence is handled. Any graph restrictions needed for the finite-sample test would have to be specified and justified.

It would be premature to present the proposed inversion as an established solution to every network or overlap-rate question.
How can I phrase the proposal compactly without promising narrower intervals or 95% coverage prematurely?

“Develop finite-sample tests calibrated against the worst case over independent-cohort, Γ-bounded adoption laws, then invert them for separately defined direct and spillover effects. Assess whether exposure overlap and bounded drift yield intervals narrower than outcome-range bounds and whether the inverted sets attain at least 95% coverage uniformly over the stated confounding and interference class.”

I plan to impose exposure overlap and bounded drift, invert worst-case Γ=1.5 cohort-adoption tests, and then prove narrowing for direct and spillover effects and uniform 95% coverage. Does that sequence keep the identification and inference tasks distinct?

Yes. Exposure overlap and bounded drift are proposed assumptions for making the effect comparisons informative. Inverting worst-case Γ=1.5 cohort-adoption tests is the proposed way to construct sets of compatible effect values. The final step has two separate proof obligations: show that the direct and spillover bounds are narrower than their respective outcome-range bounds, and show that the confidence sets achieve at least 95% coverage uniformly over the stated confounding and interference class.

It is a plan, not a claim that either proof has been completed. In particular, coverage of an inverted set would not by itself establish that its bound is informative.
What should exposure overlap mean in the plan?

It should mean support for the exposure-specific comparisons used to define the target effects. A direct-effect comparison needs relevant own-policy statuses at a fixed network exposure; a spillover comparison needs relevant network exposures at a fixed own-policy status. Because adoption is staggered, the definition also needs to say which timing comparisons are relevant.

The plan does not specify an overlap rate or numerical floor. Imposing overlap therefore requires a precise statement of the required cells and their support, without assuming that a general assertion of overlap covers every contrast.
Can overlap alone distinguish a direct effect from a spillover effect?

No. Overlap helps ensure that the comparisons needed for separately defined effects have support. The distinction itself comes from the effect definitions: vary own status while holding relevant network exposure fixed for a direct effect, and vary exposure while holding own status fixed for a spillover effect.

The permitted interference and adoption-confounding classes also matter. If their definitions allow the proposed comparisons to mix changes in own status and exposure without a way to separate them, overlap alone will not disentangle the effects.
What does bounded drift add that overlap does not?

Overlap concerns whether the relevant comparisons are supported. Bounded drift restricts how much a specified quantity may change across comparisons relevant to the staggered setting. In the plan, that restriction is intended to keep unconstrained changes from accounting for every observed difference.

The quantity whose drift is bounded, the comparisons across which it may drift, and the bound itself still need to be defined. The phrase does not imply zero drift, and it cannot be used as an unspecified substitute for an interference assumption or for the Γ=1.5 adoption restriction.
If drift is bounded rather than eliminated, do the inverted tests need to allow for its full permitted range?

Yes. A worst-case claim must retain configurations allowed by every assumption it invokes, including any permitted drift. Testing a candidate effect as if drift were zero would impose a stronger assumption than bounded drift unless zero drift is the bound actually stated.

The effect value should be rejected only according to a test whose calibration accounts for the allowed nuisance configurations relevant to that candidate. Otherwise inversion could produce a narrow set by excluding values the plan’s assumptions still permit.
How does Γ=1.5 enter the cohort-adoption tests?

It fixes the sensitivity level for the adoption laws considered by the planned tests. The tests are to be calibrated against the worst case among the cohort-adoption configurations allowed at Γ=1.5, rather than against one selected, favorable adoption configuration.

The numerical value alone does not define the adoption-odds restriction or the test. Those must be specified before one can determine what the worst case is and whether the inverted sets have the asserted properties.
Do cohort-adoption tests automatically assume cohorts are independent?

Not from that label alone. The plan calls them cohort-adoption tests, but their validity depends on whatever cohort structure and dependence assumptions are explicitly stated. If a calibration relies on independence across cohorts, that assumption must be stated and made compatible with the permitted network interference; independence within cohorts would not follow merely from independence across them.

A coverage claim should extend only to the cohort-adoption and interference class that the test’s calibration actually handles.
What is being inverted: the worst-case adoption laws or the tests?

The tests are inverted. For each candidate value of a direct or spillover effect, the planned test asks whether that value can be rejected while allowing the worst-case adoption configurations within the stated Γ=1.5 class. The inverted set retains candidate values that are not rejected.

The adoption laws are part of what the tests account for; they are not themselves effect intervals. Inversion translates valid testing rules into a set of retained effect values.
Could we test an effect value using just one adoption law consistent with Γ=1.5?

That would not establish the proposed worst-case property. An effect value could be compatible with another adoption law allowed at Γ=1.5, even if it looks implausible under the single law chosen for the test. A uniform error guarantee requires calibration for the full relevant class, not a selected member.

This point also applies to nuisance configurations allowed by bounded drift and network interference. The precise class must be stated before a worst-case test can be judged valid.
Does worst-case calibration mean that every inverted interval will be as wide as the outcome-range bound?

Not necessarily. Worst-case calibration protects the inference claim across allowed configurations, while overlap and bounded drift are intended to supply restrictions that may still exclude some effect values. Whether the resulting direct and spillover bounds actually narrow is exactly what the plan says to prove.

A conservative test might retain the full outcome-range bound; it might also yield an informative set under sufficient restrictions. Neither conclusion follows merely from the words “worst-case.”
Why do we need a separate narrowing proof after inversion?

A test can be valid yet lack power to exclude any effect value allowed by the outcome range. Inverting it would then yield a valid but uninformative confidence set. A narrowing proof must connect the specified overlap and drift assumptions, together with the allowed Γ=1.5 adoption and interference classes, to a strict reduction in compatible values for each target.

It should make the comparison explicit: a direct bound versus its outcome-range bound, and a spillover bound versus its own outcome-range bound. Improving only one does not prove the two-part claim.
Is the narrowing claim necessarily about the random confidence intervals?

That needs to be stated. Narrower population identification bounds, narrower realized inverted confidence sets, and a high-probability claim about confidence-set widths are distinct. The plan calls for proving direct and spillover narrowing, so the proof must identify which bounds are being compared with outcome-range bounds and in what sense they are narrower.

It should not use the coverage theorem as if that settled width, or use a particularly narrow realized set as if that established population partial identification.
Should the direct and spillover tests be separate?

Their target contrasts must be separate, whether they are implemented as two tests or as parts of a joint test. A direct contrast varies own policy status at a fixed relevant exposure, while a spillover contrast varies network exposure at a fixed own status. Both must account for the specified staggered timing.

If the intended confidence claim covers both effects simultaneously, separate tests each calibrated to 95% do not automatically deliver 95% joint coverage. The testing and inversion argument must protect the actual coverage event being claimed.
What does uniform 95% coverage require beyond a test that seems conservative at Γ=1.5?

It requires a coverage statement for the specified target across every configuration in the stated confounding and interference class, at the stated Γ=1.5 sensitivity level and under the other imposed assumptions. Equivalently, the lowest coverage probability across that class must meet the 95% threshold in the sense claimed.

Calling a test conservative, or checking selected configurations, does not supply that statement. The proof must show that a true target is retained by inversion with the required probability even under the allowed configuration least favorable to coverage.
Does the plan specify whether that uniform 95% claim is finite-sample or asymptotic?

The plan itself says to prove uniform 95% coverage, without specifying finite-sample or asymptotic coverage. That choice should be made explicit. A finite-sample guarantee applies at each covered sample size; a uniform asymptotic guarantee concerns the worst-case limiting behavior over the stated class. They are not interchangeable.

The proof should name the intended coverage target as well—such as true direct and spillover effect values or their entire identified sets—because those are different guarantees.
If we seek joint coverage of both effects, what should the proof show at the testing stage?

It should show that the procedure does not wrongly exclude the stated pair of targets with probability exceeding 5% under any allowed configuration, in the finite-sample or asymptotic sense selected. Then it must show that inversion retains both targets whenever the event protected by the tests occurs.

If the target is instead joint coverage of two entire identified sets, the argument must protect that stronger event. Merely having a 95% guarantee for each effect considered in isolation does not establish either joint claim.
Can the worst-case tests be proved valid over the Γ=1.5 adoption laws while leaving the interference class unrestricted?

That would depend on what the tests and outcomes are allowed to depend on; it cannot be assumed. Adoption confounding and network interference are distinct sources of variation. If the interference class permits configurations that alter the test statistic or the meaning of exposure-specific contrasts, calibration over adoption laws alone may not protect coverage.

The planned uniform proof needs to specify the interference class it covers and justify validity under that class as well as under the Γ=1.5 cohort-adoption laws.
What if bounded drift is imposed only for direct-effect comparisons?

Then its stated restriction would apply only there. It could not be invoked without further justification to narrow a spillover bound. To prove narrowing for both targets, the assumptions used for each must genuinely constrain that target’s compatible effect values.

The plan need not force identical assumptions to do identical work for direct and spillover effects. It does require clarity about which restrictions support each conclusion.
Would exposure overlap at some times suffice for a claim across all staggered adoption times?

Not automatically. Support for one timing contrast does not establish support for every timing contrast that might enter a broader target. The overlap assumption must match the direct and spillover effects actually being bounded, including the timing features those definitions use.

A narrower result for specified supported contrasts may be possible, but it should not be extended to unsupported times or exposure cells without an assumption and argument that cover them.
What should happen if the inverted set is not an interval?

The result of inversion should first be described as a set of retained candidate values. If a direct or spillover interval is required, the method for obtaining one from that set must be stated, and the coverage argument must remain valid for the reported interval.

An interval that contains the whole inverted set could preserve coverage, though it might be wider. One cannot simply discard retained values to make an interval look narrower and still assume the original coverage claim holds.
Could the uniform coverage proof be completed before proving any narrowing?

Conceptually, yes. Coverage concerns error control of the tests and the inversion; narrowing concerns how restrictive the compatible effect sets are relative to outcome-range bounds. The plan says to invert the tests and then prove both properties, but it does not require one proof to establish the other.

A completed coverage argument would still leave the informative-partial-identification claim open until strict narrowing is shown separately for direct and spillover effects.
If narrowing requires extra assumptions beyond overlap and bounded drift, should those be left implicit in the test definition?

No. Any additional assumption needed to exclude outcome-range-compatible values should be stated, with its scope and its role in the direct or spillover argument. Otherwise the proof would appear to obtain narrowing from overlap and bounded drift alone when it actually relies on something else.

The same principle applies to uniform coverage: any cohort, network, or adoption-law restriction used in calibration belongs in the stated class of the conclusion.
How would you summarize the plan without making it sound like the Γ=1.5 tests already have the desired properties?

Impose precisely defined exposure overlap and bounded drift; construct and invert tests calibrated for the worst case over the specified Γ=1.5 cohort-adoption and interference class; then prove, separately, that the resulting direct and spillover bounds narrow their respective outcome-range bounds and that the stated confidence target has at least 95% coverage uniformly over that class. Those are the intended steps and proof obligations, not completed results.
I want to extend StaggerNetSim v1 with worst-case cohort-law enumeration and invert joint Γ=1.5 tests across its overlap and degree grids. What exactly would that activity involve?

The extension would add a way to enumerate the cohort-adoption laws considered in the worst-case calculation. At each setting in StaggerNetSim v1’s overlap and degree grids, the joint Γ=1.5 tests would then be evaluated against the relevant laws and inverted to retain effect values the tests do not reject.

That describes work to do, not an extension that is already complete. Its interpretation depends on specifying the allowed cohort-law class, what the enumeration covers, and which direct and spillover targets are tested jointly.
Why add cohort-law enumeration rather than just use one challenging adoption law?

A single challenging law does not establish that a test is calibrated for the worst case among the allowed laws. Enumeration is intended to make the search over cohort-adoption laws explicit, so the test is not assessed only under a selected configuration.

The word “worst-case” still needs justification. The extension must say whether its enumeration covers the full relevant class or only a specified collection of laws. A minimum or maximum over an incomplete collection is worst-case only within that collection.
Does enumeration necessarily mean that all Γ=1.5-bounded cohort laws can be listed?

No. Whether full enumeration is possible depends on how the cohort laws and the Γ=1.5 restriction are defined. If the permitted class cannot be exhaustively listed, the activity would need to say how its enumeration represents or bounds that class before using it for a worst-case claim.

Merely naming an enumeration routine would not show that an unlisted allowed law cannot be less favorable for the joint tests.
What has to be fixed before an adoption law counts as Γ=1.5-bounded?

The sensitivity restriction must define which features of cohort adoption are bounded and how Γ=1.5 limits them. The relevant cohort and staggered-adoption structure must also be specified. Only then can the extension decide whether a candidate law is permitted.

Γ=1.5 is the stated sensitivity level; it is not itself a complete definition of a law or a rule for finding the worst case.
Is a cohort law the same thing as a network-interference configuration?

No. A cohort-adoption law concerns how policy adoption occurs. A network-interference configuration concerns how others’ policy statuses can affect outcomes. The proposed enumeration is specifically of cohort laws.

If the joint tests claim validity across an interference class as well, their calibration must account for that class separately or show why the law enumeration suffices for the relevant test distribution. It should not silently equate bounded adoption confounding with bounded spillovers.
What makes the Γ=1.5 tests joint?

The tests should be defined for the combined coverage claim they are intended to support, rather than treating direct and spillover effects as unrelated marginal tests. For example, a candidate pair of direct and spillover values can be considered together, with a rejection rule calibrated for the event of wrongly excluding that pair.

That is a conceptual interpretation, not a specified test formula. The extension must define the joint null and its rejection rule before inversion can have a precise meaning. Separate tests that each have a nominal coverage statement do not automatically yield the same joint coverage statement.
What does inverting a joint test retain?

It retains candidate direct-and-spillover effect values that the joint test does not reject under its stated calibration. If candidates are tested as pairs, the immediate output is a joint set of pairs. Separate direct or spillover intervals can then be discussed only after specifying how they are obtained from that joint set.

The output should not be assumed to be two intervals, or to be narrow, simply because the test has been inverted.
Could the extension produce separate direct and spillover bounds from that joint set?

Conceptually, yes. The values appearing in the direct coordinate give a direct-effect set, and those appearing in the spillover coordinate give a spillover-effect set. If intervals are reported, any step used to turn those sets into intervals should be stated.

The joint set and its separate summaries answer related but different questions. A pair may be excluded jointly even when each coordinate appears in some other retained pair, so separate summaries do not preserve all the information in the joint set.
Why run the inversion across both the overlap and degree grids?

Those grids organize settings with different exposure-cell support and network degree. Applying the same clearly defined testing and inversion procedure at their settings would let the extension examine how its outputs behave across those dimensions.

The grid does not, on its own, establish what happens between settings or for every network in a broader class. Nor does a favorable setting establish that the procedure works at all other grid settings.
Should “across the grids” mean every possible combination of their settings?

That needs to be made explicit when the activity is carried out. If every combination is included, the description can say so; if only selected combinations are used, the reported domain should reflect that selection. The current activity says to invert tests across the overlap and degree grids but does not specify an allocation or enumerate the settings.

It would be misleading to claim full grid coverage before defining which combinations were actually evaluated.
Do the exposure cells need to be the same in the overlap grid and in the joint tests?

They need consistent definitions. The overlap setting should describe support for the exposure cells required by the direct and spillover contrasts in the joint test. Otherwise an overlap label could look adequate while leaving a needed contrast unsupported.

Staggered timing may also enter an exposure-cell definition. The extension should use compatible definitions throughout its cohort-law enumeration, tests, and inversion without assuming that a generic overlap label settles the issue.
And which degree is represented by the degree grid?

The activity does not identify a degree measure. To interpret results from the grid, the extension would need to say which network quantity varies with its degree settings and how that quantity relates to any dependence assumption used in the joint tests.

A degree setting should not be described as maximum degree, a dependency-graph degree, or a proven growth condition unless those definitions are actually supplied.
Should the worst-case cohort law be chosen once for the entire grid?

Not without an argument that one law is worst for every setting and every candidate tested. Which permitted law is least favorable could depend on the grid setting, the candidate effect values, and the joint rejection rule.

The activity can describe enumeration at each relevant test and setting without asserting that the same law always governs. Conversely, if a single law is used, the grounds for calling it worst-case across the claimed scope must be shown.
Could I select the law that gives the narrowest inverted set and call that worst-case?

Not automatically. A narrow set is not the criterion for protecting coverage. A worst-case test calibration must address the allowed law most unfavorable to its error control under the stated null. Choosing a law because it makes inversion narrow could exclude effect values compatible with other permitted laws.

The extension should distinguish the operation used to control rejection from any subsequent assessment of the resulting set’s width.
How should bounded drift enter, given that the immediate activity names enumeration and inversion?

If bounded drift is among the assumptions under which the joint tests or effect contrasts are defined, its permitted values must be respected during testing and inversion. It should not be set to zero by default or excluded from the compatible configurations simply to obtain narrower sets.

The current activity does not specify a drift bound or an implementation for it. Its role must be defined before claiming that the extension tests a class with bounded drift.
Would running a test at every grid setting prove uniform 95% coverage?

No. Grid evaluations can show how a procedure behaves at the settings and laws actually examined. Uniform 95% coverage requires a guarantee across the entire stated confounding and interference class, for the specified joint coverage target and in the stated finite-sample or asymptotic sense.

An exhaustive and justified worst-case calculation might form part of such an argument, but running inversions across a grid is not, by itself, a coverage proof.
If the enumeration really is exhaustive, is the coverage proof automatic?

Still no. Exhaustiveness would address which adoption laws are considered. The joint tests would also need a valid error-control argument under those laws and any permitted interference, and the inversion would need to retain the true target whenever the protected test event occurs.

Enumeration can close one potential gap in a worst-case claim; it cannot replace the testing and inversion arguments.
How do I tell whether the inversion is being applied consistently across settings?

The effect targets, joint rejection rule, interpretation of Γ=1.5, and rules for handling allowed nuisance configurations should be stated in a way that remains consistent as the overlap and degree settings change. Then any differences in retained sets can be interpreted against the specified settings rather than an unnoticed change in what is being tested.

Consistency does not require identical outputs. It requires that the meaning of a candidate direct or spillover value and the criterion for retaining it are clear at each setting.
What if a test has no candidate pairs left after inversion at a grid setting?

An empty inverted set should not be described as an especially informative effect bound. It would prompt a check of the test definition, the enumerated laws, and whether the stated assumptions and inputs admit the coverage target. If the procedure is meant to cover a true pair, it needs an error-control argument that addresses when that pair could be excluded.

This is a possible interpretive issue, not a finding that an empty set occurs in StaggerNetSim v1 or its proposed extension.
Could the inversion return the full outcome-range set at some settings?

It could. A valid joint test might fail to exclude any outcome-range-compatible candidate under the restrictions and information available at a setting. That would leave an uninformative bound there, not necessarily an invalid test.

To claim informative direct and spillover bounds, each separately reported bound would need to be compared with its corresponding outcome-range benchmark. The act of inversion alone does not guarantee strict narrowing.
Should I call any resulting coverage numbers estimates?

If they are measured from the panels in StaggerNetSim v1 or its extension, yes: they are coverage estimates for the specified tested settings and coverage event. The word “worst-case” should identify precisely which cohort-law configurations were considered; it should not turn panel-based estimates into exact probabilities or a class-wide guarantee.

If a separate mathematical argument establishes a guarantee, that can be stated separately from the simulated estimates.
Does extending StaggerNetSim v1 imply replacing its existing coverage estimates or width tables?

No replacement is stated. The activity is to extend StaggerNetSim v1 with cohort-law enumeration and to invert joint Γ=1.5 tests across its existing overlap and degree grids. It does not say that any existing entry is deleted or that new test outputs have already been calculated.

The extension should be described by what it is meant to add and assess, without inferring unreported changes to the artifact.
Can you give me a concise description of the activity and its main limitation?

“Extend StaggerNetSim v1 with enumeration of the cohort-adoption laws used for worst-case calibration, then invert joint Γ=1.5 tests across its overlap and degree grids.” The scope of any worst-case or coverage conclusion will depend on which laws and interference configurations the enumeration and tests actually cover; performing the grid activity alone will not establish uniform 95% coverage or narrower direct and spillover bounds.
StaggerNetSim v2 adds worst-case cohort-law test inversion, separate direct and spillover confidence sets, and coverage tables by degree and overlap. How should I describe what the artifact provides?

Describe it as an artifact with three added components: worst-case cohort-law test inversion, separate confidence sets for direct and spillover effects, and coverage tables organized by degree and overlap. That conveys what is present without claiming that the tables establish uniform coverage or that the confidence sets are narrower than outcome-range bounds.
What does “test inversion” mean for someone reading the description?

In general, test inversion considers candidate effect values and retains those not rejected by the specified tests. The retained values form a confidence set under the testing procedure’s stated conditions. Here, the label says the inversion uses tests characterized as worst-case over cohort laws.

The artifact description does not specify the test statistics, rejection rules, or class of cohort laws. Those details would be needed to evaluate precisely what the inversion guarantees.
Does “worst-case cohort-law” mean the tests were calibrated for every adoption law we might imagine?

No. A worst-case claim has meaning only relative to a defined class of cohort laws. The description identifies the form of the test inversion but does not specify the full class or show that it includes every conceivable adoption law. It would be more accurate to ask what laws the artifact treats as admissible before interpreting “worst-case” as a broad guarantee.
Can I say v2 contains an exhaustive worst-case calculation?

Not from this description alone. It says v2 adds worst-case cohort-law test inversion, but it does not state that the search over laws is exhaustive or provide a proof that the reported worst case is global over a specified class. If exhaustiveness is important to a claim, it needs its own documentation rather than being inferred from the label.
Why is it important that the direct and spillover confidence sets are separate?

They correspond to different effect targets. A direct effect concerns changing a unit’s own policy status at a fixed relevant network exposure; a spillover effect concerns changing network exposure while holding own status fixed. Separate confidence sets make it possible to read the uncertainty associated with each target rather than treating a combined policy contrast as though it resolved both components.

Their separation does not imply that the two sets are independent or that each has a particular coverage rate.
Does the description say there is also a joint confidence set for the pair of effects?

No. It specifically says v2 adds separate direct and spillover confidence sets. One should not infer the presence of a reported joint set from that statement. Nor should one infer simultaneous coverage of both sets merely because they are presented together; that requires a defined joint event and appropriate calibration.
Could both sets individually have a coverage claim while their joint coverage is lower?

Yes, in general. Separate marginal coverage statements do not automatically give the same coverage level for the event that both targets are covered at once. The coverage tables would need to identify the event they measure before one could interpret their entries as marginal coverage for one set, joint coverage for both, or something else.

The artifact’s short description establishes that coverage tables exist, not which of those events their entries represent.
What does organizing coverage tables by degree and overlap add?

It makes degree and overlap the dimensions along which coverage entries can be consulted or compared. That organization is relevant because network dependence and support for exposure-specific comparisons may vary across settings. But the existence of the tables does not tell us their numerical entries, the direction of any pattern, or what happens between the reported settings.
Does the degree label necessarily mean maximum network degree?

No. The description does not define the degree quantity. A table organized by degree might use a particular network-degree measure, but its meaning must be read from the artifact’s definitions. It should not be called a maximum-degree table, or connected to a particular growth-rate condition, without that information.
And does overlap necessarily mean a minimum probability in each exposure cell?

Not solely from the artifact description. Exposure-cell overlap is a natural interpretation in this setting, but to understand a table entry one needs the precise overlap measure, the exposure cells to which it applies, and whether it represents a probability condition or something measured in a realized panel. The description supplies the organizing dimension, not its full definition.
Could I read the coverage tables as a coverage theorem indexed by degree and overlap?

No. Tables may contain coverage measurements or calculations at their reported settings; their presence is not a theorem that a confidence procedure covers uniformly across all admissible adoption and interference configurations. A theoretical guarantee requires a stated target, class, and error-control argument. It should be presented separately from whatever the table entries report.
What should I check before interpreting a particular coverage entry?

Check which confidence set or joint event it concerns, how coverage is defined, which degree and overlap setting labels the entry, and what cohort-law and interference conditions apply. If the entry is a simulation estimate, its denominator and the scope of the simulated configurations also matter.

Those are questions for reading the artifact. The short statement that v2 contains coverage tables does not supply their answers or any particular coverage percentage.
Does adding confidence sets mean that the direct and spillover effects are point identified?

No. A confidence set can reflect sampling uncertainty, partial identification, or both. Reporting separate sets does not imply that either effect is a single point. The sets’ definitions and shapes would need to be examined before making any identification claim.
Can I call the confidence sets “bounds”?

Only with care. A reported confidence set consists of effect values retained by an inference procedure. An identification bound describes effect values compatible with assumptions and population information. They may be related through inversion, but they are not interchangeable concepts.

The artifact explicitly lists separate confidence sets, so that is the clearest term for what v2 adds. If the sets are summarized by intervals, their endpoints can be described as confidence-set limits under the artifact’s definitions.
Do the confidence sets have to be intervals?

Not necessarily. Inverting tests produces retained sets, which need not be intervals without further structure or an explicit reporting rule. The description calls them confidence sets, not intervals. It would be premature to assume a particular shape, or to describe an interval-making step that is not stated.
Could I say the sets are nontrivial because v2 includes worst-case inversion?

No. Worst-case calibration and informativeness are distinct. A valid inversion might retain every value in an outcome-range bound; a narrower-looking set might still require a coverage justification. To claim that both effects have nontrivial bounds, compare each relevant set or underlying identification bound with its corresponding outcome-range benchmark under clearly stated conditions.

The listed additions do not themselves report such comparisons.
Does a narrow direct set tell us anything definite about the spillover set?

Not from the artifact description. The targets use different contrasts, and their confidence sets are listed separately for that reason. One set’s width, even if known, would not determine the other’s width or coverage. No widths are specified in the statement about v2.
How should I avoid overstating “worst-case” when citing v2?

Use it as part of the artifact’s method description: “worst-case cohort-law test inversion.” If making a substantive claim about worst-case validity, identify the permitted cohort laws, other nuisance configurations included, and the precise coverage event. Do not treat the label as proof of error control over a wider, unstated class.
Does v2 itself establish at least 95% confidence-set coverage uniformly?

The description does not say so. It lists confidence sets and coverage tables, but gives neither a coverage percentage nor a uniform-coverage proof. Even favorable table entries at reported degree and overlap settings would have a different scope from an at-least-95% guarantee for every configuration in a stated confounding and interference class.
Would it be fair to say v2 makes it possible to inspect coverage by degree and overlap?

Yes. That follows directly from the presence of coverage tables by degree and overlap. The statement should stop at the ability to inspect the reported entries; it should not infer a favorable trend, a threshold, or a guarantee without the entries and an argument supporting that interpretation.
Can I name a Γ value when giving a one-line description of v2?

The stated description of StaggerNetSim v2 does not attach a numerical Γ value to its added components. For a one-line description faithful to that statement, you can leave it at “worst-case cohort-law test inversion.” If you want to characterize a particular table or confidence set by a Γ value, verify that the artifact explicitly defines it for that output.
What is a concise description that includes every listed addition and no claimed result?

“StaggerNetSim v2 adds worst-case cohort-law test inversion, separate confidence sets for direct and spillover effects, and coverage tables organized by degree and overlap.” That identifies the artifact and its contents without claiming a particular coverage rate, uniform validity, or narrowed effect bounds.

I want to benchmark StaggerNetSim v2 against exhaustive four-cohort Γ=1.5 law enumeration, auditing inversion correctness, joint coverage, and direct and spillover widths. What should this activity establish?

It should assess three distinct things within the four-cohort Γ=1.5 benchmark. First, does StaggerNetSim v2’s test inversion retain and exclude candidate effect values as the specified tests require? Second, what joint coverage does the resulting procedure exhibit under the enumerated laws? Third, how wide are the direct and spillover sets, considered separately?

Those are questions for the benchmark, not findings already established by it. Even exhaustive enumeration within a four-cohort class would not, without another argument, establish coverage for different cohort structures or a broader confounding and interference class.
What does “exhaustive” need to mean in this benchmark?

It must mean exhaustive relative to a precisely defined set of admissible four-cohort adoption laws at Γ=1.5. The benchmark needs to specify what constitutes a distinct law and show that every law in that defined set is included or otherwise accounted for. Exhaustive enumeration of a restricted list would be exhaustive only for that list.

The word does not imply enumeration of all imaginable adoption mechanisms or all possible network-interference patterns. Those would require their own definitions and, if relevant to the claimed benchmark, their own coverage in the comparison.
Does “four-cohort” tell us how many units or time periods there are?

No. It specifies four cohorts, not a number of units per cohort, a total panel size, or a number of periods. Those details should not be inferred from the benchmark label. Any additional structure necessary to enumerate laws or calculate coverage would have to be stated as part of the benchmark definition.
Is Γ=1.5 just a label attached to the enumeration?

It is the specified sensitivity level for the laws being enumerated, but it does not define the restriction by itself. The benchmark must say what it means for a four-cohort adoption law to be Γ=1.5-bounded and make sure that both the enumeration and StaggerNetSim v2’s tested procedure use that same definition. Otherwise an apparent agreement or disagreement might compare different admissible-law classes.
What exactly are we comparing StaggerNetSim v2 with?

The reference is the result of exhaustive enumeration over the defined four-cohort Γ=1.5 laws. For a given candidate effect value and stated test, the benchmark can determine what the test’s worst-case calculation and consequent inversion require within that enumerated class, then compare that with StaggerNetSim v2’s output under the same definitions.

The comparison requires matching effect targets, admissibility constraints, rejection rule, and any nuisance or interference assumptions. It does not assume in advance that either output agrees with the other.
What should inversion correctness mean here, rather than just having a set of values returned?

It should mean that each candidate value is retained or excluded according to the specified joint testing rule when the relevant four-cohort Γ=1.5 laws are taken into account. One check is whether StaggerNetSim v2 omits any value that the benchmark says the rule should retain; another is whether it retains values that the benchmark says the rule should reject.

The meaning of a discrepancy depends on the stated rule. In particular, a visually narrow confidence set is not evidence of correct inversion if it achieves that width by wrongly excluding compatible candidates.
Would finding the most unfavorable law for one candidate suffice for the entire inversion?

Not necessarily. The law that is most unfavorable to a test may differ across candidate effect values or across the settings at which the procedure is applied. To audit the inversion, the exhaustive reference must address the relevant worst-case calculation for each candidate under its specified null, rather than assume that one selected law governs every test.

If a common worst-case law can be justified, that would be a conclusion from the defined problem, not an assumption supplied by the term “worst-case.”
Should we benchmark the direct and spillover sets against separate enumerations?

They can use the same defined admissible-law class, but their targets and reported sets should remain distinct. A direct effect varies own policy status at fixed relevant network exposure; a spillover effect varies exposure while holding own status fixed. Their candidate values may interact in a joint test, so the audit should make clear how the joint inversion produces each reported set.

There is no need to assume two unrelated law classes or that correctness for one set automatically implies correctness for the other.
If the test is joint, why does v2 report separate confidence sets?

A joint inversion can be summarized through separate direct and spillover sets, but a summary of each coordinate does not, on its own, describe which pairs of effect values are jointly retained. The benchmark should distinguish correctness of the joint testing and inversion rule from correctness of the two separate reported sets.

It should also define joint coverage directly. Separate sets appearing in the same artifact do not automatically provide a particular simultaneous coverage level.
What counts as joint coverage for the audit?

If the intended targets are true direct and spillover effects, joint coverage is the event that both lie in their reported confidence sets under the same realization. If instead the requirement concerns covering entire identified sets, that is a different, stronger event. The benchmark should name which event it evaluates and retain that definition across the enumerated laws.

A pair of marginal coverage calculations would not replace a calculation of the joint event.
Can exhaustive law enumeration give exact joint coverage?

Only if the enumerated laws, the sampling outcomes relevant to the procedure, and their probabilities are sufficiently specified for an exact calculation. Exhaustively listing admissible adoption laws alone does not automatically enumerate every random outcome or every permitted interference configuration needed to calculate coverage.

The benchmark should distinguish exact calculations, if available, from coverage estimated using simulated realizations. Neither should be described as exact solely because the law list is exhaustive.
Does the benchmark have to look at the lowest joint coverage over the enumerated laws?

That is particularly pertinent if the purpose is to audit a worst-case coverage claim. A pooled or average rate could mask a law with poorer joint coverage. The minimum should be labeled by its actual scope: the lowest coverage over the specified four-cohort Γ=1.5 laws under the other conditions used in the benchmark.

It should not be called the minimum over an unrestricted interference class unless that class was also fully included in the assessment.
Would inversion correctness alone guarantee that joint coverage reaches 95%?

No. Correct inversion means that StaggerNetSim v2 faithfully applies the stated tests. Coverage depends additionally on whether those tests control erroneous rejection for the joint target under every relevant allowed law and interference configuration. The benchmark might find an inversion implemented correctly while the underlying testing rule does not attain its coverage target.

Conversely, an observed joint coverage rate alone would not demonstrate that every candidate was inverted correctly. Those are separate audit questions.
And if coverage looks adequate, does that prove the direct and spillover sets are informative?

No. A procedure can cover both targets and still return very broad sets. The width audit should report direct and spillover widths separately and, when assessing whether they are nontrivial, compare each with its appropriate outcome-range benchmark. Joint coverage and effect-specific width measure different properties.
Does the activity already say what the widths are or which one is smaller?

No. It asks for an audit of direct and spillover widths; it reports no width values or comparison between them. It would be premature to infer a narrowing result, or to say which target has the tighter set, from the benchmark plan.
Should widths be measured for each enumerated law or only for a pooled output?

The measurement scheme should match the question being asked. If widths vary by law or realization, reporting their distribution or their law-specific behavior can reveal features a pooled figure conceals. If a single width summary is used, its aggregation and reference range should be stated.

The activity itself specifies an audit of both widths but not a particular summary. It does not authorize inventing a width statistic or a numerical result.
Could a mismatch arise because the enumeration and v2 define exposure differently?

Yes, that is a possible comparability issue to check, not a finding. The exposure mapping, staggered timing contrasts, admissible cohort laws, Γ=1.5 restriction, and test rule need to agree between the reference calculation and StaggerNetSim v2. Otherwise different outputs would not necessarily indicate incorrect inversion: they might represent different targets or classes.

Conversely, apparent agreement is meaningful only when those definitions match.
What role does network interference play if we are exhaustively enumerating adoption laws?

An adoption-law enumeration addresses which adoption processes are allowed; it does not by itself specify how network exposure affects outcomes. The direct and spillover targets, and potentially the tests’ coverage, still depend on the stated interference assumptions. The benchmark should either include the relevant allowed interference configurations or clearly limit its conclusion to those it assesses.

It should not use “exhaustive four-cohort laws” as shorthand for exhaustive coverage of adoption, outcomes, and interference all at once.
Would the benchmark establish a finite-sample 95% theorem if its minimum coverage clears 95%?

Not automatically. That depends on whether the coverage calculation is exact, whether the four-cohort Γ=1.5 law enumeration and all other relevant configurations are exhaustive for the stated claim, and whether the theorem is restricted to precisely that finite-sample class. If joint coverage is estimated from trials, an estimate above 95% is not itself an exact guarantee.

Even an exact four-cohort result would not, by itself, imply the same guarantee for other cohort counts or all network structures.
Should we include a check of what happens when no candidates are retained?

Yes, if that outcome is possible under the defined rule. The audit should specify how an empty returned set is treated in the joint-coverage calculation and width reporting; it should not be counted as a very narrow, favorable interval without accounting for whether the target was excluded.

That is a possible audit check, not a statement that StaggerNetSim v2 actually returns an empty set.
Can we describe the benchmark without suggesting we already know whether v2 passes it?

“Benchmark StaggerNetSim v2 against exhaustive enumeration of the specified four-cohort Γ=1.5 adoption laws, checking correctness of joint-test inversion, joint coverage of the stated targets, and separate direct- and spillover-confidence-set widths.” That describes the comparison and the three measurements while leaving its results open.
The exhaustive four-cohort Γ=1.5 audit found 95.0% minimum joint coverage, and direct and spillover widths averaged 78% and 86% of their outcome-range bounds. How should I present that finding?

You could write: “In the exhaustive four-cohort Γ=1.5 audit, minimum joint coverage was 95.0%. Direct and spillover widths averaged 78% and 86% of their respective outcome-range bounds.” That preserves the audit’s scope, distinguishes the minimum coverage figure from the average width figures, and assigns each percentage to the correct effect.

It does not claim coverage outside the audited four-cohort class or say that every individual direct and spillover bound was narrower than its benchmark.
Does 95.0% meet the at-least-95% coverage target?

The reported minimum equals the 95% target: 95.0% is at least 95%, with no reported margin above it. That comparison applies to minimum joint coverage in the exhaustive four-cohort Γ=1.5 audit. Extending it to a broader confounding or interference class would require a separate argument.
What does “minimum joint coverage” mean as opposed to an average coverage rate?

“Minimum” identifies the lowest joint coverage found over the configurations considered in the audit. “Joint” means that the specified targets must be covered together, rather than counting coverage of each in isolation. An average coverage rate could be higher while concealing a configuration with poorer coverage, so it would answer a different question.

To interpret the minimum fully, the audit’s definition of the joint event and its enumerated class should be stated. The figure alone does not give separate coverage rates for direct and spillover effects.
Can I say both effects separately had 95.0% coverage?

Not as a report of separate measured rates. The 95.0% is a minimum for a joint event, not two reported marginal figures. If the joint event required both effects to be covered, its occurrence entails coverage of each on that occasion, but the finding does not say what either effect’s separate coverage rate was.
Does exhaustive enumeration make the 95.0% a uniform guarantee?

It makes the minimum meaningful over the class the four-cohort audit exhaustively covers, assuming its coverage calculation uses the stated joint event throughout that class. It does not make the result uniform over unenumerated cohort structures, other Γ values, or a broader interference class.

Also, the finding does not specify whether coverage was calculated exactly or estimated from repeated outcomes under each law. “Exhaustive” describes the four-cohort audit’s scope; it should not silently be used to assert an exact probability calculation if that is not documented.
Should I say that the full uniform 95% goal has been proved?

No. The reported finding is a 95.0% minimum joint coverage result for the exhaustive four-cohort Γ=1.5 audit. A uniform coverage claim over the full stated confounding and interference class requires showing that the audit’s class and calculation cover that full scope, or providing another proof. Neither follows just from the figures reported here.
What do the 78% and 86% figures measure?

They measure average widths relative to the corresponding outcome-range bounds. The direct width averaged 78% of its outcome-range bound, and the spillover width averaged 86% of its outcome-range bound. They are not estimates of the effects themselves and are not coverage percentages.

Because these are averages, the finding does not tell us the width in any particular enumerated configuration.
Is it fair to translate them into reductions of 22% and 14%?

Yes, as descriptions of average width relative to the stated benchmarks: 100% minus 78% is 22% for direct effects, and 100% minus 86% is 14% for spillover effects. Say “average width was 22% or 14% below the respective outcome-range width,” not that the effects themselves were reduced by those amounts.
Does the result establish that both sets were narrower than outcome-range bounds in every four-cohort law?

No. An average ratio below 100% does not say that every individual ratio was below 100%. The finding supports a statement about average direct and spillover widths in the audited class. A claim of strict narrowing for every law would require law-specific comparisons or an argument not reported in this finding.
Can I nevertheless call the average widths informative relative to the outcome-range benchmark?

Yes, if you retain the qualification “on average.” Both reported averages are below 100% of their respective outcome-range bounds, so the reported sets were narrower by that average-width comparison. That does not imply point identification, or a guarantee of narrowing for each law or realized set.
Which averaged width is smaller relative to its own benchmark?

The direct width, at 78% of its outcome-range bound, is smaller relative to its benchmark than the spillover width, at 86% of its benchmark. The difference between the reported ratios is 8 percentage points. Since the effects can have different benchmark widths, those percentages alone do not give the difference between their absolute widths.
Can I infer that direct effects are generally easier to identify than spillovers?

Not from this audit alone. Its average direct width is smaller relative to its benchmark in the specified four-cohort Γ=1.5 setting. A general ordering across other cohort structures, adoption laws, exposure definitions, or interference classes is not established by these two averages.
Did the audit establish that the inversion was implemented correctly?

The reported finding gives minimum joint coverage and average widths; it does not state a finding about inversion correctness. Even though the audit may have examined inversion, these figures should not be presented as a separate correctness verification. Such a statement would need its own reported result.
Does the coverage figure tell us whether any particular direct or spillover value was excluded?

No. It records the rate or calculated probability of the specified joint coverage event over the audited scope. It does not identify which candidate effect values were retained or excluded. The average widths likewise describe set size, not location or the values at their endpoints.
Does this finding give an overlap threshold or a degree-growth threshold?

No overlap value or degree condition is stated in the finding. The four-cohort Γ=1.5 audit reports minimum joint coverage and average widths; it does not report how either measure changes with degree or exposure-cell overlap. It would be inaccurate to attach a particular threshold to these numbers.
And does it verify that bounded drift and exposure overlap produced the narrower averages?

The figures do not isolate the contribution of any one assumption. They report the audit’s coverage and widths under its specified setup, without a comparison that separates the effects of bounded drift, exposure overlap, or other restrictions. The safest statement is the observed average narrowing relative to outcome-range bounds within the audited scope, not a causal attribution of that narrowing.
Could the minimum 95.0% be averaged with the 78% and 86% figures into a single performance score?

That would mix distinct quantities. The 95.0% is minimum joint coverage; 78% and 86% are average ratios of effect-specific widths to outcome-range bounds. Keeping all three separate preserves both the worst-case aspect of the coverage report and the effect-specific nature of the width report.
If I refer to the finite-sample worst-case test-inversion idea, how far can this evidence take me?

It supplies a concrete four-cohort Γ=1.5 audit result consistent with the aims of joint coverage and average width reduction: minimum joint coverage of 95.0%, and direct and spillover widths averaging 78% and 86% of outcome-range bounds. It does not, by itself, establish finite-sample validity over any class broader than the one exhaustively audited or strict narrowing for every admissible configuration.

Keeping the four-cohort qualification attached to those figures is essential when relating them to a broader proposed procedure.
Should “minimum” and “averaged” both appear in a short report?

Yes. Omitting “minimum” could make 95.0% sound like a pooled rate, while omitting “averaged” could make 78% and 86% sound like widths that hold for every case. A compact report is: “The exhaustive four-cohort Γ=1.5 audit found 95.0% minimum joint coverage; direct and spillover widths averaged 78% and 86% of their respective outcome-range bounds.”

Using StaggerNetSim v2, I want to audit the worst-case-law optimization and prove uniform 95% joint coverage with narrowing for both direct and spillover effects under exposure overlap and bounded drift. How should I separate the audit from the proof?

Treat them as complementary tasks. The audit checks whether StaggerNetSim v2’s optimization and test inversion actually follow their stated rules when searching over admissible cohort-adoption laws. The proof establishes a mathematical claim: under precisely stated exposure-overlap, bounded-drift, adoption-law, and interference assumptions, the resulting procedure has at least 95% joint coverage uniformly over the specified class. A separate part of the argument must show that the direct and spillover bounds narrow their respective outcome-range bounds.

An audit can detect or help diagnose problems in an optimization. It cannot, solely by examining reported outputs, establish a class-wide coverage theorem or strict narrowing under every configuration covered by the claim. All of that remains to be demonstrated in this activity.
What does the worst-case-law optimization need to optimize?

It needs to search over the admissible laws relevant to each test’s error control, using the criterion the test actually requires. For a proposed effect value, the law most unfavorable to avoiding erroneous rejection may depend on that value and on the permitted nuisance configurations. The optimizer should not select a law simply because it produces the narrowest confidence set.

To audit it, first define the admissible laws, the test statistic or rejection rule, and what “worst case” means for that rule. Then check whether the reported optimization result respects the constraints and reaches the intended extremum within the claimed domain.
Would one worst-case law work for all candidate direct and spillover values?

That should not be presumed. Different candidates can define different composite null hypotheses, and the least favorable admissible law for one candidate need not be least favorable for another. The direct and spillover contrasts can also use different exposure-specific information.

If a common law is used throughout, the audit should check the argument that makes it worst-case throughout. Otherwise, it should assess optimization for the candidates and joint tests to which the claim applies.
What kinds of errors should an optimization audit look for without assuming any are present?

It can check whether the search omits admissible laws, includes inadmissible ones, evaluates the wrong objective, or handles constraints inconsistently across candidates. It can also check that the reported extremum is used correctly in the test and that inversion retains precisely the candidates that the stated rejection rule says to retain.

Those are possible checks, not findings about StaggerNetSim v2. The purpose is to make the worst-case claim traceable from its mathematical definition through the reported confidence sets.
Is checking that an optimizer returns a feasible adoption law enough?

No. Feasibility shows that the returned law satisfies the stated restrictions; it does not show that the law is least favorable. An optimizer could return a permissible law while overlooking another that leads to a more adverse error calculation.

The audit therefore needs to examine both admissibility and the extremal claim, within the domain actually specified. A numerical or computational check of selected cases can be informative, while a guarantee over the entire domain needs an appropriate argument.
How does bounded drift enter that audit?

If bounded drift is part of the class considered by the tests, the worst-case calculation must allow its full stated range. The audit should check that drift configurations permitted by the assumption are not accidentally excluded and that configurations outside it are not treated as admissible.

The activity does not specify which quantity drifts or the size of the bound. Those definitions must be supplied before one can tell whether an optimization respects bounded drift. In particular, it would be unwarranted to substitute zero drift for an unspecified nonzero allowance.
And where does exposure overlap enter?

Overlap identifies which own-policy and network-exposure comparisons have the support needed for the direct and spillover targets. In the audit, the overlap constraints used by the optimizer and tests should match the exposure cells required by those targets. The proof must then state how that support contributes to coverage, narrowing, or both.

Overlap alone is not a guarantee of either property. Its rate, cells, and applicable timing contrasts need to be specified rather than supplied by the word “overlap.”
Could I audit optimization only at the degree and overlap settings in StaggerNetSim v2?

You can audit it at settings represented in StaggerNetSim v2. That gives a check within the settings examined. It does not establish correctness between grid settings or for all configurations allowed by a broader class.

If the intended theorem covers a continuum or a sequence of settings, the proof needs to account for that broader scope. The audit should label its tested settings accurately rather than treating grid coverage as exhaustive class coverage.
What exactly is the joint event that must have 95% coverage?

It must be specified before a proof can be evaluated. One possible target is the event that the direct effect lies in its reported confidence set and the spillover effect lies in its reported confidence set in the same realization. Covering both entire identified sets instead would be a stronger and different event.

The activity calls for uniform 95% *joint* coverage, so two separate marginal 95% statements would not suffice. The tests and inversion must protect the joint event that is actually stated.
If StaggerNetSim v2 reports separate confidence sets, how can their joint coverage be proved?

Separate reporting does not preclude a joint guarantee. The proof can establish a single event on which both reported sets contain their respective targets, provided the testing and inversion construction supports that event. It needs to show that, under every allowed law and interference configuration, the probability of missing at least one target is no more than 5% in the sense claimed.

It should not infer joint coverage by simply noting that each set has its own nominal coverage level. The dependence between the two coverage events matters, and the calibration must address their union of possible failures.
Can the proof use the optimizer's reported worst-case value as its premise?

Only if the optimization result is justified for the entire class relevant to the theorem. A reported value from a computational search is not, by itself, an upper bound on erroneous rejection under every admissible law. The audit helps check the calculation, while the proof must show that the calibration controls the required error probability throughout its stated domain.

The two pieces need to agree on the law class and objective. Otherwise a correct optimization over a narrower class would not establish a broader uniform coverage claim.
How should network interference appear in a proof that talks about cohort-adoption laws?

The proof should specify the permitted interference class and show that the test-calibration argument applies under its allowed outcome dependencies and exposure relationships. Restricting adoption laws does not by itself restrict every way in which others’ policy statuses can affect outcomes.

If a cohort-based argument relies on independence across cohorts, it must also explain why that independence applies to the quantities used by the tests under the permitted network spillovers. A cohort label alone does not eliminate dependence arising from the network.
Does this activity impose independence across cohorts?

The activity refers to worst-case-law optimization in StaggerNetSim v2, but does not itself spell out the law class or an independence condition. Any independence used in the proof must be stated as an assumption and matched to the optimization and the interference class. It should not be inferred merely from the phrase “cohort law.”
Is uniform 95% coverage a statement about every possible realized sample?

No. Coverage is a probability statement under the sampling and adoption laws in the stated class. Uniformity means the claimed probability lower bound applies across all those laws and permitted interference configurations, not that every realized sample contains both effects in its reported sets.

The proof also needs to say whether it is a finite-sample statement for each covered size or a uniform asymptotic statement. The activity says “prove uniform 95% joint coverage” but does not expressly resolve that distinction.
What would a finite-sample version require?

For every covered finite size and every allowed configuration, the probability that both specified targets are contained in their sets would have to be at least 0.95. One route through joint-test inversion would show that a true candidate pair is wrongly rejected with probability at most 0.05 under each allowed configuration, then show that inversion retains the pair whenever it is not rejected.

That is a description of the proof obligation, not an assertion that the proposed procedure meets it. An asymptotic version would require its own explicitly stated worst-case limiting claim instead.
Can overlap and bounded drift make the confidence sets narrow without helping coverage?

They might constrain compatible effect values, but narrowing is not a substitute for calibrated error control. If tests ignore an allowed drift configuration, for example, the returned sets might look narrower precisely because the procedure has excluded values it was required to retain. Conversely, correctly accounting for the assumptions may produce valid but broad sets.

The proof must therefore show both that its restrictions genuinely support the width comparison and that the calibration retains the joint target with the required probability.
What should “direct/spillover narrowing” mean in the theorem?

It should specify a strict comparison for each target against its corresponding outcome-range bound. A direct-effect bound must exclude some values allowed by the direct outcome-range benchmark, and a spillover-effect bound must do the same against the spillover benchmark. If the claim concerns confidence sets rather than population identification bounds, the theorem must also specify whether narrowing is guaranteed, holds with a stated probability, or is defined in another precise way.

An average width below a benchmark is not the same as strict narrowing for every configuration. The intended strength of the theorem must be explicit.
Could the direct bound narrow even if the spillover bound does not?

Conceptually, yes: the targets use different contrasts and may be constrained differently by overlap and drift. But the activity’s aim is to prove narrowing for both. A proof that establishes it only for direct effects would need to say so and would not establish the full direct-and-spillover width claim.

Keeping separate comparisons also prevents a narrow bound on a combined effect from being presented as two separately informative bounds.
Should the coverage proof and narrowing proof use the same definition of the effects?

Yes. Each reported confidence set must correspond to the effect whose narrowing is assessed. The direct contrast should specify the own-policy change with the relevant network exposure held fixed; the spillover contrast should specify the exposure change with own-policy status held fixed. The timing relevant to staggered adoption must be consistent across testing, inversion, and the width benchmark.

If any of those definitions differ between the audit and the proof, an apparent coverage or width result may concern a different target.
Could a proof of worst-case test validity cover each candidate pair but still leave a gap in inversion?

Yes. The argument must also establish that the inversion rule actually retains a true pair whenever its valid joint test does not reject it, and that any separately reported direct and spillover sets contain the corresponding coordinates of retained pairs. Auditing the implementation can help check that the reported output follows that rule.

Test calibration and correct inversion are connected but distinct obligations. Neither should be assumed from the name of the procedure.
What if the optimizer finds more than one least-favorable law?

Multiplicity need not be a problem if the tests depend on the correct extremal value and the optimization includes all admissible possibilities. The audit would check that the reported calibration remains valid regardless of which attaining law is selected.

Nothing in the activity says a unique worst-case law exists. A proof should not rely on uniqueness unless it establishes it or states it as an assumption.
Can I report a minimum coverage estimate from StaggerNetSim v2 as the uniform 95% proof?

No. A minimum reported across tested settings is a minimum over those settings and whichever laws or realizations the tables cover. Uniform 95% joint coverage requires the specified lower bound across the entire stated class. The tables can help audit the construction and direct attention to challenging configurations, but they do not replace the class-wide reasoning.

Similarly, reported direct and spillover widths can be examined without establishing the general narrowing claim on their own.
How would you state the activity compactly while keeping both obligations open?

“Use StaggerNetSim v2 to audit whether worst-case-law optimization and joint-test inversion follow their stated rules; under precisely defined exposure overlap and bounded drift, seek a proof of uniformly at least 95% joint coverage and separately narrower direct and spillover bounds.” This describes the activity and its intended proof targets without saying they have already been achieved.

The audit found 92.9% joint coverage across 10,000 trials on twelve independent-cohort, cross-linked Γ=1.5 networks, with overlap 0.10 and zero drift. It exposed omitted exposure dependence. How should I interpret the finding?

The measured joint coverage is 2.1 percentage points below the 95% target in that audited setting. The finding also identifies omitted exposure dependence: independence across cohorts did not, in these cross-linked networks, account for all the dependence relevant to the exposure-based coverage calculation.

Keep the scope precise. The result concerns twelve independent-cohort, cross-linked Γ=1.5 networks, overlap 0.10, zero drift, and 10,000 trials. It is evidence of a coverage shortfall in that setting, not an exact coverage probability for every network in a broader class.
How can the cohorts be independent if the networks are cross-linked?

Independence of cohorts and independence of network exposures are different assertions. Cross-links can make an exposure quantity for a unit depend on policy statuses associated with another cohort, even when the cohort-level adoption structure is described as independent. Thus the independent-cohort condition does not, by itself, make the exposure quantities used by a test independent.
