The finding specifically identifies omitted exposure dependence. It does not specify the links, exposure mapping, or precise calculation in which that dependence was omitted, so those details should not be inferred.
Does the result tell us that cohort adoption was correlated across the twelve networks?

No. It describes independent-cohort, cross-linked networks. Cross-linked refers to the networks, while the reported problem concerns dependence in exposure. Neither phrase supplies a claim that cohort adoption was correlated across networks or that the twelve networks were generated independently of one another.
What exactly does the 92.9% cover?

It is joint coverage: the stated coverage event was met in 92.9% of the 10,000 trials. In the direct-and-spillover setting, that means the two targets were covered together under the event used in the audit. It is not a separately reported 92.9% rate for each effect.

The finding does not give the effects’ marginal coverage rates, or say which target was missed on trials where the joint event failed.
Is 92.9% just slightly below the target, or does the exact comparison matter?

The exact reported comparison is 92.9% versus 95%, a shortfall of 2.1 percentage points. Whether that difference is statistically distinguishable from an underlying 95% probability cannot be determined without assumptions about how the trials were generated and related. The observation should nevertheless be reported as below the target, not rounded into meeting it.
Does having 10,000 trials mean there were 10,000 trials for each of the twelve networks?

No. The finding says joint coverage was 92.9% across 10,000 trials involving twelve networks. It does not give the allocation of trials among networks. It also does not give a network-specific coverage rate, so the pooled figure should not be described as the minimum coverage across the twelve networks.
Could one network be responsible for most of the joint-coverage failures?

The aggregate figure does not tell us. Failures could be distributed in different ways among the twelve networks; no per-network breakdown is reported. The supported conclusion is the 92.9% joint coverage across the stated trials, together with the finding that omitted exposure dependence was exposed in the cross-linked setting.
Does Γ=1.5 indicate that these networks violated the adoption-odds restriction?

No. They are described as Γ=1.5 networks. The result should not be dismissed by asserting that their adoption laws lie outside that sensitivity level. Γ=1.5 also does not, by itself, restrict every dependence induced by cross-network links; adoption confounding and exposure dependence are distinct issues.
Does overlap 0.10 rule out a lack of exposure support as an explanation?

The audit reports overlap 0.10 and identifies omitted exposure dependence. It does not provide enough detail to attribute every missed trial to one cause or to make a general statement about all aspects of exposure support. Overlap and dependence play different roles: an overlap condition does not make cross-linked exposure quantities independent.

It is accurate to retain overlap 0.10 as a condition of the finding without treating it as a guarantee of joint coverage.
And zero drift means the bounded-drift assumption was not the issue?

Zero drift is a stated condition of these trials. The finding identifies omitted exposure dependence, rather than reporting drift as the source of the shortfall. It does not, however, prove what coverage would be under other drift values or establish that drift could never interact with exposure dependence.

Keeping “zero drift” in the report is useful because it makes clear that the observed 92.9% was measured under that condition.
Can we say what was omitted in mathematical terms?

Only at the level the finding supplies: dependence among the exposure quantities relevant to joint coverage was omitted. The evidence does not provide an exposure mapping, a covariance term, or a test formula, so naming a particular missing mathematical term would add an unsupported detail.

The substantive distinction is clear without one: independently organized cohorts do not necessarily yield independent exposure information on cross-linked networks.
Does this show that worst-case optimization over cohort-adoption laws is insufficient on its own?

For the audited cross-linked setting, the identified omission shows why an argument focused on adoption laws alone cannot simply assume that exposure dependence has been handled. A worst-case calculation over permitted adoption laws and a valid account of dependence in the exposure-based joint statistic are separate requirements.

The result does not establish that every possible worst-case test inversion fails. It reports a shortfall and a specific omitted dependence in this setting.
What does the result imply for a uniform 95% joint-coverage claim?

It supplies a concrete adverse measurement that a claim covering these cross-linked Γ=1.5 networks would have to address. A proof of uniform coverage cannot rely on cohort independence in a way that omits the exposure dependence identified here. The observed 92.9% is below the target, although a finite collection of trials alone is not a mathematical determination of the coverage probability throughout an entire class.

Nor does the result specify coverage at other network or overlap settings. Its force is the measured shortfall and the identified gap in accounting for exposure dependence within the stated audit.
Does it say anything about whether the direct or spillover sets were narrow?

No widths are reported. Joint coverage of 92.9% does not tell us either set’s width or whether either was narrower than its outcome-range benchmark. The finding addresses coverage and omitted exposure dependence, not direct- or spillover-width performance.
If the report says twelve networks, can I describe this as a twelve-cohort result?

No. Twelve counts the independent-cohort, cross-linked networks in the finding; it is not stated to be the number of cohorts in each network. “Twelve networks” preserves the reported unit of that count.
Can you put the result and its limitation in one concise statement?

“Across 10,000 trials on twelve independent-cohort, cross-linked Γ=1.5 networks with overlap 0.10 and zero drift, joint coverage was 92.9%, below the 95% target; the audit exposed omitted exposure dependence. This is a finding for the audited setting, not a class-wide coverage probability or a result about direct and spillover widths.”
Which restrictions on cross-cohort exposure dependence could preserve uniform 95% coverage without widening the direct and spillover bounds all the way to outcome-range widths?

There is no single restriction or numerical threshold determined by that question alone. A useful restriction must do two jobs: make the joint coverage calculation valid despite cross-cohort exposure dependence, and leave enough exposure-specific information to narrow the direct and spillover bounds separately. Those jobs need not be accomplished by the same assumption.

Possible classes to investigate include restrictions on which cohort pairs can share relevant exposures, limits on how many exposure summaries can be dependent, or explicit bounds on their joint dependence. Each is a candidate assumption, not a demonstrated sufficient condition. Its implications would depend on the exposure mapping, the effect targets, and how the confidence sets are constructed.
Is the simplest restriction to prohibit every cross-cohort network link?

That would be one strong way to limit potential cross-cohort exposure dependence, but it is not necessarily the restriction the question calls for. The issue is dependence among the exposure quantities used for inference. Whether a link creates such dependence depends on how exposure and interference are defined; conversely, a restriction on links alone needs to be shown to control the dependence relevant to the procedure.

The aim is to characterize conditions that support coverage without sacrificing informative bounds, not to assume that removing all cross-cohort links is required.
Could we allow cross-links but say that exposure is independent across cohorts?

That would be a substantive assumption requiring justification. Cross-links can cause an exposure summary in one cohort to depend on policy statuses associated with another. Simply declaring the resulting summaries independent could conflict with the exposure mapping.

One would need to define exactly which exposure quantities are independent and show that the allowed links and adoption laws make that statement coherent. If they are not independent, an inference procedure should accommodate the permitted dependence rather than label it independence.
What would a restriction on the pattern of cross-cohort links look like conceptually?

It might limit which cohorts can contribute to one another’s relevant exposure summaries, so the dependence among those summaries has a controlled structure. The restriction must apply to the exposures entering the direct and spillover comparisons, not just to a graph feature chosen for convenience.

Its value would be established by showing how the restricted pattern supports a valid joint coverage calculation. A separate argument would then have to show that the remaining exposure comparisons still yield bounds narrower than the appropriate outcome-range bounds.
Could a dependency graph represent that controlled structure?

Potentially. Its vertices could represent the contributions used in the exposure-specific tests, with edges recording dependencies that the stated adoption and interference class permits. The important requirement is that the graph include every dependence relevant to the coverage argument; omitting an allowed cross-cohort dependence would make the representation inadequate.

Even an accurate dependency graph is only a description of dependence. Coverage needs a test or confidence-set calibration valid for that graph class, and informative bounds require sufficient support for the target contrasts.
Would a bound on the number of dependent cohort pairs be enough?

It might form part of a sufficient condition, but the count alone does not settle the question. How the pairs are arranged, which exposure quantities they connect, and how dependence is allowed to operate can matter to joint error control. The condition also needs to be expressed in a way that applies uniformly over the class for which 95% coverage is claimed.

There is no justified numerical limit on dependent pairs in the information given. One would have to derive a condition from the specified test and dependence model rather than assume a count is sufficient.
What if we bound the strength of cross-cohort dependence instead of forbidding connections?

That is another candidate route. It would require a precise measure of dependence, a stated bound on that measure, and a proof that the coverage calibration remains valid for every dependence pattern allowed by the bound. A general phrase such as “weak dependence” is not enough to determine a uniform 95% guarantee.

The width question remains separate. A bound weak enough to support inference may still require wide confidence sets, or it may leave useful direct and spillover comparisons; neither outcome follows from the label alone.
Can independent adoption across cohorts coexist with dependent exposures?

Yes, conceptually. An exposure summary may use policy statuses from more than one cohort. Two summaries can therefore share inputs or otherwise be linked through the network even if cohort-level adoption variables satisfy an independence assumption. The dependence restriction must address the exposure quantities that enter the tests, not merely the adoption-law labels.

That is why the question specifically concerns cross-cohort exposure dependence. A restriction on adoption processes cannot silently do the work of a restriction on how network exposure is constructed.
Is this mainly a problem for the spillover effect, then?

It is especially visible for spillover contrasts because they explicitly vary exposure to others’ policies. But a direct-effect comparison may also be constructed within specified exposure cells and rely on exposure-specific quantities. Cross-cohort dependence can therefore affect its uncertainty calculation as well.

The coverage proof should encompass every quantity used for both targets. The width analysis should then ask separately whether the direct and spillover bounds improve on their respective outcome-range benchmarks.
Would a restriction on interference be equivalent to a restriction on exposure dependence?

No. An interference restriction says which other policy statuses may affect an outcome and through what permitted exposure structure. Exposure dependence concerns the joint behavior of the exposure quantities or test contributions across cohorts under the adoption and network laws. The two are related, but one does not automatically determine the other.

A coherent class would specify both sufficiently to justify the effect definitions and the joint coverage calculation.
What does it mean for the coverage guarantee to be uniform under one of these restrictions?

The coverage probability for the stated joint target must be at least 95% across every adoption, interference, and cross-cohort exposure-dependence configuration that satisfies the restrictions. It cannot be calibrated only for a convenient link arrangement or one favorable dependence pattern.

The claim must also say whether it applies at each covered finite sample size or asymptotically. Those are different guarantees; the question’s reference to uniform 95% coverage does not by itself choose between them.
Would 95% coverage for each effect separately settle the joint question?

No. If the intended target is simultaneous coverage of the direct and spillover effects, the event that both are covered must reach at least 95% uniformly. Two separate marginal 95% guarantees do not imply that joint guarantee, particularly when the two sets depend on shared exposure information.

A proposed dependence restriction needs to support calibration of the actual joint event, rather than two unrelated marginal claims.
Why might accounting for cross-cohort dependence widen the bounds?

A procedure that acknowledges additional permitted dependence may need more conservative uncertainty calibration to protect joint coverage. Inverting a more conservative test can retain more candidate effect values. But the effect of that calibration on width depends on the method and the information available; it cannot be asserted without analysis.

The question therefore asks for restrictions that allow valid calibration while still excluding some outcome-range-compatible values for both effects. It does not assume the only choices are ignoring dependence or returning the full outcome-range bounds.
Should we distinguish widening a confidence set from widening an identified bound?

Yes. An identified bound concerns which effect values are compatible with the population information and assumptions. A confidence set additionally reflects uncertainty in learning about those values. Accounting properly for exposure dependence may widen a confidence set even if the underlying identified bound is unchanged.

To answer the question precisely, state which direct and spillover widths are being compared with outcome-range widths. If the desired claim is about both identification bounds and reported confidence sets, each comparison needs its own conditions.
Could strong exposure overlap alone prevent the widened sets from reaching outcome-range widths?

Not necessarily. Overlap supplies support for the comparisons, but it does not by itself control cross-cohort dependence or guarantee that the remaining information is strong enough to exclude effect values after the permitted confounding and interference are accounted for.

The overlap condition should cover all exposure cells used for the specified direct and spillover contrasts. Then a width argument must show that the restrictions and information jointly yield strict narrowing for each target.
If we limit dependence by conditioning on some cohort-level information, would conditional independence solve it?

It could be a candidate assumption, but only if the conditioning information is defined and conditional independence of the relevant exposure quantities truly follows under every law in the claimed class. Conditioning must not be used as a verbal shortcut that discards dependence carried by shared network inputs.

Even if such an independence statement supports coverage, it leaves the bound-width question open. It must be shown that the conditioning and resulting comparisons retain information about both direct and spillover effects.
Could we instead calibrate the tests for arbitrary cross-cohort dependence and avoid restricting it at all?

That is a possible question about test construction, but arbitrary dependence may require a conservative calibration. Whether such a procedure can both guarantee uniform 95% joint coverage and keep both sets narrower than outcome-range bounds depends on the other restrictions and the available comparisons.

The present question seeks cross-cohort exposure-dependence restrictions that preserve both properties. If no dependence restriction is used, one still has to prove that the resulting worst-case calibration is valid and informative; neither property is automatic.
What would show that a proposed dependence restriction is too weak?

Under a precisely defined procedure, a permitted configuration for which the joint coverage guarantee fails would show the restriction does not suffice for that guarantee. Alternatively, if every outcome-range-compatible value remains possible for one effect despite the restriction and other stated assumptions, it would not suffice for strict narrowing of that effect.

Those are different ways a proposed condition could fall short. A finite measured coverage shortfall can motivate scrutiny, but a class-wide conclusion requires an argument matching the stated coverage claim.
And what would show that a restriction is unnecessarily strong?

A valid argument for a broader dependence class that still achieves uniform 95% joint coverage and strictly narrower direct and spillover bounds would show the stronger restriction was not needed for those conclusions. A result under one narrow class alone cannot establish that its restrictions are minimal or sharp.

The question can be answered with defensible sufficient conditions without claiming they are the weakest possible.
Do the dependence restrictions have to be the same for the direct and spillover comparisons?

A common joint coverage proof must account for all dependencies relevant to both. But the particular exposure quantities that limit informativeness can differ between direct and spillover contrasts. One could state target-specific width conditions alongside a common dependence condition for joint inference, provided the overall assumptions are explicit and consistent.

A direct bound that remains narrow cannot compensate for a spillover bound that expands to its outcome-range width when the claim concerns both.
How could the answer be structured without inventing a degree cutoff or dependence coefficient?

First define the cross-cohort exposure quantities entering the two effect contrasts and the class of allowed links, shared inputs, or other dependencies. Next derive a simultaneous testing or confidence-set rule valid for every configuration in that class and show that its joint coverage reaches at least 95% in the stated finite-sample or asymptotic sense. Finally compare each resulting direct and spillover bound with its own outcome-range bound and identify assumptions under which both comparisons are strict.

That structure answers what a sufficient restriction must accomplish. Numerical cutoffs, if any, would have to follow from the specified exposure and inference model rather than be supplied without support.
So is the question really about the interaction between dependence control and informativeness?

Exactly. Controlling cross-cohort exposure dependence is necessary to justify a uniform joint-coverage calculation under the stated class, while retaining enough supported, restricted comparisons is necessary to keep the direct and spillover bounds informative. The task is to find and prove conditions satisfying both, not to regard either property as following from the other.

Until the exposure mapping, dependence class, effect targets, and calibration are specified, no particular restriction can be declared sufficient for uniform 95% coverage without outcome-range-width bounds.

Here is a hypothesis about cross-cohort exposure dependence: with exposure components involving no more than three cohorts, overlap ≥0.10, and drift ≤0.05 of the range, joint Γ=1.5 enumeration ensures uniform coverage of at least 95% and sub-range widths for both direct and spillover effects. Is that a precise enough claim?

It is a specific working hypothesis, but several terms still need definitions before it can be evaluated. In particular, define an exposure component and what it means for one to involve at most three cohorts; identify the exposure cells subject to the ≥0.10 overlap condition; specify what can drift and the range used for the ≤0.05 limit; and state which laws and dependence configurations the joint Γ=1.5 enumeration covers.

The two proposed conclusions also need precision. Uniform ≥95% coverage needs a named joint target and a stated class. “Sub-range” should mean that the direct and spillover widths are each strictly below their respective outcome-range widths, with the scope of that width claim made explicit. None of those conclusions follows from the three numerical conditions without an argument.
Does “≤3-cohort exposure components” mean there can be only three cohorts in the entire study?

No. The proposed restriction concerns the number of cohorts involved in each exposure component, not necessarily the total number of cohorts. A study could have more than three cohorts while each relevant component involves at most three, depending on how the components are defined.

That definition matters: the hypothesis cannot be assessed simply by counting all cohorts or by counting units within a component.
What should an exposure component represent?

It should represent a grouping of cohorts whose adoption or exposure information is linked for the quantities used in the direct and spillover analysis. A precise definition would specify when cohorts belong to the same component and how cross-cohort links enter that grouping.

That is a possible interpretation to formalize, not a component construction already supplied by the hypothesis. If a component leaves out shared inputs that actually create exposure dependence, the ≤3 restriction would not control the dependence the coverage argument needs to address.
Can components overlap?

The hypothesis does not settle that. If components overlap or share exposure inputs, dependence may carry across what appear to be distinct components. A proof that treats them as separate would need to account for those connections or justify why they do not matter.

The key restriction is not just a label saying “three cohorts.” It is a mathematically defined limit on the cross-cohort exposure dependence relevant to joint inference.
Would a maximum component size of three automatically make the components independent?

No. A bound on component size says how many cohorts a component involves under its definition. It does not, by itself, say that different components are independent or that dependence within each component has been fully represented. Any independence or other restriction used for joint coverage must be stated separately or derived from the defined adoption and exposure structure.

The proposed enumeration must also reflect whatever dependence remains; otherwise the component-size condition would not establish uniform coverage.
Could a component with just two cohorts still create a coverage problem?

Conceptually, yes. A small component can contain dependence that a test fails to account for. Limiting components to at most three cohorts could make a joint worst-case calculation more manageable, but the size restriction alone does not validate that calculation.

To support the hypothesis, the joint Γ=1.5 enumeration would have to include the permitted exposure relationships within those components and correctly calibrate the event that both effects are covered.
So is three supposed to be a proven cutoff?

No. Three is the specific proposed upper limit in the hypothesis. It is neither a proved sufficient cutoff nor a demonstrated necessary one. If the proposed result were established under components involving at most three cohorts, that would not, by itself, determine what happens with larger components.
How should the ≥0.10 overlap condition be read?

It is a proposed floor of 0.10 for the probabilities of the exposure cells needed by the target comparisons. A direct contrast needs support for differing own-policy statuses at a fixed relevant exposure; a spillover contrast needs support for differing exposures at a fixed own-policy status. With staggered adoption, the relevant timing may also be part of a cell’s definition.

The hypothesis must say which cells are covered by the floor and what distribution defines their probabilities. A population probability of at least 0.10 is not a promise that every realized sample has at least 10% of observations in each cell.
Could overlap ≥0.10 hold in aggregate while a cell needed for a spillover comparison is unsupported within a component?

That possibility depends on how the overlap condition is specified. An aggregate floor might not ensure support in each component or for every timing- and exposure-specific comparison. If the proposed spillover width result needs component-level support, the hypothesis must impose it at that level rather than infer it from aggregate overlap.

The same care applies to direct effects. The overlap assumption should be no broader or narrower in the stated conclusion than the support conditions actually used in its proof.
What does “≤0.05-range drift” mean numerically?

On its intended scale, it restricts the specified drift to no more than 0.05 times the stated range—five percent of that range. It is a bound, not an assertion of zero drift.

The hypothesis does not identify the drifting quantity, the time or exposure comparisons over which drift is measured, or the precise range used as its reference. Those must be defined before the numerical limit can enter either the test or a bound-width argument.
Is the drift limit an additional restriction on adoption odds?

Not necessarily. Γ=1.5 concerns the stated sensitivity restriction used in the adoption-law enumeration. Bounded drift is a separate proposed restriction whose object has not yet been defined. Treating the drift limit as part of Γ, or Γ as a bound on drift, would conflate two conditions.

A formal hypothesis should explain how each restriction enters the admissible configurations and the effect comparisons.
If drift can reach the full 0.05 of the range, must the joint tests allow that value?

Yes, if the proposed class permits drift up to and including that limit. A test calibrated only for zero drift would not, without further justification, ensure coverage uniformly over a class that also allows nonzero drift through 0.05 of the range.

The same principle applies to exposure dependence within the permitted components and to adoption laws allowed by Γ=1.5: the claimed worst-case calculation must include the configurations its guarantee purports to cover.
What is the joint Γ=1.5 enumeration supposed to enumerate?

It is supposed to support a joint worst-case test or inversion at the specified Γ=1.5 sensitivity level. To make that meaningful, state which cohort-adoption laws are admissible, which cross-cohort exposure relationships and drift configurations are considered, and how the relevant joint rejection or coverage event is calculated.

Enumerating adoption laws alone does not automatically enumerate all permitted interference or exposure dependence. “Joint” and “enumeration” describe the intended approach; they do not by themselves establish that the worst case over the stated class has been attained.
Does joint enumeration mean separate direct and spillover tests are both run?

Not necessarily. It could be defined through a joint test of candidate direct-and-spillover effect values, whose inversion yields a set of retained pairs. Other constructions would need an equivalent argument for the same joint coverage target. What matters is that calibration protects both effects together, not merely that two marginal tests are displayed side by side.

Separate effect-specific intervals can be reported, but their joint coverage does not follow merely from each having its own nominal coverage statement.
Could Γ=1.5, the overlap floor, and the drift limit ensure coverage even if the enumeration misses a cross-cohort exposure connection?

No such implication is established. The three restrictions concern different aspects of the setup, and none excuses omitting dependence permitted by the exposure-component definition. If an allowed connection affects the joint test distribution, the calibration must account for it to support a uniform claim.

The component restriction is useful only if it accurately captures the dependencies relevant to the inference procedure and the enumeration or accompanying proof handles them.
How should I interpret “uniform ≥95% coverage” in this hypothesis?

It means that the coverage probability for the stated joint target is at least 0.95 across every configuration admitted by the specified adoption-confounding, exposure-dependence, drift, overlap, and interference class, in whatever finite-sample or asymptotic sense is claimed. A favorable average across configurations is not enough.

The hypothesis does not yet specify whether it promises a finite-sample guarantee at each covered size or a uniform asymptotic guarantee. That distinction should be settled explicitly before treating the statement as a theorem to prove.
Would 95% coverage of the direct effect and 95% coverage of the spillover effect separately meet the joint requirement?

Not automatically. The joint event is that both specified targets are covered in the same realization. Two separate statements about marginal coverage do not establish that the probability of this joint event is at least 95%.

A valid joint Γ=1.5 calibration would need to control the possibility of missing either target under every configuration covered by the proposed uniform guarantee.
Should the target be the two true effects or their entire partially identified sets?

The hypothesis needs to choose. Jointly covering the true direct and spillover effect values and jointly covering their entire identified sets are different coverage claims. The latter requires more than merely retaining each true value.

Neither interpretation is fixed by the phrase “uniform ≥95% coverage,” so an eventual proof and any reported confidence sets must name the object they cover.
What counts as a sub-range direct or spillover width?

For each effect, the stated width must be strictly less than the width of its corresponding outcome-range bound. Thus “sub-range direct/spillover widths” claims an improvement for both targets, not just a smaller combined width or an improvement for one effect.

The statement should also identify whether it concerns population identification bounds, inverted confidence sets, or both. A random confidence-set width can vary across realizations, so a claim about its width needs a scope such as a deterministic guarantee or another precisely stated criterion.
Would average widths below the outcome-range widths establish the hypothesis?

Only if the hypothesis explicitly makes an average-width claim under a defined averaging scheme. As phrased, “ensures sub-range direct/spillover widths” could be read as applying across the stated class, which is stronger than an average result. An average below the benchmark does not rule out some configurations or realizations reaching the full outcome-range width.

The proposed width conclusion should say whether strict narrowing holds for every admissible configuration, for a specified subset, or in a specified average or probability sense.
Can we infer narrower widths simply because the component-size limit makes enumeration easier?

No. Easier or more complete calibration is an inference benefit, not an identification argument. Limiting cross-cohort exposure components could help account for dependence without excessive conservatism, but it does not itself show that Γ=1.5, overlap ≥0.10, and drift ≤0.05 of the range exclude any effect values permitted by the outcome range.

Direct and spillover narrowing must be demonstrated separately using their defined contrasts and the actual restrictions on compatible outcomes.
Could the direct width be sub-range while the spillover width remains at the outcome-range width?

That is conceptually possible because the two effects rely on different exposure-specific comparisons. Such a result would not establish the hypothesis as written: its width conclusion concerns both direct and spillover effects. It would be important to report the distinct conclusions rather than let the direct result stand in for the spillover result.
Does the ≤3-cohort condition specify whether there are links between different components?

Not yet. The component definition must determine whether a link that creates shared exposure information merges components or is otherwise represented in the permitted dependence structure. If relevant links can connect nominally separate components without being counted, the at-most-three-cohort label may understate the dependence.

That is a definitional obligation for the hypothesis, not a finding about any particular network.
Do these proposed conditions claim to be necessary?

No. The hypothesis proposes them as sufficient for joint coverage and sub-range direct and spillover widths. It does not assert that a component may never involve four cohorts, that overlap below 0.10 necessarily fails, or that drift greater than 0.05 of the range necessarily prevents either result. Such necessity or sharp-threshold claims would require separate arguments.
Could an exhaustive calculation for a fixed number of cohorts establish the full uniform claim?

Only for the precisely defined class it exhaustively covers, if it also establishes the required joint error control. A component-size condition applies to exposure components, which need not limit the total number of cohorts or the number of components. A calculation restricted to one fixed overall cohort count would not automatically cover every permitted arrangement under the hypothesis.

A broader uniform statement needs an argument matching the full stated class, including how components and their dependence behave across the configurations it admits.
What are the separate proof obligations if I keep this as a working hypothesis?

First, define the exposure components and show that the at-most-three-cohort restriction captures all relevant cross-cohort exposure dependence. Next, define the required cells, the ≥0.10 overlap floor, the drift quantity and its ≤0.05-of-range bound, and the Γ=1.5 admissible-law and interference classes. Then justify joint test calibration and inversion so the stated target has uniformly at least 95% coverage. Finally, prove strict improvement over the outcome-range width for the direct effect and separately for the spillover effect in the sense of narrowing you have specified.

These are tasks required to establish the hypothesis, not results implied by stating it.
Can you give me a compact formulation that retains all three restrictions and both proposed conclusions?

“We hypothesize that, when every relevant cross-cohort exposure component involves at most three cohorts, every required exposure cell has probability at least 0.10, and the specified drift is at most 0.05 of its stated range, joint worst-case enumeration at Γ=1.5 yields uniformly at least 95% coverage of the defined joint target and direct and spillover widths each strictly below its corresponding outcome-range width.” The admissible class, coverage interpretation, and scope of the width comparison remain to be defined and proved.

I want to replace cohort-law inversion with joint enumeration of exposure components involving at most three cohorts, then prove finite-sample coverage and sub-range direct and spillover bounds under bounded drift. How should I frame that plan?

Frame the replacement precisely: the proposed inference construction will enumerate relevant cross-cohort exposure configurations jointly within components involving no more than three cohorts, rather than use cohort-law inversion as its organizing calculation. The two intended results are a finite-sample coverage proof and bounds narrower than the corresponding outcome-range bounds for direct and spillover effects under a stated bounded-drift assumption.

Neither result follows just from changing what is enumerated. The component definition must capture the dependence relevant to the coverage event, and the width argument must show separately why values allowed by the outcome range are excluded for each effect.
What is the point of enumerating exposure components instead of only adoption laws?

The point is to make cross-cohort exposure dependence part of the calculation itself. A description of how cohorts adopt does not alone specify whether exposure quantities used for different contrasts share adoption inputs through the network. Joint exposure-component enumeration is intended to account for those shared inputs when evaluating the relevant effect comparisons and coverage event.

That rationale does not imply the proposed enumeration is already complete or valid. It must be shown that its components include every exposure relationship the stated interference class permits.
What does “at most three cohorts” limit?

It limits the number of cohorts involved in each enumerated exposure component: no more than three per component. It does not, by itself, limit the total number of cohorts in a panel or say how many components there may be.

To use that restriction in a proof, the plan needs a rule for determining which cohorts belong to the same component. A group cannot be treated as a separate component if a relevant shared exposure input connects it to another group without being accounted for.
Does joint enumeration mean enumerating all possible outcomes as well?

Not necessarily. “Joint” here concerns the exposure configurations and dependence relevant to the direct and spillover contrasts. What else has to be considered for finite-sample coverage depends on the specified test or confidence-set construction, adoption process, and permitted outcomes.

The plan should say exactly what is enumerated and what is handled by other parts of the proof. Calling the enumeration joint does not mean that every possible outcome or nuisance configuration has automatically been included.
Could two components each contain three cohorts but still be dependent on each other?

They could unless the component definition or a separate assumption rules out or accommodates that dependence. Limiting each component to three cohorts controls its size; it does not establish independence between components.

If the coverage proof treats components as independent, it must justify that treatment under the permitted network links and adoption laws. Alternatively, it must calibrate coverage while allowing the dependence between components that the stated class permits.
Would it be enough to enumerate the exposure configurations separately for direct effects and spillovers?

Not if the intended coverage claim concerns the two effects jointly and they share exposure information. Separate enumerations can miss relationships between the quantities entering their respective sets. A joint enumeration should preserve those relationships when constructing or evaluating the simultaneous event.

The effect targets still need distinct definitions and bounds. “Joint” refers to accounting for their shared configurations, not merging direct and spillover effects into one undifferentiated effect.
What would the direct and spillover targets look like conceptually?

A direct contrast changes a unit’s own policy status while holding its relevant network exposure fixed. A spillover contrast changes that exposure while holding the unit’s own status fixed. Because adoption is staggered, a formal definition must also specify the timing relevant to each comparison.

The component enumeration should be built around the exposures those targets actually use. Otherwise an enumeration could be complete for one set of exposure summaries yet incomplete for the proposed effects.
Does replacing cohort-law inversion mean adoption confounding can now be ignored?

No. It changes the proposed calculation, not the need to account for permitted unmeasured adoption confounding. If adoption laws remain uncertain within a stated class, the exposure-component construction and coverage proof must accommodate that uncertainty.

Enumerating shared exposure configurations cannot, by itself, make adoption unconfounded. The plan needs to say how the allowed adoption laws enter the joint calculation or its accompanying argument.
Does this plan fix a particular sensitivity value or overlap floor?

Neither a numerical sensitivity value nor an overlap floor is stated in this plan. Its specific numerical restriction is the limit of at most three cohorts per exposure component. A formal result would need to state any adoption-confounding and exposure-support assumptions it uses; they should not be inferred from the component-size condition.

The plan does specify bounded drift, but does not give a numerical drift limit or define the quantity being bounded.
How should bounded drift enter the enumeration?

If drift can affect the outcomes or comparisons used to bound the effects, the calculation must allow every drift configuration within the stated bound. A candidate effect should not be excluded merely because it is incompatible with zero drift if nonzero drift remains permitted.

First define what may drift, between which times or exposure comparisons, and by how much. Then ensure that both the enumerated configurations and the coverage and width proofs use that same definition.
Does bounded drift control cross-cohort exposure dependence?

Not by itself. Drift limits change in a specified quantity across comparisons; exposure-component enumeration is intended to represent dependence generated by shared cross-cohort exposure relationships. They address different ambiguities.

A proof would need to explain how each contributes. It should not use a bound on drift as a reason to omit an allowed link between exposure quantities, or use a component-size restriction as if it imposed a drift bound.
What would the finite-sample coverage statement have to say?

It would need to name the coverage target, the applicable finite sample sizes, and the complete class of permitted adoption, interference, exposure-dependence, and drift configurations. For a joint claim about the effects, the relevant event is that both specified targets are covered in the same realization.

The broader objective calls for at least 95% confidence-set coverage uniformly over its stated class. If this finite-sample proof is intended to deliver that objective, it must show the joint event has probability at least 0.95 for every allowed configuration at each covered finite size. The plan has not yet proved that statement.
Why emphasize finite-sample coverage rather than a growing-network approximation?

A finite-sample proof would establish its guarantee for the sizes it covers without relying on a limiting approximation. But it still needs a valid probability calculation for the whole stated class. Enumerating components of at most three cohorts might help make such a calculation explicit; the size restriction alone does not prove finite-sample error control.

The plan does not assert that every possible panel size or network automatically satisfies its component condition.
Would proving 95% coverage separately for the two reported sets meet the joint goal?

No. Two marginal 95% guarantees need not yield 95% probability that both effects are covered together. If the construction is called joint, the proof should control the event of missing either target, with the dependence between their sets taken into account.

It should also specify whether the targets are the true direct and spillover effect values or their entire partially identified sets. Those are different coverage requirements.
How does enumeration translate into a confidence set if we are no longer describing the method as cohort-law inversion?

That translation must be specified. One possible conceptual approach is to retain candidate effect configurations that remain compatible with the joint exposure-component calculation and the stated uncertainty rule. But the plan does not prescribe a particular test statistic, rejection rule, or set-construction formula.

The coverage proof has to connect whatever rule is chosen to the true target under every allowed configuration. It cannot infer coverage solely from having enumerated exposure components.
What does “sub-range” require for each effect?

It requires the direct bound to be strictly narrower than its direct-effect outcome-range bound and the spillover bound to be strictly narrower than its spillover-effect outcome-range bound. Neither point identification nor a single shared effect interval is required.

The plan must say whether this is a statement about population identification bounds or reported finite-sample confidence sets, and whether strict narrowing is meant for every admissible configuration or under other specified conditions. A bound that happens to be narrow in one realization would not establish a general sub-range claim.
Could the component limit ensure coverage but leave the spillover bound at the outcome-range width?

Conceptually, yes. Accurately accounting for exposure dependence can support a valid coverage calculation without necessarily providing enough information to narrow a spillover effect. The direct and spillover comparisons have different support needs, and bounded drift may constrain them differently.

That is why the planned width proof must address both effects separately. A valid joint confidence procedure would not, by itself, demonstrate sub-range widths.
Could using a joint calculation make the reported confidence sets wider?

It might, if accounting for allowed shared exposure information requires more conservative uncertainty calibration. That possibility is not a prediction of the proposed method. The plan’s substantive challenge is to show that it can account for the permitted dependence while the direct and spillover bounds remain below their outcome-range widths under the stated conditions.

Coverage and width must each be established rather than inferred from the other.
What would show that the at-most-three-cohort restriction actually controls the relevant dependence?

A definition of components that places every cohort sharing an exposure input relevant to the targets within the appropriate connected structure, followed by an argument that all dependence permitted by the adoption and interference class is represented in the joint calculation. If dependence can pass between nominal components, the proof must account for that too.

Merely verifying that every listed component contains two or three cohort labels would not show that no relevant exposure connection was omitted.
Should the plan require overlap even though it is not named in the current formulation?

The sub-range proof will have to identify what support is needed for the direct and spillover contrasts. If exposure overlap is necessary for the proposed result, it should be stated as an assumption in the formal theorem, with the relevant cells defined. But this plan does not itself specify an overlap rate or threshold, so one should not attach one to its claim without doing that work.

The component-size restriction addresses the structure of dependence; it cannot silently guarantee that all relevant exposure comparisons have support.
Is three a necessary cutoff for finite-sample coverage?

The plan makes no necessity claim. It proposes joint enumeration for components involving at most three cohorts and seeks a result under that restriction. Establishing coverage and sub-range widths there would not show that a larger component makes either conclusion impossible.

Nor should a finite-sample guarantee be announced simply because components have size three or less. The proof must still handle the specified probability class.
What would count as success for the replacement, stated without assuming it has happened?

A successful argument would define the joint exposure-component enumeration and its admissible adoption and interference configurations, show that it accounts for cross-cohort exposure dependence when every relevant component involves at most three cohorts, and derive confidence sets with the stated finite-sample joint coverage. Under a precisely defined bounded-drift condition and any other explicit support assumptions needed, it would also show that the direct and spillover bounds are each strictly narrower than their outcome-range benchmarks.

Those are the intended proof obligations. Replacing cohort-law inversion specifies the method to investigate; it does not certify either outcome.
Can you state the revised plan in one compact sentence?

Replace cohort-law inversion with joint enumeration of exposure components involving at most three cohorts, and seek proofs of finite-sample joint coverage and separately sub-range direct and spillover bounds under a precisely defined bounded-drift assumption.

I want to extend StaggerNetSim v2 to enumerate three-cohort exposure-adoption laws, then audit Γ=1.5 coverage and direct and spillover widths at exposure-cell overlap ≥0.10 and drift ≤0.05 of the range. How should I describe the activity?

Describe it as an extension and audit, not as a completed coverage result: add enumeration of the specified three-cohort exposure-adoption laws to StaggerNetSim v2, then assess coverage at Γ=1.5 and report direct and spillover widths separately under overlap ≥0.10 and drift ≤0.05 of the stated range.

The important connection is that exposure and adoption are considered jointly in the laws being enumerated. The audit must make clear which laws it covers, what event counts as coverage, and what the width benchmark is before its findings can be interpreted.
Does “three-cohort exposure-adoption laws” mean that every panel has exactly three cohorts?

Not necessarily. The activity specifies enumeration of three-cohort exposure-adoption laws; it does not say that the entire panel has exactly three cohorts. An enumerated law could concern a three-cohort exposure component within a larger setting, depending on how the components are defined.

The extension should specify the unit of enumeration. It should also say whether “three-cohort” covers components of exactly three cohorts or includes smaller components. That should not be inferred silently from the label.
Why enumerate adoption and exposure together?

Because the network exposure used in an effect comparison can depend on adoption in more than one cohort. Enumerating only an adoption pattern without tracking the exposure relationships it induces may fail to represent the dependence relevant to joint inference. A joint exposure-adoption law makes those relationships part of what the audit examines.

That is the intended purpose of the extension. It does not yet establish that the enumeration includes every configuration allowed by the stated interference class.
What would count as an individual law in the enumeration?

That needs a formal definition. At a conceptual level, an enumerated law must specify the aspects of adoption and resulting exposure needed to evaluate the procedure for the relevant three-cohort component. The definition should say which configurations are distinct, which are admissible at Γ=1.5, and which network-exposure relationships each configuration includes.

There is no particular probability model or list of laws in the activity statement, so giving one now would add an unsupported specification.
Does the word “enumerate” guarantee that the audit includes all allowed laws?

No. Enumeration can be complete for a precisely defined class or limited to a specified collection. To call the audit exhaustive over a class, the extension would need to show that every admissible three-cohort exposure-adoption law in that class is represented or safely accounted for.

That distinction matters for coverage: the lowest coverage among enumerated laws is not necessarily the lowest among all laws allowed by a broader, incompletely enumerated class.
How should Γ=1.5 enter the enumeration?

It is the stated sensitivity level for the audit. The extension needs a definition of which adoption laws satisfy the Γ=1.5 restriction and must apply it consistently when constructing the law set and evaluating coverage. A law should not be excluded because it is inconvenient if it remains admissible under that definition.

Γ=1.5 does not by itself define the network exposure mapping or constrain every kind of cross-cohort dependence. Those need their own specification.
Is overlap ≥0.10 supposed to hold for every possible exposure cell?

The relevant floor should be stated for the exposure cells needed by the direct and spillover comparisons being audited. A direct contrast requires support for different own-policy statuses at a fixed relevant exposure; a spillover contrast requires support for different exposures at a fixed own-policy status. Staggered timing may further distinguish the required cells.

The activity gives the numerical condition ≥0.10 but does not list the cells. It should not be described as covering cells unrelated to the targets, nor should an aggregate overlap figure be assumed to cover a required but unsupported cell.
Would overlap ≥0.10 mean that at least one tenth of each realized panel occupies each required cell?

Not if the condition is on exposure-cell probabilities. A probability floor of 0.10 does not ensure that a realized panel has at least 10% in every relevant cell. The audit must distinguish the condition imposed on the laws from realized cell counts used in any calculations.

If empty or very small realized cells affect the procedure, its treatment of those panels should be explicit in the coverage and width measurements.
And how should I explain drift ≤0.05 of the range?

It is a permitted drift of no more than five percent of the specified range, not an assumption of zero drift. The activity does not say which quantity drifts, across which times or comparisons, or exactly how the reference range is defined. Those definitions must be supplied for the audit.

In particular, evaluating only zero-drift laws would not assess the entire class allowing drift through the ≤0.05-of-range limit.
Should the audit include the drift limit when searching for the least favorable coverage?

Yes, if it is claiming to assess coverage throughout the stated bounded-drift class. The coverage calculation must allow every drift configuration permitted by the defined limit, along with the admissible Γ=1.5 exposure-adoption laws. Looking only at a favorable drift value would have a narrower scope.

The activity does not yet specify a search rule or a numerical coverage result. It identifies the condition under which the audit should be conducted.
Could drift and overlap be treated as a single restriction?

They should remain distinct. Overlap concerns support for the exposure and own-status cells used in the contrasts. Bounded drift restricts change in some specified quantity across relevant comparisons. A cell can be well supported even if the permitted drift leaves an effect uncertain; a tight drift bound does not supply observations in an unsupported cell.

The audit should apply both conditions as defined rather than let one stand in for the other.
When it says to audit Γ=1.5 coverage, should I measure coverage of both effects together?

If the intended claim is joint coverage for the direct and spillover effects, the audit should define an event that requires both targets to be covered in the same realization. It should specify whether those targets are true effect values or entire identified sets, since those are different coverage requirements.

The activity says to audit coverage but does not itself spell out that event. Reporting two separate effect-specific rates without a joint event would not assess a joint-coverage claim.
What if I report the worst observed coverage over the enumerated laws?

That would be useful if coverage is evaluated law by law. Call it the minimum measured or calculated coverage over the enumerated three-cohort laws satisfying the stated conditions, and explain how each law’s coverage was obtained. It should not be called a minimum over the entire confounding and interference class unless the enumeration and evaluation truly encompass that class.

A pooled rate over all laws would answer a different question: it could conceal a law with weaker coverage.
Would exhaustive enumeration make the coverage number exact?

Not automatically. Exhaustively listing admissible exposure-adoption laws and calculating the coverage probability under each exactly are different accomplishments. If coverage is assessed through simulated realizations, the reported rates are estimates even if the list of laws is exhaustive. An exact calculation would need the relevant sampling outcomes and their probabilities to be handled as well.

The description of the activity does not state which kind of coverage calculation will be possible.
Can the three-cohort enumeration justify coverage for a network with many components?

Not just because each enumerated component involves three cohorts. One must also address how components relate: they may share inputs or be dependent in ways relevant to the joint statistic. A coverage claim for a larger network requires an argument that the three-cohort component calculations, together with any stated restrictions between components, cover its full dependence structure.

The audit can measure performance in the settings actually evaluated, but a component-size label alone does not extend a coverage calculation to every permitted arrangement of components.
What should be checked when attaching the enumeration to StaggerNetSim v2’s test inversion?

The allowed law class used by the enumeration should match the class used to calibrate the tests. For each candidate direct or spillover value, check that the worst-case calculation considers the appropriate admissible exposure-adoption configurations and that the inversion retains candidates according to the stated rejection rule. The exposure-cell and drift definitions must be consistent across those steps.

These are checks for the extension, not findings that the test inversion is correct or incorrect.
Would the least favorable law have to be the same for direct effects, spillovers, and joint coverage?

No such common law should be assumed. The law most challenging for the direct width, the spillover width, or the joint coverage event could differ, depending on the defined objectives and allowed configurations. Even the least favorable law for a test could change with the candidate effect values being tested.

Enumeration should apply the relevant criterion to each question rather than pick one law because it looks adversarial in general.
What widths should the audit report?

It should report the direct and spillover widths separately, identifying whether they are widths of inverted confidence sets or of underlying effect bounds. To assess whether they are sub-range, compare each with its own outcome-range bound. A single combined width could hide a spillover bound that remains broad even if the direct bound is narrow.

The activity specifies no width results. It calls for measuring them under the stated Γ=1.5, overlap, and drift conditions.
If their average widths are below outcome-range widths, would that prove sub-range bounds throughout the class?

No. An average below the benchmark can coexist with an outcome-range-width bound for some allowed law or realization. Report an average as an average if that is what is measured. A claim that both widths are strictly sub-range under every admissible configuration would require a stronger law-by-law argument or proof.

The audit should keep the width summary and its scope separate from the coverage calculation.
Does the extension itself prove uniformly at least 95% coverage?

No. It creates or uses a means of evaluating three-cohort exposure-adoption laws and audits the procedure’s coverage under specified conditions. Uniform ≥95% coverage is a claim over every configuration in the class named by a theorem, with a precise coverage target and a finite-sample or asymptotic interpretation. The extension and its measurements can inform that claim but do not establish it merely by existing.
Could it find adequate coverage but no narrowing for spillovers?

That is possible in principle. Accounting for dependence can yield a well-calibrated confidence procedure whose spillover set still spans its outcome-range benchmark. It is also possible for direct and spillover widths to differ substantially. The audit needs to retain both measurements so a favorable coverage figure does not conceal an uninformative effect bound.

No particular outcome of the proposed activity should be presumed.
How can I state the activity in one sentence without announcing its results?

“Extend StaggerNetSim v2 to enumerate the specified three-cohort exposure-adoption laws, and audit joint coverage at Γ=1.5 and separate direct and spillover widths for settings with exposure-cell overlap ≥0.10 and drift ≤0.05 of the stated range.” This gives the object, conditions, and measurements while leaving coverage and narrowing outcomes open.

Across 10,000 three-cohort Γ=1.5 panels with overlap ≥0.10 and drift ≤0.05 of the range, minimum joint coverage was 95.1%. Direct and spillover widths were 83% and 91% of range. How should I present this finding?

You could write: “Across 10,000 three-cohort Γ=1.5 panels with overlap ≥0.10 and drift ≤0.05 of the range, minimum joint coverage was 95.1%; direct and spillover widths were 83% and 91% of range, respectively.”

That preserves the conditions and distinguishes the minimum coverage figure from the two effect-specific width figures. It reports the audited panels without claiming a coverage theorem for a broader class.
Does 95.1% meet the at-least-95% target?

Yes, as a reported measurement: 95.1% is 0.1 percentage points above 95%. Because the margin is small, it is especially important to retain the wording “minimum joint coverage” and the scope of the 10,000 panels. The figure alone is not a proof that coverage is at least 95% for every admissible configuration.
What is the minimum taken over?

The finding calls 95.1% the minimum joint coverage, but it does not specify the collection of settings or laws over which that minimum was taken. To make the report fully interpretable, that domain should be identified from the audit. Without it, describe the number as the reported minimum for the three-cohort panels under the stated conditions, not as a minimum over every possible network or adoption law.
Should I treat 95.1% as pooled coverage across all 10,000 panels?

Not without clarification. A minimum across evaluated configurations and a coverage rate pooled across trials are different summaries. The finding explicitly says “minimum joint coverage,” so replacing that with “pooled coverage” could change its meaning. The 10,000 figure describes the panel count; it does not by itself tell us how coverage was aggregated to obtain the minimum.
What does joint coverage mean in this result?

It refers to a coverage event involving the targets together, rather than separate marginal events. In this direct-and-spillover analysis, the natural effect-level reading is that both targets are covered in the same panel. The exact definition of what is covered—true effect values or entire identified sets—should be stated if available.

Either way, 95.1% is not a separately reported coverage rate for the direct effect and another 95.1% rate for the spillover effect.
Can I infer which effect was missed when joint coverage failed?

No. A failure of the joint event could involve the direct target, the spillover target, or both. The minimum joint coverage figure does not provide a breakdown of those possibilities or separate effect-specific coverage rates.
Does “three-cohort panels” mean each exposure component in an arbitrary larger network involves at most three cohorts?

That broader conclusion does not follow from this finding. The reported evidence concerns three-cohort panels. It does not describe how multiple exposure components in a larger network interact, or establish coverage for all networks whose components each involve no more than three cohorts.

Keep “three-cohort panels” attached to the numerical result rather than replacing it with a more expansive network-class description.
Does it say how many panels were assessed at each permissible overlap or drift value?

No. It specifies 10,000 panels under overlap ≥0.10 and drift ≤0.05 of the range, but not their allocation among particular overlap or drift values. It would be inaccurate to say there were 10,000 panels at every combination, or that the minimum applies separately at each value, without further information.
How should I interpret overlap ≥0.10?

It is a lower-bound condition of 0.10 on overlap for the reported panels. To give it a technical interpretation, the audit should define the relevant exposure cells and what its overlap measure is. If it is a probability floor, it should not be described as a guarantee that at least 10% of observations appeared in every required cell of every realized panel.

The concise result can simply retain “overlap ≥0.10” rather than supplying a definition that is not stated here.
Does the finding establish the same 95.1% coverage at overlap exactly 0.10?

It does not report a separate coverage result for overlap exactly 0.10. The stated condition is ≥0.10. Unless the audit identifies coverage at that boundary, the 95.1% minimum should be reported with the condition as given, not reassigned to one particular overlap value.
And is drift ≤0.05 of the range the same as zero drift?

No. It allows drift up to five percent of the specified range, including but not limited to zero. The finding does not identify the quantity whose drift was bounded or give results separately for different permitted drift values. Reporting the condition as ≤0.05 of the range avoids treating the entire audited setting as zero drift.
Does “range” have to mean the same thing in the drift limit and the width ratios?

The report should define each reference so readers can tell. The finding expresses the drift limit as ≤0.05 of the range and the direct and spillover widths as percentages of range. It does not independently specify the scale behind each use of “range.” One should not add an unstated equality between reference ranges if the technical definitions differ.

A concise account can retain the original wording; a technical account should name the relevant range for each quantity.
What do 83% and 91% tell us about the effects?

They describe widths, not effect magnitudes. The reported direct width is 83% of range, while the spillover width is 91% of range. Neither percentage says where an effect lies within its set or gives its sign or value.
Can I say the direct bound was narrower relative to range than the spillover bound?

Yes. The direct width is 83% of its stated range and the spillover width is 91%, an 8-percentage-point difference in those ratios. That is a relative-width comparison. Without the absolute reference widths, it need not imply any particular difference between the two widths in outcome units.
Would it be accurate to describe reductions of 17% and 9% from range?

As arithmetic comparisons of width to the reported range, yes: 83% leaves a 17% difference from full-range width for the direct effect, and 91% leaves a 9% difference for spillovers. Specify that these are differences in width, not reductions in the effects themselves.

The original ratios—83% and 91% of range—are also clear and avoid ambiguity about what is being reduced.
Does that establish that every direct and spillover interval in the audit was sub-range?

The finding does not specify whether the two width figures are averages, values at the least-favorable coverage setting, or some other summaries. It therefore cannot, by itself, establish that every individual direct and spillover interval was narrower than its range benchmark. Report the widths as stated and avoid adding an “every panel” claim.
Can I at least say that both reported widths are below full-range width?

Yes. Both reported ratios are below 100%: 83% for direct and 91% for spillover. That is a comparison of the two reported width figures with full-range width. It should not be expanded into a claim about each admissible law or every realized confidence set without further evidence.
Do the figures prove the direct and spillover effects are point identified?

No. A width below the reference range can still leave many compatible values. Neither 83% nor 91% is zero, and the finding reports no effect endpoint or point estimate. Its width results concern how broad the reported bounds or sets are, not point identification.
Should I call the width figures confidence-set widths or identification-bound widths?

Use whichever term the audit’s measured objects actually warrant. The finding says “direct/spillover widths” without identifying whether they refer to inverted confidence sets or underlying identification bounds. Those are different objects, so the one-sentence report can retain “widths” unless the audit supplies that distinction.
Can I infer a numerical uncertainty interval around the 95.1% from the 10,000 panels?

Not responsibly from the panel count alone. The reported value is a minimum, and its uncertainty would depend on how the panels and the configurations contributing to that minimum were evaluated. The finding gives neither an allocation nor a calculation of uncertainty. It is accurate to report 95.1% as the measured minimum without presenting it as an exact underlying probability.
If 95.1% of 10,000 is 9,510, can I report that count?

The multiplication is correct, but it may not describe this finding. Because 95.1% is reported as a minimum, it need not be a single pooled fraction with all 10,000 panels as its denominator. Without knowing how the minimum was calculated, retain the reported percentage rather than converting it to a count of covered panels.
Does the result prove finite-sample joint coverage at or above 95%?

It reports a minimum of 95.1% in the audited three-cohort Γ=1.5 panels. A finite-sample guarantee would need to establish that the joint coverage probability is at least 95% for every configuration in a precisely stated class at each covered finite size. The panel measurement alone does not supply that class-wide proof.
Could I describe it as uniform coverage across all networks whose exposures involve at most three cohorts?

No. The reported scope is 10,000 three-cohort panels under the specified Γ, overlap, and drift conditions. It gives neither an exhaustive characterization of all such networks nor a coverage argument for arbitrary arrangements of three-cohort exposure components. “Minimum joint coverage in the audited panels” is the supported description.
Does Γ=1.5 explain why the widths are 83% and 91%?

Γ=1.5 is part of the setting under which those widths were reported, but the finding does not isolate its contribution to either width. The observed widths could depend on the defined contrasts, exposure support, permitted drift, and the way the sets or bounds are constructed. No causal explanation for the particular percentages is supplied.
Do overlap ≥0.10 and drift ≤0.05 of the range by themselves imply these width ratios?

No. Those conditions delimit the reported setting; they are not a formula for widths. The 83% and 91% figures are reported results across the three-cohort Γ=1.5 panels under those conditions. They should not be asserted for every procedure or every law satisfying the same inequalities.
Is there a way to state the encouraging part of the finding without turning it into a theorem?

Yes: the reported minimum joint coverage of 95.1% exceeds the 95% target in the audited panels, and both reported effect-specific widths are below full-range width. Those are meaningful comparisons within the finding’s stated scope. They do not establish a uniform coverage guarantee or strict narrowing in every admissible configuration.
Can you give me a compact final wording with that limitation attached?

“Across 10,000 three-cohort Γ=1.5 panels with overlap ≥0.10 and drift ≤0.05 of the range, minimum joint coverage was 95.1%; direct and spillover widths were 83% and 91% of range, respectively. These audited measurements do not by themselves establish class-wide uniform coverage or sub-range widths for every configuration.”

How should I describe StaggerNetSim v3? It replaces cohort-independent inversion with joint enumeration of exposure laws involving at most three cohorts and includes separate direct and spillover coverage audits.

A concise description is: “StaggerNetSim v3 replaces cohort-independent inversion with joint enumeration of exposure laws involving at most three cohorts and provides separate coverage audits for direct and spillover effects.” That states the replacement and the artifact’s contents without claiming that the enumeration is exhaustive over a broader class or that either audit establishes a coverage guarantee.
What does the replacement change conceptually?

It changes what the construction explicitly accounts for. Joint exposure-law enumeration focuses on the configurations that determine exposure across the relevant cohorts, rather than relying on cohort-independent inversion as the organizing method. That distinction matters when exposure quantities may be connected across cohorts.

The description identifies a change in method, not a finding that the new method has solved every dependence or coverage issue.
Does “joint” mean the exposure laws for direct and spillover effects are treated together?

It indicates that exposure-law configurations are enumerated jointly rather than treating the relevant pieces as unrelated. The exact object being enumerated still needs a definition: which exposures are included, how laws are represented, and what relationships between cohorts are retained.

It does not, by itself, say that v3 reports a joint confidence set or a joint coverage percentage. The stated audits are separate for direct and spillover effects.
What does the ≤3-cohort qualification limit?

It limits the exposure-law enumeration to the stated at-most-three-cohort scope. It should not be read as saying that an entire panel can contain only three cohorts, or that a result automatically extends to every larger network assembled from small components. The precise meaning depends on how the relevant exposure laws and their cohort involvement are defined.
Is it accurate to say v3 enumerates exactly three cohorts at a time?

That would narrow the stated condition without justification. “At most three” allows fewer than three as well as three. If a description uses “three-cohort” as shorthand, it should not obscure the ≤3-cohort limit actually specified.
Does the version name imply that the exposure-law enumeration is exhaustive?

No. StaggerNetSim v3 is the artifact’s name. The description says it uses joint ≤3-cohort exposure-law enumeration, but does not establish that every admissible law in a defined class has been enumerated. An exhaustiveness claim would need the admissible class and a demonstration that the enumeration covers it.
What makes an exposure law relevant to the coverage audits?

It must describe exposure configurations used in the direct or spillover comparison being audited. Direct effects concern changes in own policy status at a fixed relevant exposure; spillover effects concern changes in exposure while own status is fixed. The enumeration and audits need compatible definitions of those contrasts.

The artifact statement does not specify an exposure mapping or particular contrast. It tells us what kind of enumeration v3 uses, not every detail of the laws included.
Why are there separate coverage audits?

Direct and spillover effects are different targets, so auditing their coverage separately lets each be examined on its own terms. A single undifferentiated coverage figure could conceal which target is being evaluated.

Separate audits do not imply that the effects are statistically independent. They also do not automatically establish simultaneous coverage of both effects.
If each separate audit looks favorable, can I say the pair has joint coverage at the same level?

Not from separate audits alone. Coverage of each target individually is a marginal property; coverage of both in the same realization is a joint property. A joint claim would require an explicitly defined joint event and an argument or measurement for that event. The v3 description specifies separate direct and spillover coverage audits, not a joint coverage guarantee.
Do the audits prove that the confidence sets cover uniformly?

No such conclusion is stated. An audit can assess coverage for the laws and configurations it actually examines. Uniform coverage is a claim over every configuration in a stated class, with a specified coverage target. The presence of coverage audits in v3 does not supply their findings or a class-wide proof.
Does v3 report particular coverage percentages for the two effects?

Not in the artifact description given here. It identifies separate direct and spillover coverage audits, but supplies no numerical results. It would be inaccurate to assign either audit a percentage or to infer that the two percentages are equal.
Does it say anything about the widths of the direct and spillover bounds?

No width result is specified for StaggerNetSim v3 in this description. Its stated features are the replacement with joint ≤3-cohort exposure-law enumeration and the separate coverage audits. Whether either reported bound is narrower than an outcome-range bound would require an explicit width comparison.
Could I say that enumerating exposure laws guarantees correct inversion?

No. Enumeration and inversion are distinct steps. The description says joint exposure-law enumeration replaces cohort-independent inversion; it does not state that a particular inversion has been proved correct, or even give the rule by which effect values are retained.
