Accuracy and coverage would have to be established for the procedure v3 actually applies.
How should I explain why the enumeration is joint while the coverage audits are separate?

Those words describe different aspects of the artifact. “Joint” describes how exposure laws involving the relevant cohorts are considered. “Separate” describes how coverage for the direct and spillover targets is audited and reported. A common representation of exposure configurations can inform both effects without turning two effect-specific coverage audits into one joint coverage audit.
Does a limit of three cohorts necessarily control dependence between different enumerated exposure configurations?

No. A size limit alone does not say whether two configurations share inputs or are dependent. The enumeration needs a definition that represents the relevant exposure connections, and any inference claim needs to account for dependencies permitted between the pieces it uses.

The stated ≤3-cohort scope tells us what v3 enumerates; it does not by itself establish an independence assumption or a coverage result.
Can I describe the replacement as eliminating the need to think about cohort adoption?

No. Exposure may depend on adoption across cohorts, and the allowed adoption processes remain relevant to what an exposure law permits. The stated replacement changes the organizing construction from cohort-independent inversion to joint exposure-law enumeration. It does not declare adoption irrelevant or remove the need to define the admissible laws.
Does the v3 description specify a sensitivity value, overlap floor, or drift bound?

No. It specifies StaggerNetSim v3, joint exposure-law enumeration involving at most three cohorts, and separate direct and spillover coverage audits. It does not attach a numerical sensitivity value, overlap floor, or drift limit to this artifact description. Those conditions should not be added to a one-line characterization of v3 without an explicit statement tying them to the outputs being described.
Is it fair to call v3 a solution to uniform 95% joint coverage?

That would go beyond the stated artifact. Separate coverage audits do not establish a uniform guarantee, much less uniform joint coverage of both effects at 95%. It is accurate to describe v3’s method and what it audits; any numerical or theorem-level conclusion would need to be stated and supported separately.
What is the safest compact wording if I want the methodological change and both audits in one sentence?
“StaggerNetSim v3 replaces cohort-independent inversion with joint ≤3-cohort exposure-law enumeration and includes separate direct- and spillover-effect coverage audits.”

I want to stress-test StaggerNetSim v3 under cross-component adoption correlations, comparing its worst-case p-values against exhaustive six-cohort binary-adoption laws. What should that comparison tell us?

It should test whether v3’s worst-case p-value calculation still accounts for the adoption dependence relevant to its tests when correlations extend across exposure components. The exhaustive six-cohort binary-adoption calculation supplies a reference within a precisely defined class; comparing p-values for the same test and candidate effect can reveal whether v3’s calculation agrees with that reference or misses a more adverse law.

This is an activity to perform, not a reported finding. The comparison does not, by itself, establish a coverage rate or a result for networks outside the six-cohort binary-adoption class.
What is meant by cross-component adoption correlation?

It means adoption variables associated with different exposure components may be statistically related. A component boundary used to organize exposure laws need not also be a boundary for dependence in adoption. If a worst-case calculation treats components separately, the stress test asks whether permitted correlations between them change its p-values.

The activity does not specify a correlation measure or magnitude. Those would need to be defined to say which correlated laws the test includes.
Does this imply that a component contains more than three cohorts?

No. Correlation can connect adoption across distinct components even if each component individually involves at most three cohorts. Component size and independence between components are different properties.

The six-cohort reference is a way to examine such cross-component relationships. It does not imply a particular partition of the six cohorts, or say that all six belong to one exposure component.
Why use six cohorts for the reference calculation?

Six is the specified size of the exhaustive binary-adoption-law comparison. It permits the reference to consider joint laws across more cohorts than a single at-most-three-cohort component. That makes cross-component correlations a meaningful feature to check if the components are defined accordingly.

The activity does not claim that six is a sufficient size to reveal every possible dependence problem or that findings at six cohorts automatically generalize to an arbitrary number of cohorts.
Does “binary adoption” mean each cohort has only one adoption decision over the whole panel?

Not necessarily. Binary adoption indicates a two-valued adoption status in the reference laws, but the activity does not say whether the binary variable is defined for a particular time, an adoption history, or some other specified cohort-level quantity. That definition must be matched to what v3’s test uses.

It would be premature to infer a number of time periods or a count of admissible laws from the phrase alone.
If the enumeration is exhaustive, does it include every correlation across those six cohorts?

Only relative to the admissible six-cohort binary-adoption laws as formally defined. To make an exhaustive claim, the reference calculation must specify which probability laws and restrictions it permits, then account for all laws in that class, including any allowed cross-component correlations.

Enumerating possible binary adoption patterns is not automatically the same as enumerating every joint probability distribution over them. The scope of exhaustiveness needs to be explicit.
What has to be held constant when comparing the p-values?

The candidate effect or null hypothesis, test statistic, observed data or specified test input, exposure definition, and admissibility restrictions should match. Otherwise two different p-values may simply answer different questions. In particular, v3 and the six-cohort reference should agree on which adoption laws and cross-component correlations count as allowed for the comparison being made.

If their law classes intentionally differ, report that difference instead of interpreting a numerical gap as an implementation error.
What exactly makes a p-value worst-case over adoption laws?

That depends on the test’s definition. For a common composite-null construction, one takes the largest valid tail probability across the admissible laws for the candidate null, so the resulting p-value does not rely on a favorable law. If that is the construction used here, the stress test compares v3’s reported extremum with the extremum from the exhaustive six-cohort calculation.

The activity does not specify a p-value formula. The optimization direction and the laws included must be documented before calling either quantity the worst-case p-value.
Could the worst-case law differ across candidate direct-effect values?

Yes, that is possible. The candidate null and its rejection statistic may change with the effect value, so the least favorable admissible adoption law need not stay the same. The same caution applies to spillover candidates and any joint direct–spillover null.

The stress test should therefore compare p-values for matched candidate tests; it should not assume that finding one adverse law settles every inversion.
If v3 reports a lower worst-case p-value than the exhaustive calculation, what would that indicate?

If both calculations use the same test and admissible class, and the exhaustive calculation truly finds the relevant supremum, a lower v3 value would indicate that v3 has not attained the stated worst case for that comparison. At a fixed rejection threshold, such an understatement could lead to rejecting a candidate that a correctly calibrated worst-case calculation would retain.

That is a conditional interpretation of a possible discrepancy, not a finding that a discrepancy exists. The first check would be that the p-values are defined on exactly the same inputs and law class.
What if v3’s p-value is higher than the exhaustive reference?

Under matched definitions and an exact exhaustive reference, a higher value would also call for an explanation. It could mean v3 includes laws outside the reference class, uses a more conservative calculation, or computes the p-value differently. It would not demonstrate a coverage failure merely by being higher; retaining more candidates may instead widen an inverted set.

The comparison should identify why the numbers differ before assigning an error or a coverage implication.
Would agreement of all compared p-values prove uniform 95% coverage?

No. Agreement would support the correctness of v3’s worst-case p-value computation for the six-cohort tests and admissible laws actually compared. Coverage additionally requires a valid test-calibration argument and a correct inversion rule for the stated coverage target and full class.

It would also not establish behavior for more cohorts or other adoption and interference laws unless a separate argument extends the comparison.
Would disagreement necessarily show that cross-component correlation caused it?

No. A disagreement could arise from differing null definitions, exposure mappings, admissibility constraints, numerical calculations, or how the worst case is taken. The stress test is designed to probe cross-component adoption correlations, but attributing a discrepancy specifically to them requires a controlled comparison in which the other definitions match.

No discrepancy or causal explanation has been reported in the activity as stated.
Should the comparison cover direct and spillover tests separately?

If v3 produces p-values for distinct direct and spillover targets, both types of test should be matched to their corresponding exhaustive-reference calculations. A joint test, if used, needs its own matched comparison. Correctness for a direct-effect test would not automatically establish correctness for a spillover-effect or joint test, since their exposure contrasts may involve different dependencies.

The activity specifies worst-case p-values generally; it does not report which of these tests have already been compared.
Does checking p-values also check whether direct and spillover confidence sets are narrow?

Not directly. P-values determine which candidate effects would be retained under a specified inversion rule, so differences may affect resulting sets. But the activity specifically compares worst-case p-values; it does not report confidence-set widths or a comparison with outcome-range bounds.

A coverage or width conclusion would need additional definitions and calculations rather than being read off the name of the stress test.
How do we avoid ignoring adoption correlations merely because exposure components were enumerated jointly?

Define both the components and the permitted *joint law across* them. Enumerating exposure possibilities within each component does not automatically capture correlations between the adoption variables of different components. The exhaustive six-cohort reference can assess whether those correlations alter the relevant worst-case p-value when they are allowed.

A proof based on componentwise enumeration would need either to incorporate the permitted cross-component laws or to state and justify a restriction that rules them out. Component size alone does neither.
Does the activity prescribe a particular strength or sign for the correlations?

No. It says to stress-test under cross-component adoption correlations without assigning a coefficient, sign, or range. Any tested class of correlations must be stated before the resulting comparison is interpreted. A result for a selected collection would apply to that collection, not automatically to all possible correlated adoption laws.
Should we call the exhaustive calculation a ground truth for every aspect of StaggerNetSim v3?

No. It can be a reference for the specified worst-case p-values within the defined six-cohort binary-adoption class, provided the enumeration and probability calculations are complete for that class. It does not automatically validate or invalidate v3’s other outputs, coverage audits, confidence-set widths, or calculations outside the matched setting.

Calling it a reference calculation for the p-value comparison expresses its role more accurately.
Does “exhaustive laws” mean that a finite list of six-cohort adoption outcomes is enough?

Not necessarily. An adoption outcome is one realization, whereas an adoption law specifies probabilities over possible realizations. Comparing worst-case p-values generally requires accounting for the admissible laws, not just listing binary outcomes. Whether those laws can be enumerated finitely or optimized over another way depends on the restrictions imposed.

The activity says exhaustive six-cohort binary-adoption *laws*, so its reference calculation needs to justify that stronger description.
Could the six-cohort reference include correlations that v3 is not intended to allow?

It could if the two admissible classes are defined differently. In that case, their worst-case p-values need not coincide, and a difference would not on its own show that v3 implemented its own rules incorrectly. The comparison should identify both classes and, where the goal is a matched audit, apply the same restrictions to each.

If the purpose is deliberately to test v3 outside its claimed class, describe it as an external stress test rather than a correctness check within the claimed class.
What about dependence from network exposures, as distinct from correlated adoption?

The two interact but are not identical. The adoption law governs the joint behavior of policy statuses; the network exposure mapping determines how those statuses enter the quantities used in the tests. To compare p-values meaningfully, the six-cohort reference and v3 must use compatible exposure definitions as well as compatible adoption-law restrictions.

Cross-component adoption correlation should not be used as shorthand for every form of network interference. Any claimed inference result still needs a stated interference class.
Is comparing only the worst-case p-values enough to audit the entire inversion?

It audits a crucial input to inversion, but not necessarily the full process. Even if the p-values match, one must apply the same rejection threshold and retain candidate effects according to the defined rule to conclude that inversion matches. The current activity names p-value comparison; it does not state that every resulting confidence set or endpoint is being independently checked.

That narrower scope is useful: it makes clear exactly what the stress test is designed to assess.
Could the result be different at different observed adoption configurations?

Yes, potentially. A p-value calculation is tied to a specified test input, and different observed configurations may produce different test statistics and least-favorable laws. To characterize agreement or disagreement, the stress test should say which inputs were compared.

The activity does not provide any observed configurations or comparison results, so no pattern across them can yet be asserted.
What would count as a successful stress test, without treating it as a theorem?

For matched six-cohort candidate tests and admissible correlated binary-adoption laws, close agreement between v3’s worst-case p-values and the exhaustive reference would support the accuracy of those calculations in the tested domain. Any discrepancies would identify cases requiring examination. Neither outcome, on its own, settles uniform coverage or sub-range direct and spillover bounds across a broader class.

That frames success as a property of the proposed comparison, not a result already observed.
Can you put the activity into one sentence with its scope clear?

“Stress-test StaggerNetSim v3 under cross-component adoption correlations by comparing its worst-case p-values with an exhaustive reference over the specified six-cohort binary-adoption laws, using matched tests and admissibility conditions.” The comparison is intended to audit p-value calculations; it reports no result yet.
On six-cohort adoption grids with cross-component correlation ≤0.15, StaggerNetSim v3 p-values exceeded the exact values, and minimum joint coverage was 95.2%. How should I state that result?

“On six-cohort adoption grids with cross-component correlation ≤0.15, StaggerNetSim v3 p-values exceeded the corresponding exact values; minimum joint coverage was 95.2%.” This preserves both findings and their scope. The result does not give the size of the p-value differences or establish a coverage guarantee beyond the evaluated grids.
Does “exceeded” mean that every v3 p-value was larger than its exact counterpart?

That is the direction of the comparison as reported for the p-values on these grids. To interpret it pair by pair, the v3 and exact values must correspond to the same tests and inputs. The statement supplies no numerical differences, so it does not say whether the excess was small or large, or constant across the comparisons.
Can I describe those p-values as conservative?

You can describe them as higher than the exact reference values in the reported comparisons. If the same rejection rule rejects for sufficiently small p-values, higher values would tend to retain rather than reject more candidate values in those comparisons. Calling the whole procedure conservative for every admissible law or test would be stronger than this result establishes.
Do the higher p-values prove that v3 calculated the exact worst-case p-values correctly?

No. The reported comparison is that v3’s values exceeded the exact values, not that they equaled them. Whether the difference is an intended conservative calibration or reflects a mismatch in definitions cannot be determined from the direction alone. The result establishes the comparison on the six-cohort grids, not an explanation for it.
Does the result tell us what the cross-component correlation actually was in each case?

No. It specifies the condition ≤0.15, not a list of correlation values for individual grid cases. Nor does it define the particular measure of cross-component correlation. The safe wording retains the upper bound and does not recast it as a correlation of exactly 0.15 in every case.
Could I say the comparison applies to arbitrary cross-component correlations?

No. Its stated scope is cross-component correlation ≤0.15 on six-cohort adoption grids. It gives no p-value comparison or coverage figure for correlations outside that condition. Even within it, the result concerns the grids evaluated, not automatically every possible adoption law satisfying the inequality.
What is the difference between six cohorts and six exposure components here?

The finding says six-cohort adoption grids: six refers to cohorts. It does not state a number of exposure components or specify how the cohorts are partitioned among components. Cross-component correlation describes a permitted relationship between components, but the reported result does not identify their count or structure.
How should I read the 95.2% figure?

It is the reported minimum *joint* coverage on the stated grids. It is 0.2 percentage points above 95%. “Joint” concerns covering the specified targets together; “minimum” distinguishes the reported lowest coverage from an average or pooled coverage rate. The finding does not give separate direct- and spillover-coverage figures.
Can I say minimum joint coverage was at least 95% in this stress test?

Yes, as a comparison of the reported measurement with that threshold: 95.2% exceeds 95%. Attach “in the evaluated six-cohort adoption grids with cross-component correlation ≤0.15” so the statement does not sound like a guarantee over a broader class.
Is 95.2% the joint coverage at every grid point?

Not necessarily. A minimum of 95.2% says the lowest reported joint coverage across the collection used for that minimum was 95.2%; it does not say that each point had exactly 95.2%. The precise domain over which the minimum was computed would have to be stated to make a more detailed grid-by-grid claim.
Can I infer that direct-effect coverage was 95.2% and spillover coverage was 95.2%?

No. A joint coverage figure does not provide the two marginal percentages. If the joint event requires both effects to be covered, either or both could be missed when that event fails. The finding does not give the separate failure counts.
Do higher p-values explain why the minimum joint coverage was 95.2%?

They could affect which candidate effects are retained under a matched inversion rule, but the finding does not isolate a causal explanation for the coverage figure. The p-value comparison and the minimum joint coverage are two reported observations on the grids. Connecting them quantitatively would require details of the rejection rule, inversion, and coverage calculation that are not supplied here.
Would higher p-values necessarily make the confidence sets narrower?

No. Under the usual rule that smaller p-values prompt rejection, higher p-values would tend to retain more candidates, which can make inverted sets wider rather than narrower. But the result reports no direct or spillover widths, and it does not specify enough of the inversion rule to calculate a width change. No sub-range-width conclusion follows from these two figures.
Could I use the 95.2% to claim uniform 95% joint coverage over all network-interference configurations?

No. A minimum computed on six-cohort adoption grids under the stated correlation condition is not automatically the infimum of coverage over every allowed network-interference and adoption configuration. The result is bounded by the scope of the grids and the coverage event actually evaluated. A broader uniform guarantee would require an argument spanning the broader class.
What if I call the exact values the true p-values for every six-cohort network?

That would exceed what is reported. They are exact reference values for the comparisons on the specified six-cohort adoption grids. “Exact” does not, by itself, extend the reference to every network, exposure mapping, or adoption law involving six cohorts. Describe them as the corresponding exact values for these comparisons.
Does the ≤0.15 condition prove that cross-component adoption dependence is harmless?

No. The result shows how v3’s p-values compared with exact values and what minimum joint coverage was reported on these grids under that condition. It does not isolate the effect of correlation or establish that every dependence pattern with correlation ≤0.15 is harmless for inference. The correlation measure, admissible laws, and grid scope matter.
Is there any numerical conclusion about direct and spillover bound widths in this finding?

No. It contains two numerical statements: the correlation condition ≤0.15 and minimum joint coverage of 95.2%, plus the directional p-value comparison. It supplies no width values and no comparison with outcome-range widths for either effect.
Could “minimum joint coverage” be treated as an exact finite-sample probability because the p-value reference is exact?

Not on that basis. Exact reference p-values and an exact calculation of joint coverage are different things. The finding does not specify whether 95.2% is an exact calculation or a measured coverage rate, nor does it state the full set of configurations over which its minimum is taken. Keep the reported term “minimum joint coverage” without adding an exact-probability claim.
Can you give me one final sentence that makes the favorable comparison but keeps its limit clear?

On the evaluated six-cohort adoption grids with cross-component correlation ≤0.15, StaggerNetSim v3 p-values exceeded their exact reference values and minimum joint coverage was 95.2%, above the 95% target for those grids; the result does not establish broader uniform coverage or direct and spillover width guarantees.

I want to audit StaggerNetSim v3 against joint-law optimization and assess finite-sample superuniformity and sub-range direct and spillover bounds when overlap is ≥0.10 and drift is ≤0.05 of the range. What should this activity cover?

It has three distinct checks. First, compare v3’s calculations with an optimization over the full joint law specified for the audit, including any permitted dependence between exposure components. Second, assess whether the p-values used for inference are superuniform in finite samples throughout that law class. Third, examine direct and spillover bounds separately against their respective outcome-range widths under overlap ≥0.10 and drift ≤0.05 of the stated range.

Those are assessments to carry out, not findings. Agreement with an optimization, valid p-values, and informative bounds are related but distinct properties; none should be inferred solely from the others.
What is a joint law in this comparison?

It is a law for the relevant adoption and exposure quantities considered together, rather than a collection of componentwise laws whose relationship is left unspecified. To make the audit meaningful, define which quantities the law covers, what dependencies between components are permitted, and what other adoption or interference restrictions it must satisfy.

The phrase “joint-law optimization” does not itself say that every conceivable network or adoption mechanism is admissible. The comparison must name the class over which it optimizes.
Why isn't it enough to optimize each exposure component separately and combine the answers?

Separate optimization can miss constraints or dependencies linking components. If those links are permitted, the combination of componentwise extremes might not describe the correct worst case for the joint test: it could omit an adverse joint law or combine componentwise choices that cannot coexist under one admissible law.

The audit should check the relationship between v3’s calculation and the extremum over admissible *joint* laws. Whether a componentwise shortcut is valid is something to demonstrate, not assume.
Does this mean StaggerNetSim v3 necessarily gets its worst-case calculation wrong?

No. The activity is an audit; it does not announce a discrepancy. Its point is to compare what v3 returns with a well-defined joint-law reference and determine whether the calculation covers the dependence allowed by the audit’s class. Neither agreement nor disagreement has been specified as an outcome.
How should the joint-law reference be defined so that the comparison is fair?

For each comparison, use the same effect candidate or null hypothesis, test statistic, exposure definition, observed test input, and admissibility restrictions for v3 and the reference optimization. Define the optimization objective as well as the domain. Otherwise differing outputs might reflect different questions rather than a problem in either calculation.

If the reference deliberately permits laws outside v3’s specified class, that can be an external stress test, but the difference should not be called an inversion error within v3’s own class without further analysis.
What if the law that maximizes a p-value changes across candidate effects?

Then the comparison should be carried out for the relevant candidates rather than relying on a single selected law. A composite null can have a different least-favorable law for different direct, spillover, or joint candidate values. The audit needs to match the law optimization to the test it is assessing.

Finding one adverse law does not, without an argument, certify a worst-case p-value for the entire inversion.
Can you define finite-sample superuniformity precisely?

For a p-value p under a true null, superuniformity means that, for every threshold α between 0 and 1, the probability of p ≤ α is no greater than α. In a finite-sample, class-wide claim, this inequality must hold at the finite sample sizes covered by the claim for every admissible law relevant to that null.

At the 5% rejection threshold, the inequality gives a false-rejection probability of at most 5%. Checking only that one threshold can address a 95% coverage aim, but full superuniformity is a statement across thresholds, not merely at 0.05.
Does superuniformity require the p-values to be exactly uniform?

No. A superuniform p-value may be conservative: it can fall below a threshold less often than the threshold’s value. Discreteness can also make equality unnecessary. The essential requirement is that it not fall below any threshold too often under any true null in the stated class.

A few relatively large reported p-values would not establish that probability inequality. It concerns the distribution of the p-value across repeated realizations under each admissible law.
Is the superuniformity check supposed to be for the direct and spillover p-values individually?

That needs to match the desired coverage target. If a joint test of a direct–spillover candidate pair is inverted, its p-value must be valid for the joint null. Marginal superuniformity of two separate p-values does not automatically give at least 95% coverage of both effects together.

The audit should specify whether it assesses a joint p-value, separate effect-specific p-values, or both, and not use a marginal finding as a joint guarantee.
How would valid joint p-values lead to joint coverage?

If the true candidate pair satisfies the specified joint null, a finite-sample superuniform p-value for that null makes rejection at the 0.05 threshold occur with probability at most 0.05 under every admissible law. If inversion retains every pair whose test does not reject, the resulting joint set contains the true pair with probability at least 0.95. Separately reported direct and spillover sets can inherit coverage of both coordinates if they include the corresponding projections of that joint set.

Each ‘if’ is part of what must be verified: the null must contain the true target under the stated assumptions, the p-value must be valid over the full class, and the inversion must apply the test as defined.
Would checking only that the v3 p-values are no smaller than an optimized reference p-value prove superuniformity?

Not by itself. That comparison can help audit v3’s optimization if the reference and v3 address the same null and law class. The reference p-value must itself have a valid finite-sample calibration, and the comparison needs to hold for the inputs and admissible laws covered by the claim. Agreement or a conservative ordering at selected inputs is not automatically a distributional proof across all true nulls and realizations.

The activity should keep optimization correctness and superuniformity as separate checks.
Can a worst-case p-value be computed correctly yet fail finite-sample superuniformity?

Yes, if the underlying tests or the reference class do not support the claimed error control. Correctly optimizing a miscalibrated p-value, or optimizing over a class that omits an allowed law, does not create validity. Conversely, an optimization audit can confirm that v3 follows a stated computation without establishing that the stated computation has the required distributional property.

A superuniformity argument must start with a valid test definition and account for every law within its claimed scope.
How does permitted cross-component dependence figure in the superuniformity assessment?

The probability inequality must continue to hold when components have any dependence permitted by the joint-law class. One cannot assume independent component contributions simply because each exposure component is small. If the test statistic uses information from multiple components, correlations between them may affect its distribution.

The joint-law optimization should either represent that permitted dependence or be accompanied by a justification for restricting it. Otherwise a finite-sample guarantee would have a narrower scope than advertised.
Does the overlap ≥0.10 condition itself help make p-values superuniform?

Overlap can make the required exposure comparisons well supported, but it is not by itself a calibration rule. The finite-sample p-value argument still has to account for the permitted adoption, exposure-dependence, and interference laws. A supported cell can contribute dependent information.

The audit should specify which required exposure cells satisfy the ≥0.10 condition and distinguish that support assumption from the superuniformity proof.
Should ≥0.10 be read as a realized proportion in every sample?

Not without an explicit definition saying so. If overlap is a floor on exposure-cell probabilities, a realized sample can have different cell shares. The audit needs to say whether the condition applies to every cell needed by the direct and spillover contrasts and how samples with sparse or empty realized cells are handled by the test.

The numerical floor must remain ≥0.10; its statistical interpretation should be defined rather than inferred.
Does drift ≤0.05 of the range mean drift is fixed at five percent?

No. It allows drift up to the specified limit, including smaller values. The audit must identify what quantity drifts and what range supplies the reference. If its coverage or width claim covers all admissible drift values through 0.05 of that range, evaluating only zero drift or exactly the upper limit would not, by itself, establish the whole claim.
Could the joint-law optimizer ignore drift if it is used only for the width calculation?

That depends on the formally defined test and law class. If permitted drift affects the null distribution, compatibility of candidate effects, or any nuisance configuration used by the p-value, the finite-sample calibration must account for it. If a particular test is shown not to depend on drift, that independence needs to be justified rather than assumed.

For the bound-width assessment, the full permitted drift range must be included wherever it affects the direct or spillover contrasts. Otherwise the resulting sets could look artificially narrow.
What exactly should be compared to decide whether the direct and spillover bounds are sub-range?

For each target, compare its reported width with the width of its corresponding outcome-range bound: direct with direct, and spillover with spillover. ‘Sub-range’ calls for a strict reduction in the stated sense. A narrow direct bound does not compensate for a spillover bound that reaches its full outcome-range width.

The audit must also identify whether it measures population identification bounds or inverted confidence sets. Those are distinct objects, and a width claim for one does not automatically transfer to the other.
Could both widths be below their benchmarks on average while one of them reaches full-range width for an admissible law?

Yes. An average-width improvement does not establish strict narrowing for every law or every realized sample. The activity should state whether it seeks average width ratios, a worst-case bound on width, or a condition under which each target is strictly narrower. Each supports a different conclusion.

Likewise, finite-sample superuniformity can hold while some inverted sets remain as wide as their outcome-range benchmarks. Error control and informativeness are independent proof obligations.
Can a valid p-value produce a particularly narrow realized set that still misses the true effect?

A valid procedure can miss its target in some realizations; a 95% guarantee permits a failure probability of up to 5% under the stated laws. The mere fact that a realized set is narrow says nothing about whether it covers on that occasion. A width assessment should therefore not replace the finite-sample coverage assessment.

Conversely, removing retained values merely to improve width could break the inversion’s coverage guarantee.
Does this audit already assume that StaggerNetSim v3 achieves ≥95% coverage?

No. Finite-sample superuniformity is being assessed, and the width comparison is also an assessment. The activity supplies the artifact to audit and the overlap and drift conditions under which to examine it; it reports no result establishing that either property holds.
What would a failure of the p-value comparison demonstrate?

It would first demonstrate a discrepancy between v3 and the specified joint-law reference for the matched comparison. Interpreting that discrepancy requires checking the domains, nulls, inputs, and optimization objectives. If the reference is valid and exhaustive for the same class and v3 understates the relevant worst-case p-value, that could lead to erroneous exclusions on inversion. But the discrepancy alone would not identify a particular coverage rate or width.

A discrepancy in the other direction could indicate conservatism or a definitional difference. The audit should report what it establishes, rather than assign a cause in advance.
If the optimizer agrees with v3 and the p-values are superuniform, is the sub-range-width part automatic?

No. Correct optimization and superuniform p-values concern whether the tests are calculated as stated and protect their error rate. They do not show that the direct and spillover contrasts are restricted enough to rule out values admitted by the outcome range. A procedure could return valid but full-range confidence sets.

The width check must separately use the defined overlap ≥0.10 and drift ≤0.05-of-range conditions, along with whatever other admissible-law and interference restrictions the bounds rely on.
Can we call the audit finite-sample without giving a degree-growth condition?

A finite-sample property can be assessed without stating an asymptotic degree-growth rate, but it still needs a clearly defined class of finite networks, exposure laws, and sample sizes to which its guarantee would apply. Nothing in the activity specifies a degree threshold. One should not infer one from the fact that the method enumerates exposure laws.

The audit can examine v3 for the stated overlap and drift conditions while leaving any broader graph restrictions to be stated where the test requires them.
How can I describe the activity compactly without implying that the audit has succeeded?

“Audit StaggerNetSim v3 against optimization over the specified joint laws; assess finite-sample superuniformity of the relevant p-values and compare direct and spillover bounds separately with their outcome-range widths under overlap ≥0.10 and drift ≤0.05 of the stated range.” That identifies the artifact, comparisons, and conditions while leaving both validity and sub-range narrowing open.

Shared adoption shocks with correlation 0.30 yielded 91.7% joint coverage across 10,000 Γ=1.5 panels with three-cohort components, overlap 0.10, and drift 0.05 of the range. How should I report this finding?

“Across 10,000 Γ=1.5 panels with three-cohort components, overlap 0.10, and drift of 0.05 of the range, shared adoption shocks with correlation 0.30 yielded 91.7% joint coverage.” That preserves the reported setting and measurement. The observed rate is 3.3 percentage points below the 95% joint-coverage target; it should not be presented as an exact coverage probability for every admissible law.
Does joint coverage mean that each effect separately had 91.7% coverage?

No. Joint coverage concerns the event that the specified targets are covered together in a trial. The 91.7% figure does not give separate direct-effect and spillover-effect coverage rates, or identify which target was missed when joint coverage failed.
Why keep the shared-shock description alongside the correlation number?

They identify the dependence setting associated with this measurement. “Shared adoption shocks” describes the feature being examined, while 0.30 is its reported correlation. Omitting either could make the result sound like it applied to adoption laws with different dependence. The finding does not specify how the shocks were generated or precisely which variables were correlated, so those details should not be supplied without further information.
Is correlation 0.30 a bound, or the value used in these panels?

It is stated as the correlation of the shared adoption shocks in this finding. It is not described as an upper bound applying to a range of correlations. Report “correlation 0.30,” not “correlation ≤0.30,” unless a separate description establishes such a range.
Does Γ=1.5 restrict that correlation to a lower value?

The finding describes the panels as Γ=1.5 while also reporting correlation 0.30. Nothing in the stated result establishes that the correlation violates the Γ restriction. Γ concerns the specified adoption-confounding sensitivity class; its numerical value does not, by itself, define a limit on shared-shock correlation. Those are different properties unless the underlying model explicitly connects them.
Could the shared shocks correlate adoption across different exposure components even when each component contains three cohorts?

Conceptually, yes. Limiting the number of cohorts involved in an exposure component does not automatically make adoption in different components independent. The reported shared-shock correlation is relevant precisely because component size and the joint dependence of adoption are distinct features.

The finding does not describe the exact arrangement of components or shock assignments. It therefore does not establish a specific pathway through which the correlation affected the coverage calculation.
Does “three-cohort components” mean that each panel contained exactly three cohorts in total?

No total cohort count is specified. The phrase describes the exposure components as three-cohort components; a panel could in principle have more than one such component. The numerical result should retain that wording rather than being recast as a result for panels with exactly three cohorts overall.
Does overlap 0.10 mean the finding applies to every setting with overlap at least 0.10?

No. It reports overlap 0.10 for these panels, not a measurement across all overlap values ≥0.10. It also does not say that each realized panel had exactly 10% of observations in every exposure cell. The precise overlap definition would be needed for that interpretation; the concise report should use the value as stated.
And is drift 0.05 of the range the same as a bound allowing any drift up to that value?

The finding reports drift 0.05 of the range. That is a particular stated level, not an observation of coverage across all smaller drift levels. If an assumption elsewhere permits drift ≤0.05 of the range, this reported setting is at that numerical boundary; the result alone does not describe performance throughout the permitted interval.

It also does not identify the drifting quantity or the reference range, so the technical definition would need to accompany any more detailed interpretation.
Can I call 91.7% a minimum over the adoption laws considered?

Not from this finding. It says joint coverage was 91.7% across 10,000 panels under the specified shared-shock setting. It does not call that figure a minimum or specify law-by-law rates. Describing it as a minimum would add a comparison that has not been reported.
If the percentage is exact, is that 9,170 jointly covered trials?

If each of the 10,000 panels contributes one binary joint-coverage event and 91.7% is unrounded, then 9,170 trials were jointly covered. If the percentage was rounded or aggregated in a different way, the exact count is not determined by the figure alone. The reported percentage and trial count are sufficient.
Does this establish that the true joint coverage probability is below 95%?

It establishes that the *measured* joint coverage was below 95% across these 10,000 panels. A finite set of trials does not, by itself, establish an exact underlying coverage probability or a class-wide mathematical guarantee. The finding is a concrete adverse measurement that any claimed 95% joint-coverage result encompassing this setting needs to address.
Should I describe the observed gap as 3.3 percent?

Call it 3.3 *percentage points*: 95.0% minus 91.7% equals 3.3 percentage points. Saying “3.3 percent lower” could suggest a relative percentage calculation, which is different. The absolute comparison with the 95% target is clear.
Does the result show that the p-values failed finite-sample superuniformity?

It does not report p-values or their distribution. Joint coverage below 95% in the panels is relevant to an inversion procedure’s error control, but it is not, by itself, a reported test of superuniformity across all p-value thresholds or all admissible laws. A claim about which p-values fail and why would require additional evidence.
Could we attribute the shortfall specifically to an error in joint-law optimization?

The finding does not isolate that cause. It reports shared adoption shocks with correlation 0.30 and the resulting 91.7% joint coverage in the stated panels, but gives no comparison of optimized p-values with a reference or a diagnosis of the inversion rule. It is appropriate to investigate whether the permitted cross-component dependence was fully accounted for; it is not appropriate to announce an optimization error from this coverage rate alone.
Would it be fair to say that limiting exposure components to three cohorts did not, by itself, ensure 95% measured coverage in these panels?

Yes, with that scope. The panels had three-cohort components, yet their measured joint coverage was 91.7%. Component size alone therefore should not be presented as a sufficient explanation for achieving the 95% target in this reported setting. The finding does not show what would happen under every possible law with three-cohort components or identify which additional restriction, if any, would suffice.
Can overlap and the drift condition still be described as satisfied here?

Report the stated conditions: overlap 0.10 and drift 0.05 of the range. They coincide numerically with floors or upper limits at those values if such assumptions are defined to include their endpoints. Neither condition, however, changes the reported joint-coverage rate of 91.7%, and neither alone establishes how shared-shock dependence was treated in the coverage calculation.
Is the joint-coverage shortfall evidence that the direct and spillover bounds reached outcome-range widths?

No. This finding gives no direct or spillover widths. Coverage and width are different properties: a set can miss a target despite being broad, and an informative-looking set can still fail to cover. The 91.7% figure cannot establish whether either bound was sub-range or equal to its outcome-range benchmark.
Could we conclude which of the direct and spillover effects is responsible for the missing joint coverage?

No. The joint event fails whenever at least one target is not covered. Without separate effect-specific coverage measurements or a breakdown of failures, this result does not identify whether misses involved the direct target, the spillover target, or both.
Does this finding justify a statement about coverage at other correlations?

No. It gives a measurement for shared adoption shocks with correlation 0.30. It does not report a trend, a correlation cutoff, or results for other strengths or forms of cross-component dependence. Any comparison across correlation levels would need its own reported measurements or theoretical argument.
How can I express its bearing on a uniform 95% goal without declaring a theorem disproved?

Say that the measured 91.7% joint coverage is below the 95% goal in the specified Γ=1.5 shared-shock setting. A purported uniform guarantee whose stated class includes that setting would need to account for it, including the possibility of dependence across exposure components. Do not turn the finite-panel measurement into an exact worst-case probability or a mathematical impossibility result.
What would be a compact results sentence that also makes clear what we have not measured?

“Shared adoption shocks with correlation 0.30 yielded 91.7% joint coverage across 10,000 Γ=1.5 panels with three-cohort components, overlap 0.10, and drift 0.05 of the range—3.3 percentage points below the 95% target. This finding reports neither separate direct/spillover coverage rates nor their bound widths.”

I want to limit StaggerNetSim v3 to cross-component adoption correlation ≤0.15 and pursue joint-law calibration. The failures under 0.30-correlated shared adoption shocks preclude unrestricted coverage claims. How should I state that decision?

State the scope and the next task separately: “Limit StaggerNetSim v3’s coverage claims to settings with cross-component adoption correlation ≤0.15, and pursue calibration over the permitted joint adoption laws. Failures under shared adoption shocks with correlation 0.30 preclude claiming coverage without a restriction on cross-component correlation.”

The ≤0.15 limit defines the intended scope; it is not, by itself, a proof of coverage within that scope. Joint-law calibration remains work to pursue.
Does limiting v3 to correlation ≤0.15 mean that coverage at or above 95% has been established there?

No. The decision limits the class for which a coverage claim would be sought. It does not establish that the procedure attains at least 95% coverage uniformly over every admissible joint law with correlation ≤0.15. That still requires a calibrated inference rule and an argument covering the stated class.
Why specify the restriction as cross-component adoption correlation rather than just saying adoption dependence is limited?

Because the decision identifies both the kind of dependence and its numerical limit. Correlation *across components* in adoption is the restriction being imposed, and the bound is ≤0.15. The vague phrase “limited dependence” would not tell a reader what is constrained or which configurations the claim is intended to cover.

A formal statement would also need to define the correlation measure and the adoption quantities to which it applies. The decision itself does not supply those definitions.
Does the ≤ symbol include correlation exactly 0.15?

Yes. As stated, the proposed restriction includes the boundary value 0.15, as well as smaller values that otherwise satisfy the defined class. A proof of a uniform claim over that class would need to cover its boundary too; it should not silently treat ≤0.15 as <0.15.
Could we describe 0.15 as the largest possible correlation compatible with coverage?

No. This is a decision to limit v3’s stated scope to ≤0.15, not a demonstrated sharp cutoff or a necessity result. It does not prove that a correlation just above 0.15 makes valid coverage impossible, or that every procedure must use the same limit.
What exactly is precluded by the failures with 0.30-correlated shocks?

They preclude an *unrestricted coverage claim* for v3 that simply includes those shared-shock configurations without accounting for their behavior. The stated reason does not establish failure under every correlation above 0.15, nor does it rule out a different calibration that handles stronger dependence.

The decision’s narrower response is to restrict the contemplated v3 class and pursue joint-law calibration, not to announce an impossibility theorem.
Since 0.30 exceeds 0.15, can we just say those shared-shock configurations are outside the restricted scope?

Yes, insofar as the same defined cross-component correlation measure is used in both statements: 0.30 exceeds the proposed ≤0.15 limit. But being outside that restricted class does not establish that everything inside it has the desired coverage. The limit sets the claim’s domain; joint-law calibration and its validity argument remain necessary.
What is meant by pursuing joint-law calibration?

It means calibrating the inference procedure while accounting for the permitted adoption variables *together* across components, rather than relying only on component-by-component behavior when their joint dependence matters. The calculation should be matched to the class actually allowed under the ≤0.15 restriction and to the coverage event being claimed.

“Pursue” is deliberate: the decision does not say that the joint-law optimization has been completed, that a critical value has been obtained, or that coverage has been proved.
Would restricting correlation alone make componentwise calibration sufficient?

Not automatically. A bound of ≤0.15 permits some cross-component adoption correlation. Whether a componentwise calculation remains valid under that permitted dependence would need to be shown. Joint-law calibration is being pursued precisely so that a coverage argument can account for the relationships the restricted class still permits.
Should the joint law include network exposures as well as adoption?

A calibration meant to support direct and spillover inference must account for how permitted adoption dependence propagates into the exposure quantities used by the tests. The adoption law, exposure mapping, and allowed interference must therefore be specified consistently. The decision does not prescribe a particular mathematical representation of the joint law, but merely limiting adoption correlation is not a license to omit relevant exposure dependence.
Does limiting v3 mean every output of StaggerNetSim v3 is meaningless outside the ≤0.15 class?

No such blanket conclusion is part of the decision. The limitation concerns the coverage claims being contemplated for v3. It does not declare every calculation outside the restricted class meaningless, nor does it make a claim about the performance of some other procedure there. It says that unrestricted coverage claims cannot be maintained in light of the 0.30-shock failures.
What would a properly qualified 95% statement eventually need to include?

It would need to identify the joint coverage target, the applicable adoption and interference class, the precisely defined cross-component correlation bound ≤0.15, and whether the guarantee is finite-sample or asymptotic. The calibration would then need to justify at least 95% coverage uniformly across every configuration admitted by that class.

That describes the proof obligation. The decision to pursue joint-law calibration does not announce that such a statement has already been established.
Does this decision also guarantee that direct and spillover bounds stay narrower than outcome-range bounds?

No. A correlation restriction and a coverage calibration address the validity of inference under the stated dependence class; they do not automatically yield informative bounds for either effect. Direct and spillover narrowing each require their own comparison with the corresponding outcome-range benchmark under the assumptions actually used.

The decision specifically sets v3’s correlation scope and the calibration direction. It does not report a new width guarantee.
Could we still distinguish direct-effect coverage from spillover-effect coverage under this limitation?

Yes. They remain different targets: changing own policy status at fixed relevant network exposure for a direct effect, and changing exposure at fixed own status for a spillover effect. If a joint coverage claim is sought, its calibration must protect the event that both are covered together; separate effect-specific statements should not be substituted for that joint event.

Restricting cross-component adoption correlation does not merge the two effects or establish their separate or joint coverage by itself.
Would averaging performance over the allowed correlations demonstrate uniformity?

No. Uniformity is concerned with the least favorable allowed configuration, not average performance over configurations with correlation ≤0.15. A calibration or audit should not conceal an unfavorable admissible joint law within a favorable average. The proposed correlation bound defines which laws may be considered, while the uniform guarantee requires error control throughout that class.
Can we say that 0.30-correlated shocks explain every possible failure of joint coverage?

No. The decision identifies failures under shared adoption shocks with correlation 0.30 as the reason unrestricted coverage claims are precluded. It does not diagnose every possible coverage failure or say that correlation alone fully explains them. The intended joint-law calibration still has to account for the specified dependencies within its restricted scope.
How do I make the limitation clear without making ≤0.15 sound like a theorem?

Call it a *scope restriction* and describe calibration as a task: “For StaggerNetSim v3, restrict the contemplated coverage class to cross-component adoption correlation ≤0.15 and pursue joint-law calibration.” Then give the stated reason: “Failures under 0.30-correlated shared adoption shocks rule out unrestricted coverage claims.” This avoids claiming that the restricted class has already been proved safe or that 0.15 is a sharp threshold.

I have a hypothesis for controlling cross-cohort exposure dependence: observed-shock-conditional independence of exposure components involving at most three cohorts, together with Γ=1.5, exposure-cell overlap ≥0.10, and drift ≤0.05 of the range, yields uniform 95% joint coverage and sub-range direct and spillover bounds. How should I state its scope?

State it as a hypothesis, not a guarantee already established. It proposes that, conditional on the observed shocks, the relevant components are independent; each involves at most three cohorts; the adoption sensitivity level is Γ=1.5; the required exposure cells satisfy overlap ≥0.10; and the specified drift is ≤0.05 of its reference range. Under those conditions, the proposed conclusions are at least 95% joint coverage uniformly over the stated class and widths strictly below the respective outcome-range bounds for both direct and spillover effects.

The statement still needs definitions of the observed shocks, components, overlap cells, drift, coverage target, and permitted interference and adoption laws. Those definitions determine what the hypothesis actually covers.
What is the important distinction between conditional and unconditional independence here?

Conditional independence says that, after conditioning on the specified *observed* shocks, the relevant component-level quantities have the independence property needed by the proposed argument. It does not say those quantities are independent before conditioning. Components may remain associated when observations are pooled across different shock values.

The hypothesis must specify which quantities are independent conditional on which observed shocks. Independence of one set of quantities—for example, adoption variables—would not automatically establish conditional independence of the exposure-based contributions used by the joint test.
Does observing a shared shock make conditional independence automatic?

No. Observing it makes conditioning possible; it does not prove that all remaining dependence has been removed. Components could share other inputs or be linked through the exposure mapping in a way that survives conditioning. The conditional-independence assumption needs to be stated for the quantities the inference procedure actually uses and justified within the proposed class.

Nor does “observed” mean the shock can be treated as if its value were fixed without specifying how the conditional tests and their coverage probabilities are defined.
Should the hypothesis say the adoption components are conditionally independent, or the exposure components?

Its wording identifies *observed-shock-conditional independence of the ≤3-cohort components*. To use it for joint coverage, the formal version needs to make clear whether this is a claim about adoption laws, exposure quantities, test contributions, or a combination of them. Those are not interchangeable.

A condition that concerns adoption alone must be connected to the exposure dependence relevant to direct and spillover inference. Otherwise the coverage proof could still omit dependence generated when network exposures share adoption inputs.
If the shocks are observed, can the inference procedure condition on them while keeping Γ=1.5?

That is the proposed approach, but the Γ=1.5 restriction must be defined consistently with the conditioning. The procedure should specify which adoption laws remain admissible at Γ=1.5 for the observed shock values and ensure the conditional calculation considers the full permitted class.

Conditioning on observed shocks does not make unmeasured adoption confounding disappear. Γ=1.5 still represents the stated sensitivity level for whatever unmeasured confounding the formal model allows.
Does the hypothesis also impose a numerical cap on correlation across components?

Not as written. Its dependence restriction is conditional independence given observed shocks, not a stated numerical correlation bound. Conditional independence need not translate into a particular unconditional correlation limit, because marginal associations can depend on how the observed shocks vary.

A numerical correlation cap should not be added to this hypothesis unless it is expressly made another assumption.
Could unconditional cross-component correlation coexist with the conditional-independence assumption?

Conceptually, yes. If components respond to a common observed shock, they can be associated before conditioning even if the defined component quantities are independent once that shock is held fixed. That is why the coverage calculation must use the conditioning argument it claims, rather than assume unconditional independence.

This is a general distinction, not a finding that conditional independence holds for any particular network or set of shocks.
What must a component include for the ≤3-cohort restriction to be meaningful?

A component definition must capture the cohorts connected through the exposure information relevant to the effect contrasts and joint test. Every relevant shared exposure input must be represented. If the construction labels two groups as separate while an unaccounted link makes their test contributions dependent even after conditioning on observed shocks, the component restriction would not supply the assumed independence.

The “≤3” limit applies to cohorts per component, not necessarily to the number of components or the total number of cohorts.
If each component is small, can I simply multiply component-level probabilities to calculate joint coverage?

Only if the particular events or contributions being combined are conditionally independent given the observed shocks under every law in the stated class, and if the calculation handles the conditional distributions correctly. A small component size does not itself authorize multiplication.

Even where conditional factorization is valid, one still needs to calibrate the *joint* direct-and-spillover coverage event. Component-level or effect-specific probability calculations cannot just be multiplied without establishing that the necessary independence applies to those events.
Does overlap ≥0.10 have to be conditional on the observed shocks too?

That must be decided in the formal statement. An unconditional exposure-cell probability floor and a floor that holds at each relevant observed-shock value are different assumptions. If the conditional calculation needs support within shock strata, aggregate overlap ≥0.10 might not provide it.

The hypothesis supplies the numerical floor, not its conditioning level or the list of required cells. A proof should state exactly where ≥0.10 holds and which direct and spillover contrasts it supports.
Can overlap at 0.10 guarantee that both effect bounds are sub-range?

No. It ensures a proposed level of support only once the relevant exposure cells are defined. Γ=1.5, bounded drift, and the permitted interference configurations may still leave an effect compatible with every value allowed by its outcome-range bound. The width argument must demonstrate actual exclusion of some outcome-range-compatible values for the direct target and separately for the spillover target.

The ≥0.10 floor is a specific condition in the hypothesis, not a formula for either bound’s width.
What is drift ≤0.05 of the range meant to allow?

It allows the specified quantity to drift by no more than 0.05 times its stated reference range—five percent of that range. It does not require zero drift. The hypothesis must identify what drifts, across which timing or exposure comparisons, and which range supplies the scale.

Both the coverage calculation and the width calculation must accommodate the drift values permitted by the formal bound wherever drift affects them. Assuming zero drift would test a narrower class.
Could the range in the drift condition be different from the outcome-range benchmark for a direct effect?

The wording alone does not establish that they are identical. The ≤0.05 drift condition needs a specified reference range, while the sub-range-width claim needs the appropriate outcome-range benchmark for each effect. A technical statement should define each so the numerical drift restriction and the width comparisons are unambiguous.

One should not infer a particular outcome scale or an equality of reference ranges merely from the shared word “range.”
How should the proposed 95% claim deal with different observed-shock values?

It must state whether the ≥95% joint coverage guarantee is intended conditionally for each shock value in a specified support, or marginally after averaging over shocks while holding uniformly over the stated law class. A conditional guarantee that holds for every relevant shock value can support a corresponding marginal guarantee, but a marginal claim alone need not imply conditional coverage for each value.

The hypothesis currently says “uniform 95% joint coverage” without making that choice. Naming the conditioning and the uniformity domain is essential to a precise proof.
What exactly is joint coverage in this hypothesis?

For an effect-value target, it is the event that the reported direct set contains the true direct effect *and* the reported spillover set contains the true spillover effect in the same realization. If the goal is instead to cover both entire partially identified sets, that is a stronger event and must be named explicitly.

Two separate marginal 95% statements do not automatically imply the desired joint 95% statement. The tests or confidence-set construction must control the event of missing at least one target under every law it claims to cover.
Is the 95% guarantee supposed to be finite-sample?

The hypothesis states uniform 95% joint coverage but does not expressly say finite-sample or asymptotic. If the intended claim is finite-sample, it must establish the coverage probability at each sample size within its stated scope for every allowed configuration. If it is asymptotic, the uniform worst-case limiting statement needs to be specified instead.

The component-size limit and conditional-independence assumption do not settle that distinction on their own.
Could a joint-law enumeration establish coverage if it enumerates only exposure patterns, not the conditional probabilities given shocks?

Not merely by listing patterns. A coverage argument needs the conditional or joint laws governing the relevant test outcomes under the admissible adoption and interference configurations. An enumeration of possible exposures that leaves their probabilities or cross-component relationships unspecified may identify candidates but not calibrate a joint error probability.

A proposed enumeration must match the formal observed-shock-conditional class. Whether it can be exhaustive or yields finite-sample error control remains something to demonstrate.
If each conditional p-value is superuniform, does that prove joint coverage of direct and spillover effects?

Only if “each” refers to a correctly calibrated *joint* test for the relevant candidate pair, or an alternative construction whose combined error is controlled at the required level. Separately superuniform direct and spillover p-values do not alone ensure 95% joint coverage after inversion.

The argument must connect the conditional testing event, the permitted Γ=1.5 laws and interference, and the final two reported sets. It then needs to establish uniformity over the stated class and any shock values included in the conditional claim.
Does conditional independence ensure sub-range widths as well as coverage?

No. It may permit an appropriate coverage calibration, but it does not create informative exposure comparisons by itself. The separate width claim must show that overlap ≥0.10, drift ≤0.05 of the range, Γ=1.5, and the defined interference assumptions together restrict the compatible effect values enough that both widths are strictly below their outcome-range benchmarks.

A conservative joint procedure can be valid and still return a full-range bound for either effect.
Should “sub-range widths” apply to every realized confidence set?

That has to be specified. Strict narrowing of population identification bounds, strict narrowing of every realized confidence set, and narrowing under an explicitly stated probability or averaging criterion are different claims. The unqualified phrase “yield sub-range direct/spillover bounds” may sound universal, so a proof should define both the object and the scope of the width comparison.

Whatever is chosen, direct and spillover widths must each be compared with their own outcome-range benchmark; a result for only one does not establish the paired conclusion.
Can a shock value make an exposure cell rare even when the overall overlap floor is ≥0.10?

Conceptually, yes: an aggregate probability floor need not persist within every conditioning stratum. That is why the formal overlap condition must match the conditioning required by the inference and width arguments. If support at particular shock values is necessary, the hypothesis should state a conditional floor there; if only aggregate support is needed, the proof must explain why.

This is a possible distinction in definitions, not a claim that any cell is rare in a particular panel.
What class must the word “uniform” range over?

It must range over the full class actually stated in the theorem: Γ=1.5-bounded adoption laws, the permitted network-interference and exposure relationships, the observed-shock-conditional independence structure for components of at most three cohorts, the defined overlap ≥0.10 condition, and drift ≤0.05 of its range. If some shock values or component arrangements are excluded, those exclusions must be explicit.

A guarantee over a selected enumerated collection is not automatically uniform over a broader class with the same short labels.
Does this hypothesis say that conditional independence is necessary for 95% coverage?

No. It proposes conditional independence, together with the other stated restrictions, as a sufficient route to the two desired conclusions. It does not assert that coverage or informative bounds are impossible when components remain dependent after conditioning, nor that three cohorts, 0.10 overlap, or 0.05-range drift are sharp cutoffs.
What would a proof need to show, in a compact sequence?

Define the observed shocks and the component quantities, and show that the permitted cross-component exposure dependence is captured by their conditional-independence assumption. Specify the Γ=1.5 adoption class, interference class, required exposure cells, ≥0.10 overlap condition, and drift bound of ≤0.05 of the stated range. Calibrate the joint procedure for the defined coverage target and prove its 95% guarantee uniformly in the stated finite-sample or asymptotic sense. Finally, establish separate strict comparisons of direct and spillover widths with their respective outcome-range bounds.

That is a list of proof obligations for the hypothesis, not a statement that any obligation has already been met.
Can you phrase the working hypothesis in one sentence without turning it into an established result?

“We hypothesize that, when relevant exposure components each involve at most three cohorts and are independent conditional on the specified observed shocks, Γ=1.5-bounded adoption, exposure-cell overlap ≥0.10, and drift ≤0.05 of the stated range suffice for uniformly at least 95% joint coverage of the defined direct-and-spillover target and for each effect’s bound to be strictly narrower than its corresponding outcome-range bound.” The conditioning, admissible class, coverage interpretation, and width claim remain to be defined precisely and proved.

I want to condition StaggerNetSim v3 on observed shocks, test whether its joint-test p-values are superuniform, and simulate coverage and separate direct and spillover widths at Γ=1.5. How should I frame the activity?

Frame it as an evaluation with three connected parts. First, specify how the observed shocks enter StaggerNetSim v3’s joint exposure-law calculation. Second, assess whether the resulting joint-test p-values are superuniform under the relevant conditional laws. Third, simulate Γ=1.5 panels to measure joint coverage and the widths of the direct and spillover sets separately.

These are checks to perform, not results. In particular, conditioning on observed shocks does not itself establish superuniformity, and simulated coverage does not by itself prove a uniform guarantee.
What does it mean to condition v3 on an observed shock?

It means that the test and its law calculation use the observed shock value as part of what is held fixed when defining the relevant conditional distribution. The procedure must say which shock is observed, which quantities are conditioned on it, and which admissible adoption and exposure laws remain possible at that value.

Conditioning is more than adding a shock label to the output. The p-value calculation and the interpretation of its coverage claim must use the same conditional law.
Does an observed common shock make exposure components independent once we condition on it?

Not automatically. The intended conditional-independence property has to apply to the component quantities used by the joint test. They might still share exposure inputs or have other permitted dependencies after the shock is held fixed.

The activity can test the procedure under a specified conditional class, but merely observing a shock is not evidence that every remaining cross-component relationship has disappeared.
Would it be enough to condition the adoption-law enumeration but leave the test statistic unchanged?

That depends on how the statistic and its reference distribution are defined. If the statistic uses exposure information whose conditional distribution changes with the observed shock, the law calculation used to calibrate it must reflect that change. An unchanged statistic is not inherently a problem; an inconsistent pairing of statistic and conditional calibration would be.

The audit should trace the conditioning through the joint-test calculation and its inversion, rather than assume that changing one input makes the entire procedure conditional.
What exactly should be tested for superuniformity?

For a joint null that is true under an admissible conditional law, its p-value should satisfy Pr(p ≤ α | observed shock) ≤ α for thresholds α between 0 and 1, if conditional finite-sample superuniformity is the intended property. The probability and the conditioning event must be defined for the shock values to which the claim applies.

A test at the 0.05 threshold is directly relevant to a 95% coverage aim, but full superuniformity is stronger: it concerns every threshold, not just 0.05.
Why emphasize the joint test rather than separately testing direct and spillover p-values?

Because the intended coverage event may require the direct and spillover targets to be retained together. Separate superuniform p-values for two marginal nulls do not automatically make the probability of covering both targets at least 95%.

The activity specifically calls for testing *joint-test* superuniformity. Its joint null, p-value, and inversion rule should therefore be defined for the pair of effects or for another explicitly named joint target.
Could a joint-test p-value be superuniform at some observed shock values but not others?

Yes, that is a possibility the scope of a conditional claim must address. If superuniformity is asserted for every relevant observed-shock value, a favorable average across shock values is not enough. If the intended claim is only marginal coverage after averaging over shocks, it should be stated as such instead.

The proposed assessment should distinguish results by the conditional domain it actually examines; it should not silently move from selected shock values to all possible values.
Does conditioning on observed shocks remove Γ=1.5 adoption confounding?

No. Γ=1.5 remains the stated sensitivity level for the simulated coverage assessment. The conditional procedure still has to account for the adoption laws allowed at that level after the observed shocks are taken into account. An observed shock and unmeasured adoption confounding are not interchangeable concepts.

To assess the activity consistently, the conditional joint test and the Γ=1.5 simulations should use the same defined sensitivity restriction.
What if the set of admissible laws changes with the shock value?

Then the conditional joint-test calculation must use the admissible laws appropriate to the value being conditioned on. A law that is permissible at one shock value need not be assumed permissible at another, and a law that remains allowed should not be dropped merely because it challenges calibration.

The activity does not specify how those law sets are constructed. Making them explicit is part of evaluating whether the conditional p-values have the claimed property.
Can the simulation test superuniformity as well as coverage?

Simulation can probe both by examining how often joint-test p-values fall below chosen thresholds under the simulated conditional laws, and by checking how often the inverted sets cover the specified targets. Those measurements are related but not identical: a p-value assessment concerns the distribution of the test under its null, whereas a coverage assessment concerns the sets returned after inversion.

Finite simulations cannot establish the probability inequality for every threshold, shock value, and admissible law. A claim of uniform finite-sample superuniformity would require an argument covering that stated domain.
If the p-values satisfy the inequality at α=0.05 in the simulations, may I call them superuniform?

Not on that observation alone. Performance at α=0.05 addresses one rejection threshold in the simulated settings. Superuniformity concerns all α in the claimed range and all relevant true-null laws. It is more precise to say that a simulation assessed rejection frequency at the 0.05 threshold if that is what was measured.

Nor does a simulated frequency, by itself, certify an exact finite-sample inequality even at that threshold.
