It does not itself state an overlap floor or a numerical drift allowance. Any support or drift restrictions needed to derive bounded weights or sub-range widths must be made explicit in the formal argument; they should not be silently supplied by the component count.
What if the sensitivity envelope remains broad no matter how small the Hoeffding radius gets?

Then increasing the number of independent components would address sampling error without necessarily narrowing the final compatible effect bound below the outcome-range benchmark. The derivation should expose that possibility by separating the envelope allowance from the sampling radius and evaluating the resulting width for each effect.

The plan to certify 4,000 components calls for ruling out full-range width under its stated assumptions, not assuming that a small concentration radius is enough.
Does a proof for exactly 4,000 components extend automatically to more components?

Not without showing that the relevant contribution bounds, exposure support, collection of simultaneously covered quantities, and envelope width behave appropriately as the count increases. The plan names 4,000 as the certification point; a conclusion for every count above 4,000 requires a justified extension.

Likewise, proving sufficiency at 4,000 would not establish necessity: a smaller count might also work under some assumptions.
Could some of the 4,000 components be irrelevant to the spillover contrast?

If so, counting all 4,000 as informative repetitions for the spillover band would be unjustified. The derivation must identify which conditionally independent component contributions support each required exposure-specific quantity, and use the relevant count and bound in its radius. A total component count cannot replace adequate information for a least-supported spillover comparison.

The same check applies to the direct contrast, though its limiting cells need not be the same.
How should I ensure the claimed conditional independence matches the actual weighted statistics?

Define components from the exposure and adoption inputs that enter the Horvitz–Thompson contributions, then state independence for those contributions conditional on the specified observed shocks. Check that no permitted cross-component shared input or dependence in the joint conditional law has been omitted. A component partition that is convenient for computation but fails that requirement would not support the Hoeffding radii.

This is part of the proposed proof, not an assertion that the property already holds.
Can a proof be uniform over Γ=1.5 laws yet fail to be uniform over observed-shock values?

Yes. A worst-case argument over conditional adoption laws at one observed-shock value may still rely on weight or contribution bounds that change at other values. A uniform claim needs to specify both its law class and its shock-conditioning scope. If the radii and envelopes vary with shocks, their validity must be established wherever the stated coverage guarantee applies.

If only particular shock values are covered, the conclusion should be expressly restricted to them rather than described as uniform without qualification.
What is the logical order between deriving the radii and proving the width inequalities?

The width inequalities need the actual justified radii, so deriving the latter first makes the 4,000-component certification check meaningful. The coverage proof then verifies that those radii and the envelope yield the intended simultaneous guarantee. Finally, compare the resulting effect-specific widths with their benchmarks.

The coverage and width arguments may share derivations, but neither substitutes for the other. It would be premature to announce sub-range widths from a proposed Hoeffding formula before showing that formula is valid for the shock-conditional components.
Can you state this as a compact plan without implying that 4,000 has already passed?

Derive the Γ=1.5 shock-conditional envelope-bias allowances and simultaneous component-level Hoeffding radii; prove that their combination gives the stated uniform joint coverage; then check whether, at 4,000 qualifying components, both the direct and spillover widths are strictly below their respective outcome-range bounds. The coverage guarantee and the 4,000-component certification remain proof targets.
I want to compute worst-case Hoeffding radii at 1,000–8,000 independent components, then verify Γ=1.5 direct and spillover widths and joint 95% coverage. How should I describe the activity?

Describe it as an assessment across component counts from 1,000 to 8,000. At each count examined, compute Hoeffding radii valid for the worst case in the specified class, use those radii with the Γ=1.5 sensitivity envelopes to assess direct and spillover widths separately, and check the intended joint 95% coverage property.

The activity states what will be computed and verified; it supplies no radii, widths, coverage results, or component-count threshold yet.
Does 1,000–8,000 mean we already have a radius for every integer count in that range?

No. It specifies the range of independent-component counts to examine, not the spacing of evaluated counts or any completed calculation. If only selected counts are checked, results should be reported for those counts rather than described as calculations for every integer from 1,000 through 8,000.
Why examine a range of counts instead of just one count?

The range allows the proposed uncertainty and width calculations to be checked as the number of independent components changes. It can help identify whether a candidate count is sufficient under the defined assumptions, rather than relying on one calculation without context.

No particular direction or threshold in the results is given. Even if radii decrease over evaluated counts, that would not alone establish that both effect bounds become sub-range.
What makes a Hoeffding radius worst-case?

Its calibration must protect the intended sampling-error event for every component-contribution distribution admitted by the stated class, not just one favorable law. That requires identifying the bounded component-level quantities, the independence condition, the observed shocks if conditioning is used, and the allowable Γ=1.5 adoption and interference configurations relevant to the calculation.

“Worst-case” is meaningful only relative to that defined domain. A radius calculated for one selected weighting law cannot simply be called worst-case over all permitted laws.
Is Γ=1.5 itself the Hoeffding radius?

No. Γ=1.5 is the stated adoption-sensitivity level. A Hoeffding radius quantifies sampling uncertainty for specified bounded, independent contributions at the required coverage calibration. Its numerical value depends on the contributions and the number and collection of quantities being protected; it cannot be read off Γ alone.
What would the component count refer to in the calculation?

It should count the independent component-level contributions actually relevant to the weighted exposure quantities being bounded. It is not automatically a count of units, cohorts, or network links. If an effect contrast uses only some of those components, the radius for its required quantities must reflect the support it actually has.

The activity does not specify the component construction, so that definition is an essential part of carrying it out.
Can I regard components as independent simply because they were partitioned into separate groups?

No. Independence must hold for the contributions used in the Hoeffding calculation under the claimed adoption and interference class. Components that share an unaccounted exposure or adoption input may remain dependent even when they have different labels. If the intended argument conditions on observed shocks, the corresponding conditional independence must be established for those same contributions.
Does the activity itself specify shock-conditional independence?

It says to compute at 1,000–8,000 independent components, but does not independently specify a shock variable or how conditioning works. If the radii are meant to be shock-conditional, the activity needs to define the observed shocks, the conditional component contributions, and the shock values over which validity is claimed. It would be premature to attribute a conditional guarantee to the calculation without those definitions.
What needs to be bounded to use Hoeffding here?

The component-level contributions entering each relevant exposure-specific statistic need applicable bounds, along with the independence structure used in the inequality. Horvitz–Thompson weighting can magnify outcome contributions, so the outcome range alone need not bound the weighted quantities tightly enough; relevant exposure probabilities and permitted weights matter.

A worst-case radius must use contribution bounds that remain valid throughout the claimed Γ=1.5 and interference class. The activity does not provide numerical bounds or a resulting radius.
Should we compute a separate radius for every direct and spillover quantity?

That depends on the construction. Different exposure-specific quantities can have different contribution bounds and component support, so they may need different radii. A common radius could instead be used if it is proved valid for every quantity it purports to protect.

In either case, if the coverage claim is joint, the calibration must protect all quantities needed by both effects simultaneously. Separate marginal 95% radii do not automatically give a joint 95% event.
What is the distinction between verifying the radii and verifying joint coverage?

A valid radius controls sampling deviations for its specified quantity or simultaneous collection under the stated assumptions. Joint *effect* coverage additionally requires that the Γ=1.5 envelopes and the rule forming the direct and spillover sets retain both true targets whenever the protected deviation event occurs.

The coverage check must therefore trace the calculation through the envelopes to the final sets. Having correctly computed a concentration radius is not, on its own, a proof about the reported effect sets.
Could I check only that each set has 95% marginal coverage?

Not if the claim is joint 95% coverage. The relevant event must require both the direct target and the spillover target to be covered in the same realization. Marginal coverage of each at 95% does not generally imply that their intersection also has probability at least 95%.

The activity should define whether those targets are true effect values or entire identified sets; those are different joint coverage requirements.
What does it mean to verify joint 95% coverage uniformly?

It means establishing at least 0.95 coverage of the specified joint target for every configuration in a clearly defined confounding and interference class, in the finite-sample or asymptotic sense chosen. If the aim is finite-sample validity, the probability statement must hold at every evaluated size to which the guarantee is extended, rather than just at a favorable count.

An assessment at selected counts from 1,000 to 8,000 does not automatically extend to every count or to laws outside those actually addressed. A mathematical argument or an explicitly limited result must match the scope claimed.
Does computing a worst-case radius prove uniform coverage automatically?

No. The calculation must first truly encompass the allowed component contributions and their dependence. Then the simultaneous-band event must have the required probability across that class, and the envelope-to-effect-set step must preserve both targets on that event. Any omitted allowed weighting law or relevant exposure dependency would leave a gap in a uniform claim.

“Worst-case” describes the intended calibration, not a guarantee created by naming it.
How should direct and spillover widths be measured?

Measure them separately for the sets or bounds that the Γ=1.5 envelope-and-band procedure actually produces. State whether a width is for a population identification bound or an uncertainty-bearing confidence set, and compare it with the outcome-range bound for the *same* effect if sub-range width is the criterion.

A direct bound can improve while a spillover bound does not. A combined width or a narrow exposure-specific input band would not settle the required two effect-specific comparisons.
If both radii shrink as the count rises, does that certify sub-range widths?

No. The Γ=1.5 envelope can retain a range of effects even with precise weighted quantities, and any permitted drift or poorly supported exposure contrast can add uncertainty. A smaller sampling radius only reduces one source of width.

At each count for which narrowing is claimed, the full direct and spillover bounds need to be compared strictly with their respective outcome-range benchmarks.

If the planned widths or concentration bounds rely on an overlap condition, the relevant exposure cells and the condition must be specified as assumptions of the calculation. Does it impose a bounded-drift value?

Could a sufficient radius at 4,000 be used unchanged at 1,000?

If the radius is valid at 1,000, does that make the width informative at 1,000?

Could the width comparison be favorable on average while some counts or allowed configurations remain full-range?

Yes. An average width below a benchmark need not imply a strict improvement at every component count or for every admissible law. Could simulation verify the 95% coverage part?

Simulation could measure joint coverage for the panels and laws simulated at selected component counts. The activity does not state a simulation count or any measured rate, so neither should be supplied as a finding.
What would be a careful way to compare results across the component counts?

For each evaluated count, report the worst-case Hoeffding radius for its defined simultaneous event, the separately calculated Γ=1.5 direct and spillover widths with their respective benchmarks, and the status of the joint 95% coverage argument or measurement. Use the same effect and exposure definitions across counts, and document if the admissible law class or required cells change.

This makes it possible to distinguish a smaller radius from actual narrowing and from a demonstrated coverage guarantee. It prescribes reporting categories, not numerical results.
Can we infer from the activity which count first makes both widths sub-range?

No. The first qualifying count, if there is one in 1,000–8,000, can be identified only after the radii, envelopes, and effect-specific widths have been derived and evaluated under the declared assumptions. A finite set of checked counts also would not establish the smallest possible qualifying count between them without an additional argument.

“Compute worst-case Hoeffding radii for evaluated counts of 1,000–8,000 independent exposure components, then check Γ=1.5 direct and spillover widths separately against their outcome-range bounds and verify the stated joint 95% coverage claim.” The radii, width comparisons, and coverage conclusion remain to be established.

At 4,000 independent components, the Γ=1.5 Hoeffding calculation certified at least 95% joint coverage and direct and spillover widths no greater than 94% and 98% of range, respectively. How should I report that result?

“At 4,000 independent components, the Γ=1.5 Hoeffding calculation certified at least 95% joint coverage; direct and spillover widths were bounded above by 94% and 98% of range, respectively.” This keeps the coverage certification distinct from the two effect-specific width bounds. Does this say the coverage was exactly 95%?

No. The certification is for coverage of at least 95%. It does not give an exact coverage probability or say how far above 95% coverage might be. It is also a calculation-based certification, not a reported fraction of covered simulation trials.
What is being covered jointly?

“Joint” means that the coverage claim concerns the required targets together, not a separate 95% statement for each effect considered in isolation. For a direct-and-spillover confidence-set interpretation, the event would require both targets to be retained in the same realization.

Can I report separate 95% coverage rates for the direct and spillover effects?

No separate rates are given. A certified joint coverage guarantee has implications for the event it protects, but it is not a measurement that assigns each effect its own numerical coverage rate. Report the at-least-95% *joint* certification as stated.
How should I read the 94% and 98% figures?

They are upper bounds on widths relative to range. The direct width is no more than 94% of its stated range, and the spillover width is no more than 98% of its stated range. They are not effect estimates, coverage percentages, or necessarily the widths actually attained by particular reported sets.
Are both widths sub-range?

Yes, by the certified comparisons at 4,000 independent components: each stated upper bound is strictly below 100% of range. The direct bound is at most 94%, and the spillover bound is at most 98%. The spillover guarantee leaves less room below full-range width, but it is still strictly sub-range as stated.
Could I call those 6% and 2% reductions?

You can say the direct-width upper bound is six percentage points below full-range width, and the spillover-width upper bound is two percentage points below it. Because the results are inequalities, the widths may be narrower still. Avoid saying the effects themselves were reduced by 6% and 2%; the comparison is about width.
Does the direct bound have to be narrower than the spillover bound?

Not in absolute width based on these ratios alone. The direct *upper limit relative to its range* is 94%, compared with 98% for the spillover upper limit relative to its range. Their actual widths could lie below those limits, and the corresponding range benchmarks need not have the same absolute width. The precise comparison is between the stated relative upper bounds.
Is the spillover effect nearly point identified if its width is at most 98% of range?

No. A width that can be as large as 98% of range is still a bound over potentially many effect values. The result establishes strict narrowing relative to range, not point identification, a particular effect value, or a claim about its sign.
What role does the count of 4,000 play?

It is the component count at which the reported Hoeffding calculation delivered both the joint coverage certification and the two width inequalities. The result refers to *independent components*, not 4,000 units or cohorts. It does not state the number of units in a component.
Can I extend the certification to every count above 4,000?

That extension is not stated in the finding. It might follow under additional conditions that make the relevant radii and envelope-width comparisons behave appropriately as components are added, but that implication must be demonstrated. The certified result here is at 4,000 independent components; it does not claim that 4,000 is a sharp cutoff, either.
Does it tell us what happened at counts below 4,000?

No. It gives no radius, coverage conclusion, or effect-width bound for a smaller count. A result at 4,000 does not imply that fewer components fail, just as it does not by itself establish a result for every larger count.
Does independent components mean every unit within a component was independent?

No. Independence of the component-level contributions used in a Hoeffding calculation does not imply independence of units or exposures within each component. The finding states the independent-component condition; any more detailed within-component dependence claim would need to be specified separately.
Are they necessarily independent only after conditioning on observed shocks?

The finding says “independent components” but does not itself specify a conditioning event. If the Hoeffding calculation is intended to be shock-conditional, the certification should explicitly state which observed shocks are held fixed and which component contributions are independent conditional on them. Do not silently turn this reported independent-component result into a guarantee for every shock value.
Does Γ=1.5 identify the exact size of the Hoeffding radius?

No. Γ=1.5 specifies the sensitivity level used in the calculation. The result gives the coverage certification and effect-width limits, but not the numerical Hoeffding radii or the sensitivity-envelope allowances. Those quantities cannot be recovered from the two final width ratios alone.
Could I say the Hoeffding calculation has proved uniform coverage over all network spillover patterns?

Not from this finding alone. It certifies at least 95% joint coverage at 4,000 independent components under the conditions of the Γ=1.5 Hoeffding calculation. A claim of uniformity over a particular confounding and interference class must identify that class and establish that every configuration in it satisfies the calculation’s assumptions. Unrestricted spillovers are not stated as part of this certification.
Would it be accurate to call the result stronger than a simulated coverage percentage?

The word “certified” describes a calculation-based guarantee rather than a measured frequency across simulated panels. That is the appropriate distinction to make. Its strength still depends on the assumptions and scope of the calculation: certification under a stated independent-component class should not be presented as a guarantee beyond that class.
Does the certification automatically identify what the Horvitz–Thompson envelopes contain?

No. The reported finding does not provide the envelope definitions or endpoints. It says the Γ=1.5 Hoeffding calculation certified joint coverage and the two width limits. Explaining exactly how weighted quantities, sensitivity allowances, and bands combine would require the calculation’s definitions, rather than an inference from the final percentages.
Can I state that exposure-cell overlap was at least 0.10 in this calculation?

The finding itself does not state an overlap level. If an overlap assumption is part of the underlying certification, it should be given explicitly with that calculation. In reporting this result as supplied, retain 4,000 independent components, Γ=1.5, at least 95% joint coverage, and the ≤94% and ≤98% width bounds without attaching an unstated overlap condition.
What about a drift allowance?

No drift value or bound is specified in this finding either. Do not describe the width certification as covering a particular drift limit—or as assuming zero drift—without an explicit condition to that effect. The reported conclusion is meaningful at the scope defined by the Hoeffding calculation; the short finding does not list every assumption behind it.
Do the width limits concern confidence sets or identification bounds?

The finding calls them direct and spillover widths but does not expressly say whether they are widths of reported confidence sets or population identification bounds. A technical presentation should identify the objects and their range benchmarks. Until then, “direct/spillover widths ≤94%/98% of range” is accurate, while switching to one more specific type of width without support could change the claim.
If the underlying identification bound is sub-range, could a confidence set still be broader?

Yes, in general: a confidence set can include sampling uncertainty beyond a population identification bound. That is why it matters to label the certified widths correctly. The reported finding provides two upper limits on widths at the stated component count but does not separately state an identification-bound width and a confidence-set width for either effect.
Can the two width limits be combined into one guarantee about a joint direct–spillover set?

They give effect-specific width comparisons. They do not, on their own, specify the shape or volume of a joint set of direct–spillover pairs. The coverage conclusion is joint, while the two reported width inequalities remain separate; keeping those statements distinct avoids attributing an unstated joint-set geometry to the result.
What is the safest concise statement of the result and its scope?

“At 4,000 independent components, the Γ=1.5 Hoeffding calculation certified at least 95% joint coverage, with direct and spillover widths no greater than 94% and 98% of range, respectively.” The certification is for the calculation’s stated conditions at that component count; no result for other counts or a broader interference class is supplied here.
ShockHT v1 records Γ=1.5 envelope formulas, component Hoeffding radii, and certified 4,000-component direct and spillover width thresholds. How should I describe the artifact?

You can say: “ShockHT v1 documents the Γ=1.5 sensitivity-envelope formulas, the component-level Hoeffding radii, and certified direct- and spillover-width thresholds at 4,000 components.” That identifies what the artifact records without adding a formula, a numerical radius, or a coverage claim not stated in its description.
Does “records” mean the envelope formulas have already been applied to every possible network?

No. It says that ShockHT v1 contains the formulas. Their applicability to a particular network depends on the definitions and assumptions under which they were derived. The artifact description does not assert that every network satisfies those assumptions or that the formulas have been evaluated everywhere.
What does Γ=1.5 attach to in that description?

It identifies the sensitivity level for the envelope formulas recorded in ShockHT v1. The short description does not provide the exact adoption-law restriction or numerical envelope endpoints. To interpret the formulas technically, one would need those definitions from the artifact rather than infer them from the symbol Γ alone.
Could I call the envelopes effect estimates?

That would be imprecise. An envelope represents a range allowed by the stated sensitivity construction, not necessarily a single estimated direct or spillover effect. The artifact records envelope formulas; it does not say that they collapse to point estimates.
Are the Hoeffding radii the same thing as the sensitivity envelopes?

No. They address different parts of the uncertainty calculation. The Γ=1.5 envelopes concern what the permitted adoption-sensitivity configurations allow. Component Hoeffding radii address sampling variation for the component-level quantities under the assumptions required by their concentration calculation.

Recording both makes their roles visible. It does not mean the two quantities are numerically equal or can be substituted for one another.
Does the artifact description give numerical values for those radii?

No numerical radius is supplied in the description. It says ShockHT v1 records component Hoeffding radii, so the artifact can be identified as containing them, but a particular value should not be quoted unless it is actually provided for the relevant conditions.
Why are the widths certified separately for direct and spillover effects?

They concern different contrasts. A direct effect varies own policy status while holding the relevant network exposure fixed; a spillover effect varies that exposure while holding own status fixed. Their sensitivity allowances and the exposure-specific quantities informing them need not be identical.

Separate width thresholds prevent a result for one effect from being treated as a result for the other. The description says both thresholds are recorded at 4,000 components, not that they are the same.
Can I infer the actual numerical width percentages from the artifact description alone?

No. It identifies certified 4,000-component direct and spillover width thresholds but does not state their numerical values. A one-line artifact description can name the thresholds without inventing numbers or treating them as effect magnitudes.
Does the 4,000 count mean 4,000 units were observed?

No. It refers to components, not units. The description does not tell us how many units or cohorts are in a component, how components are formed, or what independence property the Hoeffding calculation requires. Those details belong to the conditions of the certification.
Is the threshold certified for every count at or above 4,000?

The description says “certified 4,000-component” thresholds. That directly identifies the result at 4,000 components. An extension to every larger count would need to be explicitly established; it should not be inferred solely from the threshold label.
Could I say ShockHT v1 proves uniform 95% joint coverage?

The artifact description itself does not say that. It lists Γ=1.5 envelope formulas, component Hoeffding radii, and certified width thresholds. Any uniform 95% joint-coverage claim would need its stated target, class, and proof conditions. Do not attribute that conclusion to the artifact solely because it records radii and width thresholds.
Would the certified widths imply coverage even if the Hoeffding assumptions fail?

No. A width comparison and a coverage guarantee are different properties, and a Hoeffding-based inference statement relies on the assumptions that justify its radii. If those assumptions do not apply, neither the concentration argument nor an associated coverage inference can simply be carried over.

The artifact’s recorded thresholds should be cited within the conditions under which they were certified, not treated as unconditional network results.
Does the description say whether the width thresholds concern identification bounds or confidence sets?

It does not specify which type of width is certified. A technical account should identify the object and its outcome-range benchmark for each effect. In a short artifact description, “direct and spillover width thresholds” preserves the stated scope without silently choosing identification-bound or confidence-set widths.
Can the recorded formulas be used to check both effects even though there is one Γ value?

The artifact says it records Γ=1.5 envelope formulas and separate direct and spillover width thresholds. A shared sensitivity level can enter distinct effect-specific contrasts, but it does not imply that their formulas or widths are identical. How the recorded formulas feed each target must be read from their definitions.
Why mention component Hoeffding radii rather than just say “uncertainty bounds”?

Naming them identifies the stated concentration method and the component level at which the radii are defined. “Uncertainty bounds” would obscure that distinction and could be confused with the Γ=1.5 sensitivity envelopes or the final direct and spillover widths.

At the same time, the term “Hoeffding” is not a substitute for the boundedness and independence assumptions needed to use the radii validly.
Could ShockHT v1 be described as a simulation artifact?

Not on the description given. Its stated contents are envelope formulas, component Hoeffding radii, and certified width thresholds. It does not say that it contains panel simulations or coverage tables. Calling it a documentation or calculation artifact for those recorded items is more faithful.
Does “certified” mean we can ignore the assumptions behind the 4,000-component thresholds?

No. A certification has the scope of its stated assumptions and definitions. The one-line description does not enumerate those assumptions, so a technical use of the width thresholds should refer to the conditions under which the formulas and radii justify them. It should not turn “certified” into “unconditionally valid.”
What is the shortest faithful description?
“ShockHT v1 records Γ=1.5 envelope formulas, component Hoeffding radii, and certified direct and spillover width thresholds at 4,000 components.”
I want to stress-test ShockHT v1 on 10,000 shock-conditioned Γ=1.5 panels with 4,000 components, auditing joint coverage and direct and spillover widths. How should I describe the activity?

Describe it as a stress test of ShockHT v1 at the specified sensitivity level and component count. Apply its envelope formulas and component Hoeffding radii to the 10,000 shock-conditioned Γ=1.5 panels, then measure whether the direct and spillover targets are covered together and examine their widths separately.

That states what will be audited, not what the audit will find. It supplies no measured coverage rate or width.
What does the count of 4,000 refer to?

It refers to components in the panels, not to 4,000 units, cohorts, or independent simulation trials. Should I call those components independent?

Only if independence of the relevant component-level contributions is part of the panels’ stated construction and has been checked at the conditioning level used by ShockHT v1. What needs to match between the stress-test panels and ShockHT v1?

The meaning of Γ=1.5, the observed shocks being conditioned on, the exposure and adoption quantities entering the envelopes, and the component-level contributions used by the radii must be consistent. The reported direct and spillover contrasts should also match the targets whose coverage and widths are measured.

If a panel permits a dependence pattern that the calculation excludes, that is useful to identify as a stress-test condition, but its coverage measurement should not be presented as though the calculation’s assumptions held without qualification.
Does shock-conditioned mean we can pool all 10,000 panels into one coverage figure?

A pooled figure can be reported if its construction and interpretation are clear, but “shock-conditioned” does not say which observed-shock values appear or whether the intended guarantee is conditional at each value. Pooling could conceal different performance across values.

Before reporting coverage, define the conditioning used by the procedure and the event being counted. Then make clear whether a result is conditional on a specified shock value, summarized across values, or broken out by value.
What should count as joint coverage?

For a joint effect-value audit, a panel counts as covered only when its reported direct set contains the specified direct effect and its reported spillover set contains the specified spillover effect in the same realization. Do not replace the joint event with the average of two separate coverage rates. Those rates would not say how often both targets were covered together.
Would it be useful to audit the Hoeffding bands as well as the final sets?

Yes, as a diagnostic distinction. The activity’s stated coverage outcome should still identify which of those events is reported as joint coverage.

If they differ, the intervening envelope and set-construction step needs examination. This is a possible diagnostic, not a claim that ShockHT v1 has such a discrepancy.
Are the Γ=1.5 envelopes just another name for the Hoeffding bands?

No. The envelopes accommodate the conditional adoption laws allowed by the Γ=1.5 sensitivity restriction. The Hoeffding radii address sampling deviations of the specified component-level quantities under their required assumptions. What makes this a stress test rather than simply applying the formulas?

The purpose is to examine how the procedure behaves across the specified panels, particularly for the joint event and the two effect-specific widths, rather than merely calculate one set of outputs. To interpret the word “stress,” the panel conditions and any challenging configurations considered should be described accurately.

Nothing in the activity specifies a particular adversarial law or shock pattern. It would be inaccurate to claim that the panels exhaust all worst-case configurations solely because the exercise is called a stress test.
Should I report the lowest coverage across panel configurations or the coverage pooled over panels?

They answer different questions. A pooled rate describes the joint-coverage frequency across the panels being pooled. If coverage is estimated separately for specified configurations, the lowest of those rates can show the weakest measured performance among them. The activity does not prescribe either aggregation or say how the 10,000 panels are allocated.

Report whichever quantity is actually computed, and identify the configurations over which any minimum is taken. Neither a pooled rate nor a minimum over selected configurations is automatically a uniform guarantee over the full class.
Can the simulation verify the 95% joint-coverage certification?

It can provide an empirical check at the 4,000-component setting: measured joint coverage can be compared with the 95% target under the simulated shock-conditioned Γ=1.5 laws. It cannot establish coverage for every law and interference configuration admitted by a broader mathematical claim.

A discrepancy would warrant checking the panel assumptions, the envelope and radius calculations, and the coverage-event definition. Agreement would be reassuring for the simulated settings, not a substitute for the argument behind a certification.
If measured coverage comes in below 95%, would that immediately identify a faulty Hoeffding radius?

No. A shortfall in the final joint event would not by itself locate its cause. And if the rate is above 95%?

Then the measured joint coverage meets the target in the reported panels. It still does not show that the conditional coverage probability is at least 95% for every observed-shock value or every allowed Γ=1.5 law. What exactly should the width audit measure?

Measure the widths of the direct and spillover outputs separately under the same procedure and panel setting. Identify whether those outputs are confidence sets formed with the Hoeffding radii or sensitivity bounds before adding sampling uncertainty; those are different width objects.

If the question is whether the widths are sub-range, compare each with the outcome-range width for that same effect. Joint coverage does not tell you either width.
Could we report just the narrower of the two widths?

If the average direct and spillover widths are sub-range, would that establish that every panel produced sub-range sets?

No. An average can lie below its benchmark even if some individual sets reach full-range width. Specify whether the audit reports averages, maxima, a distribution of widths, or panel-specific comparisons. Each supports a different statement about informativeness.

Does a small Hoeffding radius guarantee a sub-range spillover width?

Not by itself. The final spillover width also reflects which exposure contrasts have support and which values remain compatible with the Γ=1.5 envelopes. Should we assume the 4,000-component width thresholds recorded in ShockHT v1 will appear as the measured widths?

No. A certified threshold is a bound under its stated conditions, whereas measured widths are outputs or summaries from the stress-test panels. The two should be compared using the same definitions, but an upper threshold need not equal an attained width. The activity itself supplies no measured percentages.
Does the stress test cover component counts above and below 4,000?

Not as stated. It is at 4,000 components. Findings for that setting should not be turned into a trend across component counts, a claim that fewer components fail, or a guarantee for every larger count.
Does it impose a particular overlap floor or drift allowance?

Neither a numerical overlap floor nor a drift limit appears in this activity. If either is part of the conditions needed to apply ShockHT v1’s envelopes, radii, or width thresholds, the stress-test description should state the condition actually imposed on its panels. It would not be faithful to silently add a particular value—or assume zero drift—to the stated activity.
Should failures to calculate a set be included when auditing coverage?

The procedure should specify what it returns in that situation. Silently omitting a panel for which a required band or effect set cannot be calculated could change the meaning of the reported coverage frequency. A missing set also cannot simply be assigned a favorable width.

Separate the procedure’s claimed calibration from what is measured in the panels, and separate coverage from width. The stress test uses 10,000 shock-conditioned Γ=1.5 panels at 4,000 components to audit the joint coverage event and two effect-specific widths. “Stress-test ShockHT v1 on 10,000 shock-conditioned Γ=1.5 panels with 4,000 components, measuring joint coverage of the specified direct and spillover targets and auditing their widths separately against the appropriate range benchmarks.”

ShockHT v1’s marginal exposure weights yielded 93.1% minimum joint coverage across 10,000 shock-conditioned Γ=1.5 panels with 4,000 independent components. What is the most accurate way to report that?

“Across 10,000 shock-conditioned Γ=1.5 panels with 4,000 independent components, ShockHT v1’s marginal exposure weights yielded 93.1% minimum joint coverage.” The measured minimum is 1.9 percentage points below the 95% joint-coverage target.
