Conditional independence of components does not automatically imply conditional overlap of the histories they contribute.
Does a cell probability of at least 0.10 mean it appears in at least 10% of components in every realized panel?

No. A floor on a probability does not impose that realized frequency in every panel. Some realizations may still provide little observed information for a required cell. A claim that every reported confidence set is sub-range would therefore need more than population overlap alone; the width claim must say precisely what it applies to.
What is being counted by the 4,000?

The hypothesis counts 4,000 components, not units, cohorts, or observed histories. The relevant independent objects must be the component-level contributions used in the inference argument, conditional on the specified observed shocks. Components can contain internal dependence, and merely naming 4,000 groups does not establish that their contributions satisfy the required conditional independence.
Can I infer a maximum of three cohorts per component?

No. This hypothesis states the component count and conditional independence but does not impose a numerical limit on cohorts within each component. If component size is needed to bound their contributions or define admissible histories, it should be stated as an additional assumption rather than read into the number 4,000.
What if the components share an adoption input that is not explained by the observed shocks?

Then their relevant contributions might not be independent after conditioning. The formal component definition and law class must rule out that shared dependence or account for it in the inference calibration. Observing shocks does not, by itself, establish that all remaining cross-component inputs are independent.
Does conditional independence imply they have the same distribution?

No. Independence conditional on observed shocks does not imply identical conditional distributions. If the proposed coverage calculation relies on a common distribution or common contribution bound, it must justify that property separately or accommodate heterogeneity. The 4,000-component count cannot supply it.
Could many of the 4,000 components contribute nothing to a required spillover history?

That is possible under an inadequately specified support condition. The count of components and the overlap probabilities need to be connected to the component-level quantities used for each target. An inference calculation cannot automatically treat all 4,000 as informative repetitions for a spillover cell that they do not contribute to.

Likewise, support for a spillover comparison cannot stand in for support for a direct comparison. Both must be checked.
How should I explain the drift restriction numerically?

It permits the specified drift to be no greater than 0.05 times its reference range—five percent of that range. It includes permitted nonzero drift; it is not a zero-drift assumption. The formal hypothesis must define the drifting quantity, the comparisons across which it may drift, and the reference range before the restriction can enter a width or coverage argument.
Can the tests be calibrated at zero drift and still claim coverage for drift ≤0.05 of the range?

Only if an argument shows that zero-drift calibration protects every drift value allowed by the stated class. Otherwise the calibration must accommodate the full permitted allowance, including the boundary at 0.05 of the range. The same care applies to the width calculations: excluding admissible drift could make an effect bound appear narrower than the assumptions justify.
Does this hypothesis fix a value of Γ?

No numerical Γ value appears in the hypothesis as stated. If a sensitivity restriction on unmeasured adoption confounding is part of the intended class, it must be specified and applied consistently in the coverage and narrowing arguments. A numerical sensitivity level cannot be inferred from the component count, overlap floor, or drift limit.
How do we keep the direct and spillover effects separate?

Define the direct contrast by varying own policy status while holding the relevant network-exposure history fixed. Define the spillover contrast by varying exposure to others’ policies while holding the relevant own-policy history fixed. Specify the timing needed for both staggered-policy comparisons.

The joint histories and assumptions may constrain both contrasts, but each requires its own bound and its own outcome-range benchmark. A narrower combined policy-effect bound would not establish both separate conclusions.
Does sub-range mean each effect is point identified?

No. It means that the width of each specified effect bound is strictly less than the width allowed by its corresponding outcome-range bound. Each may still contain multiple effect values. The direct bound must be sub-range on its own, as must the spillover bound.
Are we talking about the widths of population identified bounds or reported confidence sets?

The hypothesis needs to say. Population identified bounds express compatibility under assumptions and population information; confidence sets also reflect sampling uncertainty. They can have different widths. If “sub-range” concerns reported confidence sets, specify whether the inequality is required for every realization, with a stated probability, or under some other explicit criterion. A guarantee about population bounds should not be silently extended to every random confidence set.
Could the identified bounds both be sub-range while a realized confidence set is full-range?

Yes. Sampling uncertainty may require a reported set broader than an informative population bound in some realizations. That can be compatible with a valid coverage guarantee. It is another reason to keep the width object and the coverage target distinct in the proposed statement.
What does uniform coverage of at least 95% require here?

It requires the probability of covering the stated target to be at least 0.95 for every configuration in the specified class, not just on average across shock values, component arrangements, adoption laws, or interference patterns. The statement must say whether coverage is conditional at each specified observed-shock value or marginal over them, and whether it is a finite-sample or asymptotic guarantee.

A favorable measurement at 4,000 components would not, by itself, prove the required worst-case probability statement.
Is coverage of each effect separately at 95% enough?

Not if the intended claim is joint coverage of the direct and spillover effects. The event that both targets are contained in their respective sets in the same realization must itself have probability at least 95% uniformly. Two marginal 95% statements do not automatically establish that joint event.
Does the overlap floor itself ensure that joint coverage?

No. Joint-history overlap can help ensure supported comparisons and may help bound contributions used for inference. Coverage also requires correctly calibrated uncertainty across the permitted conditional adoption and interference laws, plus a construction that retains both effect targets on the protected event. The ≥0.10 floor is not a substitute for those steps.
Could a procedure cover uniformly but produce full-range spillover bounds?

Yes. Validity and informativeness are separate. A procedure may retain the spillover target with the required probability yet exclude no values beyond its outcome-range bound. In that case the joint coverage conclusion could hold while the hypothesis’s paired sub-range-width conclusion would not.
What would a proof at 4,000 components need to demonstrate?

It would need to justify conditional independence and any boundedness of the relevant contributions, define a simultaneous coverage procedure for all histories used by both effects, and show its error control uniformly over the stated class. It would then need to connect the protected quantities to the reported effect sets and prove two strict width inequalities at 4,000 components: one for direct effects and one for spillovers, each against its corresponding outcome-range bound while allowing drift through ≤0.05 of the range.

Those are obligations for establishing the hypothesis, not consequences of choosing the numbers 4,000, 0.10, and 0.05.
Would proving the claim at exactly 4,000 components establish it at every larger count?

Not automatically. Larger counts could come with different component contributions, histories, or support patterns. An extension requires an argument showing that the coverage calibration and both width inequalities continue to apply under the stated assumptions. This hypothesis identifies the 4,000-component setting; it makes no necessity or sharp-cutoff claim.
Can I say 0.10 is the minimum floor needed to preserve both properties?

Not yet. The hypothesis proposes ≥0.10 as sufficient at 4,000 qualifying components. Establishing that it is a *minimum* would additionally require showing that no smaller floor can ensure both properties over the same stated class. The coverage and direct/spillover width conditions might impose different requirements, so their sharp thresholds need not coincide.
How could I state the hypothesis in one sentence without overclaiming?

“We hypothesize that, with 4,000 exposure components independent conditional on specified observed shocks, probabilities ≥0.10 for every joint-history cell required by the direct and spillover contrasts, and drift ≤0.05 of its stated range, both effect bounds are strictly narrower than their respective outcome-range bounds and the defined joint confidence target has uniformly at least 95% coverage over the specified class.” The class, width criterion, and sufficiency of these conditions remain to be established.

I want to reproduce the 0.01 joint-history-cell failure at 4,000 components, require joint-history overlap ≥0.10, and then prove uniform 95% coverage and sub-range bounds for both direct and spillover effects. Is that a sensible plan?

Yes, as a plan with two distinct purposes. Reproducing the 0.01-cell failure checks that the support problem can be recovered at the stated component count. Requiring probabilities of at least 0.10 for the relevant joint-history cells proposes a more targeted overlap condition. The remaining work is to prove, under a precisely stated class, both uniform 95% coverage and strict narrowing relative to outcome-range bounds for the direct and spillover effects separately.

Reproducing the failure would not itself show that 0.10 is sufficient, and imposing the floor would not itself prove coverage or narrowing.
When I say reproduce the failure, what should be held constant?

The reproduction should preserve the definitions needed to identify the 0.01 joint-history cell and the resulting failure at 4,000 components. If the target contrasts, relevant histories, or bound-construction rule change at the same time, it may become unclear whether the same problem was reproduced.

The plan does not specify the full configuration or a reproduction procedure. Those would have to be documented before describing any new calculation as a successful reproduction.
Is the 0.01-cell check already a proof that overlap below 0.10 cannot work?

No. It is a check of a particular failure involving a joint-history cell with probability 0.01 at 4,000 components. It does not show that every probability below 0.10 leads to the same outcome, or that 0.10 is the smallest possible sufficient floor. The proposed ≥0.10 requirement still needs its own width and coverage arguments.
What exactly should the ≥0.10 requirement apply to?

It should apply to every joint-history cell needed for the direct or spillover contrast covered by the claim. The histories, their timing, and the probabilities used to define overlap must be specified. A floor on a broader or marginal exposure category would not, without an additional implication, establish the same floor for its constituent joint histories.

If the proof ranges over multiple admissible laws or observed-shock values, it should say whether the ≥0.10 condition holds under each law and at each relevant conditioning value.
Does every possible history need probability at least 0.10?

The plan requires joint-history overlap ≥0.10, but it does not enumerate the histories. For a precise sufficient condition, identify the cells necessary to define and bound the claimed effects and impose the floor there. It need not be silently extended to histories unrelated to the targets, nor can a required history be omitted because its support is inconvenient.

The number and definition of required cells matter to whether such a floor is coherent and useful.
Should the same set of cells be used for both effects?

Not necessarily. A direct contrast changes own policy status while holding the relevant network-exposure history fixed; a spillover contrast changes exposure while holding the relevant own-policy history fixed. They can require different joint-history cells. You can state one overlap condition over the union of the cells needed by both, then assess the resulting direct and spillover bounds separately.
How does the 4,000-component count enter the proposed proof?

It fixes the count at which the failure is to be reproduced and at which the proposed overlap condition and resulting bounds are to be examined. It is a count of components, not automatically a count of independent observations in every required history cell. The proof needs to define the component-level information relevant to each contrast and any dependence assumptions used for inference.

A result at 4,000 components would not by itself establish the same conclusions at every other count.
Would ≥0.10 probability mean that at least 400 of the 4,000 components realize each required history?

No. Multiplying 4,000 by 0.10 gives 400, but a probability floor is not a deterministic guarantee of 400 realized components per cell. Nor does the plan say that each component has exactly one opportunity to realize each required history. The relationship between the probability floor and the information available at 4,000 components must follow from the defined sampling and component structure.
What should the coverage proof establish, rather than just checking a reported percentage?

It should show that the probability of covering the stated target is at least 0.95 for every configuration allowed by the specified confounding and interference class. If the target is joint coverage of the two effect values, the event must contain both the direct and spillover effects in their reported sets in the same realization. Coverage of entire identified sets would be a different, stronger target.

The proof also needs to say whether the 95% guarantee is finite-sample at the covered component count or asymptotic. A measured coverage frequency is not by itself a uniform probability bound.
Can the ≥0.10 overlap assumption deliver that uniform coverage on its own?

No. It may provide support for the histories used by the inference rule and help control quantities that depend on their probabilities. Coverage also requires valid calibration under the permitted adoption and network-dependence laws, and a demonstrated implication from the protected testing or band event to both reported effect sets.

The floor and the coverage argument should refer to the same joint histories and admissible class; otherwise a nominally strong overlap condition might miss the configurations most relevant to coverage.
What should sub-range mean in this plan?

For the direct effect, the relevant bound must be strictly narrower than the outcome-range bound for that direct contrast. The spillover bound must independently be strictly narrower than its own outcome-range bound. A result for one effect, or a narrow combined policy contrast, would not establish both conclusions.

The plan should also identify whether these are population identification bounds or reported confidence sets. Those objects can have different widths, and an unqualified statement about every realized confidence set is stronger than a population-width result.
Could the proposed overlap floor preserve coverage but still leave one effect at full-range width?

Yes, that remains possible until the width inequalities are established. A procedure may be calibrated to cover the effects uniformly yet be unable to exclude any outcome-range-compatible spillover values, or any direct-effect values, under its stated assumptions. That is why the plan explicitly calls for proving sub-range bounds for both effects rather than treating overlap or coverage as sufficient evidence of informativeness.
Does the reproduction step tell us which of the two width proofs will be harder?

Not from the plan alone. Reproducing a 0.01-cell failure shows what should be checked when joint-history support is sparse; it does not quantify how the proposed ≥0.10 restriction changes each effect’s compatible set. Direct and spillover comparisons may rely on different histories, so their strict width comparisons must be derived independently.
Should the uniform proof permit the cell probability to equal exactly 0.10?

Yes. The stated condition is ≥0.10, so it includes the boundary. If the argument only works when every required probability is strictly greater than 0.10, it would establish a different claim. Likewise, the coverage and width conditions should be checked for the least favorable admissible configurations at the stated boundary if those configurations are permitted.
Could the floor hold on average across histories rather than for each history?

An average could mask a required cell with much less support, so it would not be the same as a minimum joint-history-cell probability. To use ≥0.10 as a floor, state it for each required history under the specified probability law or laws. If a different aggregate overlap condition is intended, its ability to support both contrasts would need a separate argument.
Do I need to specify interference as well as the history probabilities?

Yes. The interference class determines which network-exposure histories can affect outcomes and which contrasts count as direct versus spillover effects. It can also affect dependence among the quantities used for inference. A uniform coverage theorem cannot silently rely on a narrower interference class than the one it claims, and a width proof needs to use the same effect definitions and admissible histories.
What about unmeasured adoption confounding?

That too belongs in the stated class. A joint-history probability floor does not make adoption unconfounded. The confidence procedure and the compatible-effect calculations must allow every adoption process admitted by the specified confounding restriction. This plan does not give a numerical sensitivity parameter, so one should not attach one without stating it explicitly as an assumption.
Does the plan impose a drift bound?

No numerical drift condition is stated here. If the intended effect comparisons allow drift, its definition and permitted range must be included in both the width and coverage arguments. One should not assume zero drift or insert a particular allowance into this plan without specifying it.
If the probability floor makes weighted quantities well behaved, is that enough to prove strict narrowing?

Not necessarily. Better-controlled weighted quantities can reduce sampling uncertainty, but the allowed confounding, interference, and any other stated ambiguities may still leave the effects compatible with their full outcome-range bounds. Derive the final bound for each effect—including the uncertainty and restrictions the chosen construction actually uses—then compare it strictly with the matching outcome-range benchmark.
Is the proposed ≥0.10 condition necessary?

The plan makes no necessity claim. It proposes requiring at least 0.10 to pursue a sufficient result. Even if that result is proved, a lower floor might also work under some or all of the stated conditions. Establishing a sharp minimum requires a separate argument about what happens below a proposed threshold.
What if the reproduction does not yield the same failure?

Then the reproduction task would need clarification: check whether the history definitions, probability condition, component count, effect targets, and bound rule match the intended 0.01-cell case. A failed reproduction would not, on its own, prove that ≥0.10 suffices or that no support issue exists. The plan contains no reproduction outcome, so it should leave that possibility open.
How should the proof use the reproduction without treating it as a theorem?

Use it to identify and verify the specific support issue the new overlap condition is meant to address. The sufficient-condition proof must then stand on its own: under ≥0.10 support for all required joint-history cells and the rest of its expressly stated class, show uniform 95% coverage and strict effect-specific width improvement. A single reproduced failure cannot establish either universal implication.
Can you state the plan compactly without suggesting the threshold has already been proved?

Reproduce the 0.01 joint-history-cell failure at 4,000 components; impose a ≥0.10 probability floor on every joint-history cell needed by the direct and spillover contrasts; then seek proofs of uniform 95% coverage and separately sub-range direct and spillover bounds over a precisely stated class. The reproduction, coverage guarantee, and sufficiency of the overlap floor remain to be established.

Using ShockHT v2, I want to enumerate shock-conditional Γ=1.5 joint-history laws at overlap values from 0.01 to 0.15, allowing drift ≤0.05 of the range, and calculate coverage and effect-specific widths at 4,000 components. What should the activity say it is doing?

It is an assessment across joint-history overlap values from 0.01 to 0.15. Using ShockHT v2’s shock-conditional law enumeration and confidence-set inversion at Γ=1.5, it would calculate coverage and the widths associated with the direct and spillover effects separately at 4,000 components, while allowing the stated drift of at most 0.05 of the range.

That describes the intended calculations, not their outcomes. It does not yet identify an overlap threshold at which both widths become sub-range or establish a uniform 95% coverage guarantee.
Why specify joint-history overlap rather than just exposure overlap?

Because the procedure enumerates joint exposure histories. A history-specific cell can involve a combination of own policy status, network exposure, and relevant timing. Its probability need not be determined by a marginal exposure probability. The overlap variable being varied should therefore refer to the joint-history cells actually needed for the effect contrasts and inversion.

The activity does not list those cells, so their definition must accompany any numerical calculation.
Does 0.01–0.15 mean that every required joint-history cell has a probability in that interval?

That interpretation should not be assumed without a definition of the overlap variable. The activity says to enumerate laws at overlap 0.01–0.15; a clear implementation would specify whether each setting is a lower bound on all required cell probabilities, the minimum probability attained among those cells, or something else. These formulations can select different classes of laws.

Whatever interpretation is chosen, it must be used consistently in the enumeration, coverage calculation, and direct and spillover width calculations.
If overlap is a minimum across cells, do direct and spillover effects need the same cells?

Not necessarily. A direct-effect contrast changes own policy status while fixing the relevant network-exposure history; a spillover-effect contrast changes network exposure while fixing the relevant own-policy history. Their required cells may differ. A common minimum could be taken over the union of both sets of required cells, but the sets should first be defined separately.

A floor that protects only the cells for one contrast would not, by itself, support a width conclusion for the other.
Do the endpoints 0.01 and 0.15 have to be included?

The phrase “0.01–0.15” ordinarily describes a range including its endpoints. If the assessment uses a grid of selected settings within that range, say which settings are actually evaluated. The activity alone does not specify a grid spacing or require a calculation at every real number between the endpoints.
Could I claim that 0.10 is the cutoff just because the range crosses it?

No. The range makes it possible to examine settings below and above 0.10, but it provides no calculated coverage or widths. A cutoff would require a defined criterion and an argument about all settings to which it is claimed to apply. Results at selected overlap values would not automatically establish a sharp minimum between those values.
What should be held fixed as overlap changes?

The meanings of the direct and spillover targets, the joint histories, Γ=1.5, the drift allowance, the 4,000-component setting, and the rule used for inversion should remain clear and comparable. Changing an overlap setting can change which laws satisfy the specified restriction; the report should distinguish that intended change from a change in the effect definition or coverage event.

The activity does not prescribe how the laws are generated or enumerated at each setting. Those details would have to be specified to interpret a comparison across overlap values.
What is a shock-conditional joint-history law here?

It is an admissible probability law for the relevant histories considered together, conditional on specified observed shocks. “Joint” matters because the probability of a complete history and the relationships between histories cannot generally be recovered by treating each exposure or time in isolation. “Shock-conditional” identifies the level at which the law and its test calibration are defined.

The activity does not name the observed shocks, the exposure mapping, or the form of the Γ=1.5 restriction. Those definitions are necessary before an enumeration can be judged complete.
Is listing possible joint histories enough to say the laws have been enumerated?

No. A history is a possible configuration; a law assigns probabilities to configurations under the stated restrictions. Different admissible laws may give different probabilities to the same list of histories, with different implications for a worst-case test and its inverted set.

To describe law enumeration accurately, specify the permissible probability assignments conditional on the shocks, including the overlap and Γ=1.5 constraints, rather than just list history labels.
Does Γ=1.5 automatically tell us which joint laws are admissible?

No. It fixes the sensitivity level, but its meaning depends on the mathematical adoption-confounding restriction used by ShockHT v2. The law enumeration must apply that restriction to the joint histories as defined. Γ=1.5 alone supplies neither a history probability nor a p-value.
How does the drift condition fit into the enumeration?

The activity allows drift ≤0.05 of the range. Its calculation should state what quantity may drift, across which relevant comparisons, and which range supplies the reference. Every permitted value, including the boundary, must be accommodated wherever drift affects a test or an effect bound.

Drift is not the same restriction as Γ=1.5 adoption sensitivity or joint-history overlap. Treating it as zero while claiming results for drift through 0.05 of the range would narrow the assessed class without saying so.
Does drift ≤0.05 of the range mean that drift is exactly five percent in each enumerated law?

No. The inequality permits drift up to five percent of the specified range; it does not fix drift at that upper limit. If coverage and widths are reported for the entire allowed drift class, the calculation must account for values within it, not only zero or exactly 0.05 of the range.
Does the 4,000 count refer to histories, components, or simulated panels?

Components. The activity calls for coverage and effect-specific width calculations at 4,000 components. It supplies no number of joint histories per component and no number of simulated panels. It would change the statement to call the 4,000 components 4,000 independent observations or 4,000 simulation trials.
Can we assume the components are independent conditional on shocks?

That assumption is not expressly stated in this activity. ShockHT v2 uses shock-conditional inversion, but conditioning alone does not establish independence between component-level quantities. If a coverage calculation at 4,000 components relies on conditional independence, it must define the relevant quantities and include that property among the assumptions being assessed.

Likewise, no maximum number of cohorts per component is specified here.
What should the coverage calculation measure?

It must name the coverage target and event. If the intention is joint direct-and-spillover effect-value coverage, the event is that both true targets lie in their respective reported sets on the same realization. Coverage of entire identified sets would be a different, stronger event. A calculation of coverage for one effect alone would not establish coverage of the pair.

The activity says “calculate coverage” but does not supply its value or explicitly choose between those targets. The choice should be made before reporting a percentage.
Should the calculation take a worst case over the enumerated laws?

If it is meant to assess uniform coverage over the stated shock-conditional class, it must account for the least favorable admissible laws, rather than average over a favorable mixture. ShockHT v2’s worst-case inversion is relevant, but the law class used in a coverage calculation must match the one used by the tests, including the stated overlap and drift conditions and any allowed interference.

A minimum over a selected enumeration is a class-wide minimum only if that enumeration or its optimization is shown to cover the full claimed class.
Is a result above 95% for a few overlap settings enough for uniform 95% coverage?

No. Such a result would concern the settings and laws actually calculated. Uniform coverage requires at least 95% for every configuration in the class covered by the claim, in the stated finite-sample or asymptotic sense. Even if a reported minimum over examined settings exceeds 95%, one must know whether unexamined laws, shock values, drift configurations, or interference patterns remain admissible.

The activity itself reports no coverage result, so it should not be described as having passed that test.
Do we know whether the intended coverage guarantee is finite-sample?

The activity asks to calculate coverage at 4,000 components; it does not expressly declare a finite-sample guarantee or an asymptotic one. A probability calculation for a stated finite class at that component count would have a different scope from a theorem holding at every size or uniformly in a limit. The resulting report should say exactly which interpretation it supports.
What should “effect-specific widths” refer to?

At a minimum, keep the direct and spillover widths separate and identify the objects being measured. Widths of population identification bounds and widths of inverted confidence sets differ because the latter can also reflect sampling uncertainty. To assess whether they are sub-range, compare each width with the outcome-range benchmark for its own contrast.

Neither width is supplied in the activity. A single combined or average width would not by itself show that both effect-specific bounds improve on their benchmarks.
Could the coverage calculation be valid while the widths reach the outcome-range bounds?

Yes. A test can retain the targets with adequate probability while also retaining nearly every effect value allowed by the outcome range. The activity needs both measurements because coverage and informativeness are separate properties. Whether any overlap setting from 0.01 to 0.15 yields strictly sub-range widths for both effects remains to be calculated.
Should I report widths at each overlap setting or only the smallest width found?

To assess a support threshold, retain enough setting-specific information to see both effect widths and the associated coverage calculation at the overlap settings actually evaluated. Selecting only the smallest width would conceal settings where one bound remains full-range or where coverage is inadequate.

The activity does not dictate a particular table or summary statistic. Whatever summary is used should specify its domain and should not be read as a result for every probability in the interval unless that is justified.
Can the direct bound become sub-range at a different overlap setting from the spillover bound?

That is possible in principle because the contrasts may depend on different required histories. A common sufficient overlap floor for both would have to satisfy the stricter of the effect-specific width conditions, while also maintaining the stated coverage guarantee. The activity does not provide thresholds or say that the two widths change in the same way.
Does a probability floor alone give the width of a Horvitz–Thompson contribution?

No. The contribution depends on the defined outcome range, exposure-history assignment probability used for weighting, normalization, and the admissible conditional law. A floor may help bound weights, but a numerical radius or effect width cannot be inferred from 0.01, 0.10, or 0.15 alone. The Γ=1.5 sensitivity allowance and permitted drift must also be included in the final width calculation.
What if a required history is absent from one realized panel even at overlap 0.15?

A positive probability floor does not guarantee the history appears in every realization. The procedure should specify what it returns in that case, and the coverage and width calculations must treat that output consistently. Discarding realizations with sparse cells without stating the restriction could make a reported coverage or width summary apply only to favorable panels.

The activity does not state that any empty cells occur; this is a condition the calculation needs to handle or explicitly exclude.
Does the interval 0.01–0.15 specify an adoption-confounding strength as well as overlap?

No. In this activity, 0.01–0.15 is the range of joint-history overlap settings. Γ=1.5 is the stated sensitivity level for the conditional adoption-law enumeration. Drift ≤0.05 of the range is another, distinct restriction. Keeping their roles separate prevents an overlap probability from being mistaken for a confounding or drift parameter.
Can we use the calculations to declare 0.10 the minimum floor if both widths first look sub-range there?

That would require care. A first favorable setting in a finite grid is not necessarily the sharp minimum over all probabilities or all admissible laws. One would need to establish what was calculated at the boundary, how untested values between grid points are handled, and whether the width and coverage claims hold throughout the class above the proposed floor.

The activity provides a range for evaluation, not a threshold conclusion.
How should the shock conditioning be reflected when comparing overlap settings?

The joint-history probability used for overlap should match the shock-conditional law to which the test is applied. If the proposed guarantee ranges over multiple observed-shock values, specify whether the probability floor holds at each value and whether the coverage calculation is conditional at each value or averaged over them. A marginal overlap value across shocks could mask weak conditional support.

No particular shocks or distribution of shock values are specified in the activity, so neither kind of coverage result can be assumed in advance.
Could enumerating laws at each overlap setting by itself certify the confidence sets?

No. Even a complete enumeration would need to be linked to a valid worst-case test, a correct inversion rule, and a specified joint coverage event. The calculation must also respect any permitted network-interference and drift configurations that affect the test. Enumeration identifies or searches the admissible laws; it does not automatically establish 95% coverage or narrower bounds.
What would count as a complete outcome of this activity without overstating it?

It would identify the overlap settings actually evaluated from 0.01 to 0.15, define and enumerate the corresponding shock-conditional Γ=1.5 joint-history law classes with drift allowed through ≤0.05 of the stated range, and report coverage and direct and spillover widths at 4,000 components under clearly named targets and benchmarks. Any statement about a uniform guarantee or a minimum sufficient probability would need an argument matching the full scope claimed.

The activity description itself supplies none of those numerical results.
Can you give me a compact, faithful one-sentence description?

“Using ShockHT v2, enumerate shock-conditional joint-history laws at Γ=1.5 for overlap settings from 0.01 to 0.15 with drift ≤0.05 of the stated range, and calculate coverage and separate direct and spillover widths at 4,000 components.”
At joint-history overlap ≥0.10, 10,000 Γ=1.5 trials showed 95.3% minimum joint coverage, with direct and spillover widths ≤91% and ≤97% of range. How should I report the finding?

“At joint-history overlap ≥0.10, 10,000 Γ=1.5 trials yielded 95.3% minimum joint coverage; direct and spillover widths were no greater than 91% and 97% of range, respectively.” Keep “minimum” for coverage and the inequality signs for widths. The result reports performance under the stated conditions, not an unrestricted coverage guarantee.
How does the coverage figure compare with the 95% target?

The reported minimum is 0.3 percentage points above 95%. That is a comparison of the reported figure with the target; it does not establish that every law in a broader confounding and interference class has a coverage probability of at least 95%.
Does “minimum” mean that each of the 10,000 trials had 95.3% coverage?

No. A trial either meets a defined coverage event or does not. A coverage percentage summarizes performance over trials under a setting or law; “minimum” indicates a lowest such summary over some collection. The finding does not specify what collection was minimized over, so it should not be recast as a trial-level property or an unqualified pooled fraction.
Can I describe the 95.3% as simultaneous coverage of both effects?

If the joint event being measured required both the direct and spillover targets to be covered in the same trial, yes. “Joint” should retain that together-at-once meaning. A technical account should identify whether the targets are true effect values or entire identified sets, since those are different events. The reported figure is not two separate effect-specific coverage rates.
Could one effect have been missed more often than the other?

Possibly. The joint figure does not tell us how failures were divided between the direct and spillover targets. A trial fails joint coverage if either target is missed, but the finding supplies no effect-specific failure counts.
Is it correct to call 95.3% an exact finite-sample guarantee?

Not from the finding as stated. It says 10,000 trials showed a minimum joint coverage figure. It does not specify whether the figure is an exact calculation or a trial-based estimate, or define the complete set of laws over which the minimum was taken. A finite-sample guarantee over a class would require those details and an argument covering every admissible configuration.
Could I translate 95.3% of 10,000 into 9,530 jointly covered trials?

Only if 95.3% is an exact, unrounded pooled rate across all 10,000 trials, each contributing one binary joint event. Because the result calls it a *minimum*, it may instead be the lowest of rates computed for different settings or laws. The stated percentage is safer than an inferred count.
What is distinctive about saying joint-history overlap ≥0.10 rather than marginal overlap ≥0.10?

The stated floor concerns the histories relevant to the analysis, not merely individual exposure categories viewed separately. A history can encode a combination or sequence of own-policy and network-exposure states under staggered adoption. Support for a marginal category does not, by itself, establish the same support for a required joint-history cell. The result should therefore retain “joint-history” when naming its overlap condition.
Does overlap ≥0.10 mean every history anyone could define has probability at least 0.10?

That is not specified. The technical definition needs to identify which joint-history cells the overlap restriction covers—especially those required for the direct and spillover contrasts—and the laws under which their probabilities are assessed. The result supplies the floor but not a list of cells. It should not be extended to unrelated histories.
Is the overlap exactly 0.10 in these trials?

Not necessarily. The condition is ≥0.10, so it includes 0.10 and larger overlap values. The finding does not give a separate coverage or width result at exactly 0.10, or say how the 10,000 trials were distributed across qualifying overlap settings.
Does the floor guarantee a realized 10% share in every required cell?

No. A probability floor and a realized cell share are different. If ≥0.10 is a restriction on joint-history probabilities, a particular trial can have a different realized frequency. The reported result does not give realized cell counts.

How should I read the two width inequalities?

The direct width is at most 91% of its stated range benchmark, and the spillover width is at most 97% of its stated range benchmark. These are upper limits, not claims that either width equals 91% or 97% in every trial. They concern the breadth of the bounds or sets, not the sizes of the effects.

The finding calls them direct and spillover widths without specifying which object is being measured. Does the result specify how many components were in the trials?

Can I mention ShockHT v2 as the method without adding further conditions?

Yes, if you are identifying the calculation from which this finding arose. You can say “In the ShockHT v2 assessment” and then give the reported Γ=1.5, joint-history overlap, coverage, and widths. Can I say the overlap check is performed separately for the direct and spillover effects?

Can we infer any component count or correlation restriction from the artifact description?

No. The stated features specify the ≥0.10 joint-history overlap check, drift constraints, and separate worst-case Γ=1.5 bound certificates. No component count or cross-component correlation limit is given in this description; attaching one would add an unstated condition.

The artifact name is not enough to establish the conditioning used in each certificate. The reader should identify the effect contrast and timing, the joint histories subject to the ≥0.10 check, the exact drift constraints, the admissible Γ=1.5 laws and interference assumptions, and the object and inequality that each certificate establishes. “ShockHT v3 adds a ≥0.10 joint-history overlap check, drift constraints, and separate worst-case Γ=1.5 bound certificates for direct and spillover effects.”

I want to exhaustively enumerate small-network Γ=1.5 laws and use them to audit ShockHT v3’s 95% joint coverage and its sub-range direct and spillover certificates at 0.10 joint-history overlap. What should the audit establish?

What needs to be specified before the enumeration can be called exhaustive?

Specify what constitutes a small network, which joint exposure histories are relevant, how Γ=1.5 restricts the admissible laws, and which network-interference configurations are included. Does “small-network” specify a particular number of units or components?

Could the enumerated laws cover adoption but omit network exposure?

They could if the class were defined too narrowly for the intended audit. How should the 0.10 overlap condition enter the enumeration?

The relevant joint-history cells and their probability definition should be specified, and the laws assessed at overlap 0.10 should be identified accordingly. The wording of this activity says *at 0.10 overlap*; it does not, by itself, report an audit at every overlap value above 0.10.

Can the overlap check use only marginal exposure probabilities?

Not if the claim under audit is expressly about joint-history overlap. Support for an exposure at one time, or for a marginal category, need not establish support for a complete history. The check should use the histories required by the effect contrasts and by ShockHT v3’s calculations.

It should not treat support for a direct-effect history as proof that all histories required by a spillover contrast are supported.
Does overlap 0.10 mean every realized small network must have exactly 10% of observations in each history cell?

No. If overlap is defined through assignment probabilities, a probability of 0.10 is not a guarantee about realized shares in every sample. Why use exhaustive laws rather than a large collection of simulated panels?

An exhaustive reference can address the full *defined small-network law class*, whereas a collection of simulated panels samples particular realizations and laws. That makes enumeration potentially useful for checking a worst-case claim within the small class.

It is not automatically an exact coverage calculation, though. One must also account for the probabilities of the realizations on which the confidence procedure runs, and for every other configuration that the stated small-network claim permits.
Can an exhaustive enumeration establish the exact minimum joint coverage?

Potentially, if the law class and all random outcomes relevant to the coverage event have specified probabilities and the calculation evaluates them for every admissible law. If only the laws are listed while coverage is estimated by simulation under each, the reported minimum would still depend on those estimates.

What joint coverage event should be checked?

The audit needs to name the target. For joint coverage of true effect values, the event is that the direct confidence set contains the true direct effect and the spillover confidence set contains the true spillover effect in the same realization. Joint coverage of both entire identified sets would be a different, stronger event.

A separate 95% calculation for each effect is not enough to establish at least 95% coverage of both together.
How do I calculate coverage under one admissible law, conceptually?

Define the target values and the joint event under that law. For each realization the law allows, apply ShockHT v3’s stated procedure and determine whether both targets are covered. Would 95% joint coverage on average across the enumerated laws suffice?

Does Γ=1.5 itself guarantee that the worst-case law can be enumerated finitely?

No. Γ=1.5 is the specified sensitivity level; it does not define the space of probability laws or make it finite on its own. If a calculation replaces literal listing with optimization, its completeness for the stated class needs justification.
Does ShockHT v3’s use of worst-case certificates settle the coverage question?

What should the direct certificate be checked against?

Against the direct-effect contrast and its corresponding outcome-range bound. The audit should check that every configuration the stated assumptions allow is respected by the certificate, and that the certified width is strictly less than the direct outcome-range width in the sense claimed.

The finding for the direct effect cannot be borrowed from a spillover certificate, because the two contrasts hold different aspects of policy and network exposure fixed.
And what is different for the spillover certificate?

The spillover contrast varies the relevant network exposure while holding the unit’s own policy status fixed. Its required joint histories and its outcome-range benchmark must match that target. What does “sub-range” mean for the two certificates?

Do we need to check that ShockHT v3’s worst-case search matches the exhaustive reference?

That is a useful part of the audit. For matched candidate effects, observed inputs, Γ=1.5 restrictions, joint histories, and test rules, compare the procedure’s worst-case calculations with the exhaustive small-network reference. Agreement within the small-network class would not, on its own, establish correctness for larger or differently structured networks.
Could the least favorable law differ between the joint-coverage calculation and the two width checks?

Yes. They optimize different quantities: the probability of covering both targets and the extremes defining the direct and spillover bounds. Should the audit test the boundary at overlap exactly 0.10?

If the claimed condition includes 0.10, the boundary deserves inclusion in the stated audit scope. The precise law class must make clear whether 0.10 is an attained minimum across required cells or a floor all those cells meet.
What role do drift constraints play?

If a certificate or test relies on ShockHT v3’s drift constraints, the audit must use the same definition of what can drift and which values are allowed. A worst-case calculation should not exclude a permitted drift configuration merely because it makes coverage or width less favorable.

This activity does not state a numerical drift limit. The audit should read the applicable constraint from the procedure’s specification rather than attach an unstated value to its findings.

Not expressly. It identifies ShockHT v3, exhaustive small-network Γ=1.5 laws, and the audit at 0.10 overlap. No. An exhaustive result could establish uniform coverage within its precisely defined small-network class if it truly includes every relevant law and outcome. The activity does not announce such an extension.

State exactly what was exhaustively enumerated: the defined small-network Γ=1.5 laws, with their specified joint histories and 0.10 overlap condition. Identify whether the coverage probabilities are calculated exactly or estimated, and specify the coverage event. Report direct and spillover certificate comparisons separately. Does six cohorts mean six exposure components?

What would we need to check about inversion to translate this into a confidence-set statement?

The true direct–spillover candidate must belong to the null whose erroneous rejection is bounded, and the inversion must retain that candidate whenever its joint test does not reject. Could an exhaustive six-cohort audit support a finite-sample uniform statement?

Does the 4.8% result by itself prove that the p-values are superuniform?

No. Full superuniformity requires that, for every threshold α, the probability of a true-null p-value at or below α is at most α under each law in the claimed class. A rejection maximum of 4.8% relevant to a 5% threshold speaks to that threshold, assuming the reported rejection event is defined that way. It gives no result for all other thresholds.
Could I claim that no additional dependence assumptions are needed?

No. The scope of the enumerated Γ=1.5 laws and the test’s treatment of network interference determine which dependencies are covered. The finding does not describe an unrestricted dependence class. How should I present the positive implication without promising informative bounds?

Say that the reported maximum joint-test rejection rate of 4.8% is below the 5% benchmark at 0.10 joint-history overlap in the exhaustive six-cohort Γ=1.5 enumeration. What if the maximum was attained at an especially unfavorable admissible law?

It would still be a maximum over the stated class; identifying an attaining law could clarify which configuration is limiting. But the finding neither names an attaining law nor gives its other properties. There is no basis to attribute the 4.8% to a particular shock, history, network link, or drift value.
Can I call the margin below 5% a safety margin?

You can state the numerical gap—0.2 percentage points—but “safety margin” could suggest robustness beyond the enumerated conditions that has not been shown. The comparison at 0.10 joint-history overlap does not say how rejection changes when the law class, Γ value, or overlap condition changes.
Does this result tell us what happened to the direct and spillover certificates in the same audit?

No. Although the broader audit concerns those certificates, this particular finding reports only the exhaustive six-cohort Γ=1.5 maximum joint-test rejection rate at 0.10 joint-history overlap. It gives no certificate endpoints, widths, or verdict on sub-range narrowing for either effect.

Exhaustive enumeration of the specified six-cohort Γ=1.5 laws found a maximum joint-test rejection rate of 4.8% at 0.10 joint-history overlap, below the 5% benchmark. A joint-coverage implication requires a true-null and correct-inversion argument; no direct or spillover width result or extension beyond the enumerated class is supplied.

I want to prove ShockHT v3’s worst-case-test superuniformity and sub-range direct and spillover widths at 4,000 components, assuming joint-history overlap ≥0.10 and drift ≤0.05 of the range. How should I separate the proof obligations?

Treat them as two proofs with a common set of definitions. Superuniformity concerns whether a true-null worst-case p-value is small too often under any law in the stated class. The width proofs concern whether the resulting direct and spillover bounds each exclude values permitted by their respective outcome-range bounds at 4,000 components.

The joint-history overlap floor and drift limit must have the same meanings throughout, but a valid test can yield full-range bounds, and a narrow bound can be based on an invalid test. This is work to prove, not a result implied by ShockHT v3’s certificates.
What precisely is superuniformity for the worst-case test?

For every true null and every admissible law covered by the claim, its p-value p should satisfy Pr(p ≤ α) ≤ α for every α between 0 and 1, with conditioning on observed shocks made explicit if the test is shock-conditional. “Worst-case” means the p-value calculation protects the test against the relevant least favorable admissible law; it does not replace the probability argument.

The class must say which joint exposure-history laws, adoption confounding, interference, and drift configurations are allowed. Superuniformity over a selected subset would not establish it over a larger stated class.
Would proving rejection probability at most 5% be enough?

It would address validity at the 5% testing threshold if it holds for every true null and admissible law in the claimed class. That is the threshold relevant to at least 95% coverage through correct inversion. Full superuniformity is stronger: its inequality must hold at every α, not only α=0.05.

The proof should say which of those claims it establishes. Calling a test superuniform after checking only the 5% threshold would overstate that result.
How does a worst-case test turn into a joint confidence-set coverage claim?

If the true direct–spillover candidate is a true joint null, a superuniform test rejects it at the 5% threshold with probability at most 5% under each allowed law. Correct inversion retains that candidate whenever its test does not reject it. Together, those steps yield at least 95% coverage of the true pair in the stated sense.

The inference must identify the target and the inversion rule. Covering both true effect values together differs from covering both entire identified sets, and separate marginal tests need not deliver the same joint guarantee.
Does the proposed proof require a candidate pair, or could it use effect-specific tests?

Either construction would need an argument matching the intended joint coverage event. A joint test of a candidate pair can be inverted to a set of retained pairs, with separately reported effect sets derived in a way that includes the coordinates of a retained true pair. If effect-specific tests are used instead, their combined error must be controlled so that missing either effect has probability at most 5% throughout the class.

ShockHT v3’s test and set definitions should decide which route is being proved. The phrase “worst-case-test superuniformity” alone does not specify it.
What should be checked before treating the p-value as worst-case?

Define the null, the admissible conditional joint-history laws, the p-value calculation, and what is optimized over. Then establish that every law allowed by the claim is accounted for and that the optimization takes the extremum appropriate for protecting against erroneous rejection. A selected unfavorable law need not be least favorable for every candidate.

If network interference or permitted drift affects the null distribution, the calibration must account for those configurations as well. “Worst-case” has no wider scope than the domain actually covered.
Can the same least favorable law be used for all direct and spillover candidates?

Not without proof. Different candidate effects can define different nulls and test statistics, and the law least favorable for one need not be least favorable for another. The superuniformity argument must protect each true null it claims to cover, whether the optimization is candidate-specific or a common bound is justified for them all.
What does the ≥0.10 overlap assumption have to refer to?

It must refer to probabilities of the joint exposure-history cells required by the specified direct and spillover contrasts, not merely to marginal exposure categories. Define the histories, their timing, and the conditional laws under which their probabilities are evaluated. If the claim is conditional on observed shocks, say whether every required cell has probability at least 0.10 at each shock value covered.

The boundary matters: ≥0.10 includes cells whose probability equals 0.10. The proof cannot quietly assume a strictly larger floor.
Would positive probability for each history be sufficient for the width claims?

Not by itself. Positive probabilities can be arbitrarily small, while the proposed assumption specifies a floor of 0.10. Moreover, even that floor needs an effect-specific argument: supporting the histories needed for a direct contrast does not necessarily constrain the spillover contrast. Each final bound must be compared with its own outcome-range benchmark after accounting for all permitted uncertainty.
Does ≥0.10 mean every realized panel has at least 10% of its components in each history cell?

No, if overlap is defined as a probability floor. A realized panel can have a smaller share or even an empty required cell. If the proof concerns every reported confidence set, it must specify how those realizations are handled. A probability restriction cannot silently be replaced by a deterministic realized-count condition.
What does drift ≤0.05 of the range allow?

It permits drift up to and including 0.05 times a stated reference range—five percent of that range. It is not a zero-drift assumption. The proof must define what can drift, across which timing or exposure comparisons, and what “range” measures.

Both test validity and width calculations must allow every drift configuration in the claimed class wherever drift affects them. Evaluating only zero drift would not establish the stated ≤0.05 claim.
Could drift be ignored in the superuniformity proof if it only appears in the bounds?

Only if the formal test construction demonstrates that permitted drift does not affect its true-null distribution or calibration. If drift changes which candidate effects are compatible or changes the relevant statistic, it must be included in the worst-case test argument. Its role cannot be determined merely by listing a separate drift constraint.

In the width proofs, the full permitted drift must be retained regardless of how the test handles it.
Where does the count of 4,000 enter superuniformity?

The finite-sample test has to be valid for the specified configuration at 4,000 components under the dependence and law assumptions it uses. A concentration or joint-law argument may involve the number of component contributions, but a count alone does not establish their independence, boundedness, or test calibration.

The proof should specify whether superuniformity is claimed at this count only or more broadly. A result at 4,000 does not, without another argument, extend to all component counts.
Are the 4,000 components necessarily independent conditional on observed shocks?

The activity specifies 4,000 components but does not itself state an independence condition. If ShockHT v3’s test needs conditional independence, the proof must impose and justify it for the relevant component-level quantities at the observed-shock values it covers. Merely dividing the analysis into 4,000 groups would not establish that property.

Likewise, this activity does not state a maximum number of cohorts per component; one should not attach one without making it an explicit assumption.
How do the direct and spillover width proofs differ?

The direct contrast changes own policy status while holding the relevant network-exposure history fixed. The spillover contrast changes network exposure while holding the relevant own-policy history fixed. Because the contrasts use potentially different joint-history cells, their worst-case allowances and final widths can differ.

The proof needs two strict inequalities: the direct width below its direct outcome-range width, and the spillover width below its spillover outcome-range width. A narrow bound on a combined policy change would not substitute for either one.
Does sub-range mean a zero-width interval?

No. It means strictly narrower than the outcome-range bound for the same effect. Each effect can remain partially identified with multiple compatible values. The certificate must establish strict narrowing, not point identification.
Do the width inequalities apply to identification bounds or confidence sets?

That must be stated. A population identified bound reflects compatibility with the assumptions and population information. A confidence set also reflects sampling uncertainty and can be wider. The activity calls for sub-range direct and spillover widths at 4,000 components; the proof must identify which objects are bounded and whether the comparison holds for every admissible realization or under another specified criterion.

An average width below range, for example, is not an every-realization certificate. Neither is a population-width result automatically a result about reported confidence-set widths.
If the p-values are superuniform, shouldn't the confidence sets automatically be informative?

No. Superuniformity limits erroneous rejection, not the number of false candidates retained. A test could retain all outcome-range-compatible direct and spillover values and still have excellent error control. The sub-range certificates need an additional argument showing that the overlap, drift restriction, and any other stated identifying assumptions actually exclude some values for each contrast.
Could the bound certificates be narrow while superuniformity fails?

Yes. An underestimated worst-case p-value or an incomplete law class could produce narrow-looking sets that reject true candidates too often. The width argument cannot validate the test. Conversely, establishing superuniformity cannot validate the width argument. Proving both is the point of the activity.
Should the proof be uniform over every observed-shock value?

Only if that is the stated scope, but the choice must be explicit. A shock-conditional claim at each relevant value requires error control under every admissible conditional law at each such value. A result averaged across shock values is different and could conceal a poorly covered value. Width certification also needs to state whether it is uniform across those values or confined to a specified conditional setting.
Would a numerical check at a few shock values establish that uniformity?

No. Such checks address the values evaluated. A class-wide proof needs to control all shock values and laws included in its statement. Computational checks may help audit an optimization or reveal a weak configuration, but they do not automatically establish superuniformity over unexamined conditional laws.
How should Γ=1.5 enter the theorem, given ShockHT v3’s bound certificates?

ShockHT v3’s worst-case bound certificates are described at Γ=1.5. If the proposed superuniformity and width theorem is for those certificates and their associated tests, it should specify the Γ=1.5 admissible-law restriction explicitly and use it consistently in the p-value optimization and both width calculations. The number alone does not define the adoption odds or interference class.

The current activity names ShockHT v3 and its conditions but does not warrant a conclusion for other Γ values.
Can we infer a full network-interference restriction from the overlap and drift inequalities?

No. The overlap floor concerns support for required joint histories, while the drift limit concerns a specified change across comparisons. Neither defines which network statuses may affect outcomes or how cross-component exposure dependence is handled. The interference class must be stated separately wherever it enters the test distribution or the direct and spillover targets.
Would proving superuniformity for each component suffice for the joint test?

Not automatically. The joint test uses contributions and histories from the collection of components. Its error probability depends on how they are combined and on whatever dependence remains among them. Componentwise statements alone do not control the resulting joint p-value unless the combination rule and its assumptions justify that implication.

The proof should start with the joint test’s null and show the required inequality for its p-value under each admissible law.
What if some of the 4,000 components contribute no useful histories to the spillover contrast?

Then counting them as informative contributions for the spillover width would be unjustified. The ≥0.10 joint-history overlap condition must be connected to the histories and component contributions actually used for each contrast. The direct and spillover inequalities should use their respective available information rather than assuming the total component count does identical work for both.
Would a proof at overlap exactly 0.10 cover every larger overlap value?

Only if its reasoning applies to every law satisfying the floor ≥0.10, not merely to one law whose cell probability equals 0.10. Raising a minimum changes the admitted law class, but the tests and certificates must still be valid for all relevant configurations in that class. A single boundary calculation is not automatically a uniform theorem for every qualifying overlap value.
Could a realized cell be empty even when the overlap condition holds, and what would that mean for a sub-range guarantee?

Yes, if overlap refers to probabilities. The procedure must specify its output for such a realization and include it in the coverage calculation. A deterministic claim that *every* reported set is sub-range might be especially demanding when permitted samples can have empty cells. A population-bound claim or a width guarantee under specified conditions would have a different scope.

The proof should not discard those realizations silently or call an empty returned set a favorable narrow bound.
What role would worst-case-law optimization play in certifying widths?

For each effect, the bound certificate should account for every compatible joint-history law and drift configuration when finding its extreme effect values. The law that is worst for direct width need not be worst for spillover width, and neither need be the law most adverse to test validity. Each optimization criterion has to match the claim it certifies.

Correct optimization over a narrow class would not certify bounds for a broader class that includes additional exposure histories or interference patterns.
Could a 95% joint-coverage result follow from superuniformity without proving the width certificates first?

Yes, if the joint null and inversion rule have the required link to the effect targets. Coverage and width can be proved in either logical order once the procedure is defined. A valid joint test may already yield the at-least-95% implication while the strict direct and spillover width comparisons remain open.

The stated activity asks for both; completing just one proof would leave the other conclusion unestablished.
How would you express the exact width comparison without inventing numerical percentages?

Let the direct and spillover widths certified at 4,000 components under the stated admissible class be W_D and W_S, and let R_D and R_S be the outcome-range widths for those same contrasts. The two desired conclusions are W_D < R_D and W_S < R_S, with a clear statement of whether these are identified-set or confidence-set widths and of the configurations over which the inequalities hold.

No numerical values for these widths are supplied by the activity. The inequalities express the proof obligations, not established results.
Does the condition on drift refer to the same range as R_D and R_S?

That cannot be assumed from the wording alone. Drift ≤0.05 of the range requires its own defined reference range, while R_D and R_S are effect-specific outcome-range benchmarks. If they use the same underlying scale, the formal statement can say so; otherwise the proof must keep the references distinct.
What would it take to establish finite-sample rather than merely asymptotic superuniformity?

For every covered finite configuration—including the stated 4,000-component case—and each admissible true-null law, prove Pr(p ≤ α) ≤ α at every α in the stated range without relying only on a large-sample approximation. If the guarantee is conditional on observed shocks, the conditional probability inequality must hold over the shock values claimed.

A finite collection of numerical test cases or favorable trial frequencies would not replace that probability argument.
How can the proof avoid treating two separate 95% effects as 95% joint coverage?

Define the joint coverage target before calibrating the test. Show that the probability of excluding at least one true target is no more than 5% over the entire stated class. That can be done through a valid joint test and inversion or another expressly simultaneous error-control argument. Do not infer it simply from each reported effect set having a marginal 95% property.
Should this activity also show that 0.10 is the smallest possible joint-history overlap floor?

No. It proposes a proof under overlap ≥0.10. Showing sufficiency under that floor would not prove that every smaller floor fails or that 0.10 is sharp. A minimum-threshold result would require an additional necessity argument, which this activity does not state.
Can you give me a compact statement of the activity without presenting either property as already proved?

Seek a proof that ShockHT v3’s worst-case joint-test p-values are superuniform over a precisely stated admissible class, then establish at 4,000 components that its direct and spillover bounds are each strictly narrower than their own outcome-range bounds under joint-history overlap ≥0.10 and drift ≤0.05 of the stated range. The test-validity and effect-specific width claims remain to be proved.

At 4,000 components, joint-history overlap ≥0.10 and drift ≤0.05 of the range yield superuniform p-values, uniform coverage of at least 95%, and sub-range widths for both direct and spillover effects. How should I state the result?

“At 4,000 components, under joint-history overlap ≥0.10 and drift ≤0.05 of the stated range, the p-values are superuniform, coverage is uniformly at least 95% over the stated class, and both direct and spillover widths are strictly below their respective outcome-range widths.”

That presents all three conclusions as results under their stated conditions. A technical presentation should also define the admissible class, the coverage target, the relevant joint-history cells, and the width objects; the short result does not supply those details.
Does this give three separate conclusions, or is sub-range width a consequence of superuniform p-values?

They are separate conclusions. Superuniformity is a property of the p-values under true nulls. Uniform coverage concerns how reliably the resulting confidence procedure contains its specified target. Sub-range width concerns informativeness relative to the outcome-range benchmark for each effect.

Valid p-values can yield very wide sets, so superuniformity alone would not imply the two width comparisons. Conversely, a narrow set need not have valid coverage.
What does superuniform mean precisely?

For a p-value p under a true null, superuniformity means Pr(p ≤ α) ≤ α for every threshold α between 0 and 1, under the laws covered by the result. The p-value can be conservative; it need not be exactly uniformly distributed.

The relevant null and the admissible laws must be defined to apply that statement. The result asserts superuniform p-values, not particular numerical p-values for a realized panel.
How does that relate to at least 95% coverage?

At a 5% rejection threshold, a superuniform p-value rejects a true null with probability no greater than 5% under the laws for which it is valid. When the confidence procedure correctly retains a target whenever its true null is not rejected, that error-control statement supports coverage of at least 95%.

Is coverage exactly 95% at 4,000 components?

What does uniform add to that lower bound?

It means the at-least-95% guarantee applies throughout the stated class, rather than only at one favorable adoption or interference configuration or on average across configurations. The class is part of the claim: uniformity cannot be extended to configurations it does not include.

The short result does not spell out the entire class, so its technical statement should identify that domain before anyone applies the guarantee to a particular setting.
Can I interpret uniform as saying every realized panel covers the effects?

No. Coverage is a probability guarantee across realizations under each law in the stated class. Even a procedure with uniformly at least 95% coverage can miss its target on a particular realization. Uniformity concerns the range of laws over which the probability bound holds, not certainty in every sample.
Is this a joint coverage statement for direct and spillover effects?

The result states “uniform ≥95% coverage” but does not explicitly define the coverage event. If the intended target is both effects together, the technical statement should say that both are covered in the same realization; two separate marginal 95% claims would not establish that event.

Likewise, covering two true effect values differs from covering both entire partially identified sets. The concise result should retain the coverage claim as stated until its target is specified.
What is the exact role of the 4,000 components?

It is the component count at which these conclusions are stated. It is not a count of units, cohorts, joint histories, or trials. The result does not say how many units belong to each component or how the components are formed.

It also does not, merely by stating a result at 4,000, establish the same conclusion at every other component count.
Can I describe it as holding at 4,000 or more components?

Not on the wording given. “At 4,000 components” states the result at that count. Extending it to every larger count requires an argument showing that the assumptions, test calibration, and both width comparisons continue to hold as components are added. No such extension is specified here.
Does the result imply fewer than 4,000 components cannot work?

No. A result at 4,000 does not establish a minimum necessary count. Smaller counts might or might not satisfy the same properties under their applicable conditions. The result states what holds at the specified count, not a sharp component threshold.
Are those 4,000 components independent?

The result as stated identifies 4,000 components but does not itself spell out an independence condition. What does joint-history overlap ≥0.10 actually restrict?

It restricts support at the level of the joint histories relevant to the contrasts, rather than merely at the level of a marginal exposure category. To make the inequality operational, the technical statement needs to identify those histories, the laws that assign their probabilities, and whether the floor applies to each required cell.

The number 0.10 is the stated lower bound. It should not be restated as an exact realized share in every panel.
Does the floor include a required history with probability exactly 0.10?

Yes. The ≥ sign includes 0.10 itself. A version of the result requiring every probability to exceed 0.10 strictly would have a different assumption. Any technical proof and application of the result must respect the boundary included in its stated condition.

Does overlap ≥0.10 apply to all histories, even those unrelated to either effect?

How should I interpret drift ≤0.05 of the range?

It allows the specified quantity to drift by no more than 0.05 times its stated reference range—five percent of that range. The inequality includes zero drift and the upper boundary; it does not assert that drift is always exactly 0.05 of the range.

Does allowing drift all the way to 0.05 mean the width and coverage conclusions include the boundary?

Does the 0.05 limit refer to five percentage points of coverage?

What exactly does sub-range mean for the direct effect?

Can I say both widths are at most a particular percentage of range?

Does sub-range imply that the direct and spillover effects are point identified?

Are the widths necessarily widths of the reported confidence sets?

Could a particular realized confidence set still be full-range?

If the p-values are superuniform, could the reported bounds nevertheless be nearly as wide as their outcome-range bounds?
